title: The value of knowing
author: none@none.com (David WalmsleyLiz CorbinMariya Gabriel)
content:
WE are not short of information. We have never had more of it. Yet across the world, people struggle to answer the simplest questions: What actually happened? Who decided what? Is it true?
This is the paradox of our age. The most connected societies in history are also among the most vulnerable to confusion, manipulation and distrust. Information moves faster than accountability. Algorithms reward outrage before accuracy. Artificial intelligence generates plausible falsehoods at scale. In such an environment, the right to know is not just a matter of transparency; it is the heartbeat of freedom.
Without an accurate understanding of what is going on and what is being done in your name, the fog of deceit thickens, and bad actors can mislead with impunity.
Society is most vulnerable when access to information is denied. Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition documented 313 internet shutdowns in 52 countries in 2025, the highest number ever recorded. Shutdowns block journalism, silence communities and deny people potentially life-saving information.
Disinformation is not just a communications problem. It is a governance risk, an economic liability and a direct threat to people’s ability to make informed decisions.
Access to information laws are an anchor of information integrity, and Unesco’s latest monitoring shows progress. Its 2025 survey showed that 141 countries have legal guarantees for access to information. But adoption is not implementation, and many countries still face practical gaps in oversight, appeals, enforcement, record-keeping and data management. Of the countries surveyed, 51 could not provide record-keeping data, despite reporting they had systems or procedures in place.
Information commissioners and other overseers turn legal provisions into enforceable rights. Yet many of them are hampered by weak mandates, delayed appointments, budget cuts, political interference, limits on their powers and attacks on their independence. For access to information to work, these bodies must be protected by law, given adequate powers and resources, and shielded from undue influence.
The gap was further confirmed by a 2025 test of access to information laws, jointly conducted by Unesco and the Centre for Law and Democracy. Across 146 identical requests in 76 countries, 38 per cent received no substantive response, only 42pc resulted in full disclosure, and the average response time was 22 days. A similar exercise will be repeated this year to measure any change.
Access to information has to evolve, but examples of the shortcomings are everywhere, even in countries with well-intentioned legislation.
And in an information vacuum, brave and independent journalism is indispensable. Journalism distils information into public understanding. It investigates, interrogates, corroborates and contextualises, but it also counters disinformation. It asks questions that some parties would rather avoid. And it gives citizens the means to participate meaningfully in public life.
The damage caused by disinformation is real. Unesco estimates that individual disinformation cases can incur economic and social costs of $350 billion to $510bn, annually, through weakened public health responses, distorted elections, delayed climate action, financial losses, reputational harm and the erosion of trust in institutions. Disinformation is therefore not just a communications problem. It is a governance risk, an economic liability and a direct threat to people’s ability to make informed decisions.
Public service broadcasters and independent news media organisations are a key counterweight to this problem. Their mandate is not to chase engagement at any cost, but to inform and serve all audiences. But they face the simultaneous pressures of fragmented audiences, declining trust, political interference, financial constraints, platform dependency and rampant false, synthetic and manipulated content. Their struggle to keep producing quality journalism is not a sectoral concern, it’s a democratic one.
The response must include renewed investment in public-interest journalism, editorial independence, fact-checking, open-source verification, media and information literacy, and collaboration across borders. Just as falsehoods travel globally, so purveyors of trusted journalism must cooperate transnationally.
The information ecosystem would be poorer and much more fragile without public service media — but they cannot defend it alone.
On World News Day and the International Day for Universal Access to Information, the challenge is practical, and we call on all actors in the information space to do better:
— Governments must enforce access to information laws and protect independent oversight.
— Platforms and technology companies must take full responsibility for the information spaces they create, in total alignment with international human rights law.
— And media organisations of all stripes should always choose rigour over reach. 
Free-flowing, reliable information is a shared benefit. But it depends on the authorities that protect access to information, journalists who pursue the truth above all else, and citizens’ right to the facts. The integrity dividend is real, but it is only paid when all of us play our part. 
David Walmsley is president, World Editors Forum, and editor in chief, Globe and Mail. 
Mariya Gabriel is assistant director-general for Communication and Information at Unesco. 
Liz Corbin is director of news, European Broadcasting Union. This opinion piece was commissioned to mark the International Day for Universal Access to Information and World News Day on Sept 28.
Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

Independent journalism, robust legal frameworks for information access, and responsible technology companies are indispensable for countering disinformation and fostering a healthy information ecosystem.

title: Discussions on terrorism
author: none@none.com (Ahmed Bilal Mehboob)
content:
WHILE visiting the British parliament a few years ago, I was struck by the tradition —observed by prime ministers — of paying homage and expressing gratitude at the start of the weekly question time session to British armed forces personnel who had been killed or injured in action. It was the time of the Afghan war and British troops were stationed in Afghanistan. I thought it was a great tradition that reminded everyone of the sacrifices made by the soldiers and sent a powerful message to the troops that their countrymen had the highest regard for them and their sacrifices. 
Although Pakistan follows the British parliamentary system, almost all Pakistani prime ministers have avoided personally answering questions in parliament. As prime minister, Yousuf Raza Gilani used to answer many supplementary questions himself when he was in the House — but that was not a part of the set parliamentary procedure. Imran Khan had promised to follow this British tradition when he was prime minister and personally answer questions. However, he neither tried to change the parliamentary rules nor did he ever answer any questions in parliament.
Both Houses and the provincial assemblies observe question hour but there is no parliamentary tradition of routinely acknowledging the sacrifices of the country’s shuhda and ghazis. The president, prime minister, ministers and senior civil and military officers do issue statements, and legislatures occasionally pass resolutions honouring those fighting a bloody war against terrorism; but the possibility of a weekly tribute did cross my mind. After all, hardly a day passes without hearing of security personnel — in the armed forces, paramilitaries, police and other security bodies — who have lost their lives in the line of duty.
We need committees that are more active in debating national security.
Almost all sources of information show that the number of violent terrorist incidents, casualties and fatalities in Pakistan have reached their highest level in a decade. In fact, 2025 was the bloodiest year since 2014. According to the South Asian Terrorism Portal, the number of violent terrorist incidents in 2025 was 1,077 with fatalities among the forces and civilians touching 1,229 and 655 respectively during the year. The data gathered for 2026 points to even higher figures when compared to the average monthly figures for 2025. For example, the number of terrorism incidents increased to a monthly average of 118, compared to 90 in 2025. Similarly, average monthly fatalities of civilian and security forces personnel in the first nine months of 2026 (up to Sept 21) have increased to 74 from 55 last year and to 114 from 102, respectively. These figures indicate a steep spike in attacks, particularly carried out by two major terrorist groups that the state aptly refers to as Fitna al-Khawarij and Fitna al-Hindustan.
We do not see the level of concern and debate within democratic institutions that is warranted by the rise in acts of terrorism. We have four key standing committees relating to the issue in parliament — separate Senate and National Assembly standing committees on defence and two other committees of the Senate and National Assembly on the interior. In addition, each of the four provincial assemblies has a standing committee on home affairs. Whatever little record is available on these legislatures’ official websites does not indicate that the committees have been often and actively debating the rising incidence of terrorism in the country — especially in KP and Balochistan —in detail, which should have been done in view of the situation.
The plenaries of the six national and provincial legislatures have debated the issue on and off, and passed resolutions too. I am sure that more frequent discussions in the legislative bodies would not only contribute to finding more effective ways in which the menace of terrorism can be combated at the people’s level, but the attention given by the legislators to this issue would further boost security personnel’s morale. In 2019, the Speaker of the National Assembly had constituted a joint (National Assembly and Senate) committee on national security under his own chairmanship and included the senior-most parliamentarians and ministers. But since the last election in 2024, the committee has apparently ceased to exist. It doesn’t necessarily mean that we need a parliamentary committee on national security while the committees on defence and interior already exist. However, what we need are committees that are more active in debating national security.  
The public should be confident that national security issues are being discussed and timely decisions being made at the appropriate forum. In this context, it is difficult to understand the relatively inactive state of the National Security Committee, which was created in 2013. The Committee, which brings together the top civil and military leadership under the chairmanship of the prime minister, has not met even once during the current calendar year. Given the prevailing circumstances and the mandate of the NSC, it should meet more regularly, preferably on a monthly basis. Just for comparison, Britain’s National Security Council meets every week under the prime minister although the UK has far fewer security issues than Pakistan.
It is hoped that the National Counter Terrorism Authority — a very important body especially in the present context — will not only become more active under its new national coordinator Maj-Gen Faisal Naseer but will also attempt to raise its public profile by, for example, sharing at least a sanitised version of the progress on the implementation of the National Action Plan with the people, their representatives and the media. Extending its outreach will bolster public trust.  
The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.

title: Disposable humans
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
DESCENDING into dirt, disease and uncertainty for a living is inhuman. Sanitation workers — the pillars of urban hygiene — often perish as poisonous gases fill their lungs. In eight months, 26 have died across the country. Karachi recorded eight losses, with 18 in Punjab. None of the workers were Muslim. In Pakistan, discrimination takes many forms. Among its most shameful manifestations have been job advertisements for sewerage management and garbage disposal. These have humiliated scores of underprivileged citizens with their ‘only Christians and Hindus may apply’ criteria — a practice banned by the Islamabad High Court. The Amnesty International and the Centre for Law & Justice report last year also highlighted the bigotry that stigmatises an essential service and creates social marginalisation. The call to do away with this practice at the recent Citizens Commission for Equality and Human Rights conference in Karachi deserves support. Compensation cannot persist as an escape for the government. 
The situation has remained unchanged for years. The lack of protective gear and no health cover or stable employment mean we are normalising ‘disposability’ of vulnerable segments. The government is obligated under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and domestic labour laws to provide safe working conditions for the people. Manual scavenging violates fundamental freedoms and strips away human dignity, besides exposing the state’s utter disregard for its constitutional duties. In an age when modern machinery makes urban hygiene possible, why should individuals be made to risk their health and lives by descending into gutters? Those in power must be made to answer for the illness, harm and deaths inflicted on those who live on the fringes of society. Sadly, the deaths of workers who risk life and limb to make our environment livable are a reminder of our lost humanity.
Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026
topic: Labour Rights, Social Inequality, and Human Rights Violations in Pakistan
whyMatters: This article critically exposes systemic human rights violations and deep-seated social discrimination against sanitation workers in Pakistan. Citing it demonstrates an aspirant's awareness of pressing social justice issues, governmental accountability, and the state's failure to uphold constitutional and international obligations, making it highly relevant for essays and analytical questions.
summary: Sanitation workers in Pakistan face hazardous, life-threatening conditions, leading to numerous deaths from poisonous gases, highlighting a grave human rights crisis.
Institutionalized discrimination, evident in job advertisements explicitly excluding Muslims, targets vulnerable religious minorities for these dangerous jobs, despite being legally banned.
The government implicitly normalizes the 'disposability' of these workers by neglecting to provide basic safety gear, health coverage, or stable employment.

The state's failure to eradicate manual scavenging and ensure safe working conditions constitutes a violation of domestic labour laws, constitutional duties, and international human rights commitments like the UDHR.

None of the deceased workers were Muslim, indicating a pattern of discrimination.
An Amnesty International and Centre for Law & Justice report last year highlighted the bigotry and stigmatization faced by sanitation workers.
academicReferences: Amnesty International and Centre for Law & Justice Report (a key reference point for discussing discrimination against sanitation workers in Pakistan).

Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) - specifically Articles 3 (right to life), 23 (right to just and favourable conditions of work), and 25 (right to a standard of living adequate for health and well-being).
International Labour Organization (ILO) Conventions, particularly C155 on Occupational Safety and Health and C111 on Discrimination (Employment and Occupation).

title: India’s killer tourists
author: none@none.com (Rafia Zakaria)
content:
THE date was January 2024, and Israel’s destruction of Gaza was underway for all to see. Among the Israeli soldiers demolishing Palestinian homes was a man named Eitan Gilboa. In videos obtained by the Hind Rajab Foundation, which analyses publicly available data to identify Israeli soldiers it alleges are implicated in war crimes, Gilboa and his unit can be seen detonating residential buildings and celebrating their destruction. The foundation alleges that in June of the same year, Gilboa was in Rafah ordering the demolition of multiple buildings and in July was involved in another demolition. It argues that Gilboa’s actions — and the actions of thousands of Israeli soldiers who took part in similar mayhem — are in violation of the Fourth Geneva Convention.
Where do these Israeli war criminals go to ‘rest’ after destroying the lives of innocent Palestinians? Many go to India, following a backpacking route so well known for hosting Israeli soldiers that it is called the ‘Hummus Trail’. It stretches through destinations like Kasol and the Parvati Valley, Dharamkot and Tosh in Himachal Pradesh and on to places like Pushkar in Rajasthan, and Goa. Around 80,000 Israeli soldiers are said to travel there annually.
This is also where Gilboa went. The path of guest houses frequented by Israeli travellers is well established and Indians have gone through a lot of trouble to accommodate them. Attractions include raves where visitors can lose themselves in trance music and drugs. 
So established is this trade in providing peace and ‘healing’ that one writer called towns on the Hummus Trail the “ashrams for war criminals”. Dharamsala even boasts of a ‘mini-Israel’, where shopkeepers speak Hebrew and serve Israeli food. In 2015, a cafe in Kasol was accused of refusing to serve Indian customers while admitting white tourists. 
Israeli soldiers reviled in other parts are welcome in India.
The most important thing that India provides is absolution. Here, Israeli soldiers condemned and excoriated in most other parts of the world, are welcome. They can partake of a commercialised, tourist-friendly mix of ‘healing’ from the trauma of war, without having to take accountability for their actions in Gaza.
Gilboa was no different. The Hind Rajab Foundation analysed photographs and other material from his Indian journey and filed complaints with the Himachal police, the home ministry and the Bureau of Immigration seeking his arrest. No arrest followed and Gilboa eventually left India.
India’s ties with Israel run deep and increasingly point to an ideological, economic and military alignment. Hindutva’s founder Vinayak Damodar Savarkar praised the idea of a Jewish state in Palestine, describing Palestine as the Jews’ “Fatherland and Holyland”. Zionism’s blend of attachment to a motherland and religious attachment to a holy land was precisely what Savarkar wanted for Hindus.
Modi’s India in this sense is like Zionist Israel. India’s Citizenship Amendment Act created an expedited route to citizenship for specified non-Muslim migrants from neighbouring countries while excluding Muslims from its provisions. Israel’s 2018 nation-state law similarly privileged Jewish national identity by declaring that the right to national self-determination in Israel is unique to the Jewish people. 
In contemporary India, the state supports these Israeli enclaves on the Hummus Trail even as it punishes people for expressing their support for Palestinians. An editorial published in The Edict, a newspaper at Ashoka University, noted how eager Hin­­dutva supporters want to fraternise with Israeli tourists, imagining their sha­red hostility tow­ards Muslims as a natural alignment, while some Israeli travellers treat br­­own Indians as les­ser locals there to serve them. In Pu­­shkar, The Edict re­­ported that the Chabad House has Hebrew signage and a perimeter fence, with Indians facing restrictions on entry while white tourists were admitted with less scrutiny.
So India welcomes Israeli soldiers on their ‘healing journeys’, including those facing allegations of war crimes. The Indian state — as evidenced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s eager embrace of Israeli officials — is keen to emphasise the closeness of the two countries. In his speech at the Knesset, Modi even peddled yoga and ayurveda as sources of holistic wellness that Israelis could partake in when they visited India.
This, then, is the tale of two hatreds. Men like Eitan Gilboa, accused of participating in the destruction of civilian homes, can leave Gaza and seek succour in a new environment where they can forget the cruelties of war. Hosting those accused of such acts without demanding accountability raises its own moral questions, but this is a truth that India, drowning in its own hatreds, appears unable to acknowledge.  
The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy. 
rafia.zakaria@gmail.com
Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

title: Safeguarding and harnessing AI
author: none@none.com (Shahid Ahmed MallickAftab Ahmad Khokher)
content:
THE launch of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation in Shanghai on July 16, 2026, may mark an important moment in global AI governance. Initiated by China, the body aims to promote cooperation and keep AI beneficial, safe and fair. It has attracted 29 countries, mostly from the Global South, and is expected to grow. To become globally effective, WAICO must broaden its membership across North and South and evolve into a genuinely multilateral institution. President Xi Jinping summarised its ambition: AI development, he said, should not be “a solo performance by a single country, but a symphony of international cooperation”.
WAICO emerges amid a technological dilemma. Like nuclear technology, AI promises major benefits but also raises fears of misuse, instability and harm. The new organisation’s task is not simply to control AI, but to also manage risks while widening access to benefits without discrimination. Its founders should therefore study the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which faced a similar challenge almost seven decades ago.
The atomic bomb demonstrated that nuclear technology could transform the strategic balance between nations and threaten civilisation; the same science also offered advances in medicine, agriculture, industry and energy. The challenge was to prevent destructive applications and share peaceful benefits. President Dwight Eisenhower’s ‘Atoms for Peace’ address to the UN General Assembly in 1953 proposed an international agency to make nuclear technology available for peaceful purposes “for the benefit of all mankind”. His initiative led to the IAEA’s creation in 1957.
The IAEA was never merely a nuclear policeman. Its statute covered peaceful applications, scientific exchange, training, safeguards and safety standards. Its founding principle was to make nuclear technology safer without denying humanity its benefits — a central lesson for WAICO. Safeguards became a core IAEA function, assuring states that civilian nuclear materials and activities were not diverted to military purposes. After the 1968 Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, they became central to the global non-proliferation regime. Yet the Agency also helped countries acquire knowledge, train personnel, build infrastructure and use nuclear science peacefully. An organisation that only prohibits will meet resistance; one that also advances legitimate development creates stronger cooperation.
The IAEA’s institutional logic offers five useful lessons for the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation.
The IAEA developed complementary roles in verification, peaceful uses, technical cooperation, safety and security. As nuclear technology spread, countries needed not only non-proliferation controls but also secure materials, safe operations, capable regulators, trained personnel and strong national institutions.
AI can transform healthcare, education, agriculture, energy, manufacturing, public administration and research, helping developing countries overcome barriers. Yet it also brings job displacement, misinformation, cyberattacks, fraud and potentially harmful autonomous decision-making. The question is how to keep this power aligned with progress without letting its destructive potential escape control. While the IAEA experience is relevant, WAICO should not copy the Agency. AI is software-based, diffuse, fast-moving and developed by thousands of private actors. Nevertheless, the IAEA’s institutional logic offers five useful lessons.
Risk management cannot be separated from development: Governance cannot be framed only as restriction. For many developing countries, the priority is access. A regime in which advanced states possess AI while others merely follow rules designed elsewhere will deepen inequality. So, WAICO should make capacity building a central pillar. China’s plan to offer developing countries 5,000 AI training and seminar opportunities over five years and establish international application centres could become a permanent multilateral programme. It should build national capacity — universities, research institutions, regulators, data infrastructure, etc. — much as IAEA technical cooperation has done in the nuclear field.
Develop an AI safeguards concept: Trust cannot rest on declarations. AI safeguards should not block access but identify exceptionally powerful capabilities, manage their risks and verify commitments. A risk-based system could grade capabilities, set standards, require transparency, establish testing methods, and independently assess declared advanced systems through continuous monitoring and peer review like the IAEA verification and peer review system. It should focus on consequential applications, not intrusively control every system.
AI safety should be an international public good: This is necessary because failures and malicious use can cross borders. WAICO could develop shared principles, standards, testing methods and incident-reporting mechanisms, and enable countries to share failures and near misses so others can prevent their recurrence. IAEA safety standards and operating experience systems show how consensus guidance and corrective learning can reduce risk without assigning blame.
Security must be distinguished from safety: Safety addresses accidents, failures and unintended harm; security addresses deliberate misuse, manipulation and attack. Distinguishing between them would support clearer legal, regulatory and ethical responses.
Standards aren’t enough — people and institutions matter: Standards work only when countries have capable institutions and people. WAICO could create regional centres of excellence along with training, fellowships, laboratories and regulatory capacity programmes, helping developing countries implement commitments similar to IAEA technical cooperation programmes.
WAICO should learn from the IAEA but not become the IAEA of AI. AI differs fundamentally from nuclear technology. Nuclear material can be physically controlled and is concentrated in capital-intensive facilities; AI software can be copied, modified and distributed instantly. WAICO cannot transplant the IAEA model, but it can adopt its balanced approach: enable beneficial use, build capacity, set safety and security standards, and prevent misuse.
The international community has spent nearly 70 years learning to govern a beneficial but dangerous technology. The IAEA also has its limitations and is politically constrained, yet WAICO should study its successes, failures and adaptations rather than reinvent the wheel.
Eisenhower sought to turn the atom from an instrument of destruction into a force for peace. Today, the challenge is to ensure that AI serves humanity rather than subordinates or harms it. WAICO should place safety and security alongside development and capacity building; promote cooperation without blocking developing country access; set international standards that respect national contexts; and focus oversight on the gravest risks rather than every application.
In 1953, the world answered Eisenhower’s call and created the IAEA. Today, Xi has called for AI to become “an important driver for shared prosperity and common security”. The world should respond with equal seriousness.
Shahid Ahmed Mallick was director at IAEA and Aftab Ahmad Khokher was ambassador in Austria/IAEA.
Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

title: Education for society
author: none@none.com (Faisal Bari)
content:
NOTWITHSTANDING what might be going on in other countries, Pakistan has a real problem regarding violence against women. In the past few months alone, we have seen some horrendous incidents: ‘honour’ killings, marriage-of-choice killings, rapes, domestic violence, spousal violence and killings, abduction, rape and killing of minors, and violence against employees and staff. There is no dearth of reports from national and international bodies documenting the extent and severity of these issues.
A couple of points stand out in these reports. One, we do not have good data on violence against women. Incidents are underreported, and there are no national registries or data sets of any sort. Most reported data comes from newspaper reporting, police case registrations, hotline reports, and so on.
Two, though many reasons — poor laws and weak implementation, few protections, pathetic institutional arrangements, low reporting and conviction rates, delays, social and societal taboos, etc — are cited in these reports, a primary one is the impact of patriarchy: the control of men over society. Patriarchy shapes not only laws, norms, and expectations in this society; it also shapes responses: what she was wearing, why she was out at that time, why she was driving, and so on.
Patriarchy is hard to spot, fight, and neutralise because it is embedded in almost every norm, rule, and law. Most societies have, historically and even today, used education to address society’s main issues. What it means to be educated has varied across societies and times, and one element (other than the ability to carry out tasks) has been the larger socialisation of the individual within society and the shaping of their values and norms. I want to pose the question: should we not be shaping our education to take on the issue of patriarchy and its impacts directly?
Recently, my daughter started school as a fifth-grader in a public school in London. On the very first day, after introductions and other formalities, her teacher spent a couple of hours talking about the autism spectrum and notions of inclusion, expected behaviour, and what was not expected or what would not be tolerated. This came before any conversation about the English or math curriculum. This term, the heroes the class will be introduced to include Frida Kahlo, Mahatma Gandhi, Simone Biles, and a couple of human rights defenders from across the globe.
We must address the most urgent social and cultural issues of our society through education.
Every day when I walk her back from school and ask her about her day, she tells me about the book they have been reading in class, the documentary they saw, the discussions they had, etc. I have to ask specifically about her math, English and history lessons. They are there, and she is learning the subjects she is supposed to, but the school and her education are much more than that. This has been true every school day. It is about what she needs as a human being and a citizen; it is about values and the kind of society that needs to be there. Specific skills are just a small part of the ‘education’ she is getting.
I went to some of the best schools in Lahore in the day. But when I landed in England for undergraduate studies, one of the first things I noticed, comparing my own educational experiences with those of my undergraduate peers from England, was that almost each one of my peers had been exposed to things I had not. All of them had good exposure to and knowledge of a major European language other than English. All of them had studied music for many years in their schools, and many could play one instrument fairly well or had a good understanding of it. Many of them had had singing lessons: some were good choir singers. So, language, music and singing. Their exposure to art was also more advanced than mine. The schools I attended focused much more on doing well in academic subjects and preparing for school-leaving examinations.
Though schools, especially high-fee private schools, have changed a lot, including in Pakistan over the years, even the best of them today remain narrowly focused on subject understanding and examination performance. They do not give any importance to preparing citizens and human beings. Nor is there a demand for this from parents.
In fact, the trend, at least in public schools, is the opposite. With clear evidence that most children in schools are not learning enough (77 per cent are ‘learning poor’), the focus has shifted to foundational learning to ensure students grasp the basics of language and math. But the danger is that this approach narrows the scope of education even more. We focus on only essential learning objectives and try to drill them into students. We teach these and test only these. We test only these, so we teach only these. Foundational learning is the flavour right now, and it is hard even to raise concerns about what this might mean for broader educational objectives.
Education has always been about creating citizens and human beings who can take us forward. We must address the most pressing social and cultural issues of our society through education. If we do not, what is the point of education, and how else can we plan for a better society? Violence against women, in all its forms, and the grip of patriarchy on our society is exactly the kind of embedded issue that cannot be tackled through law alone and has to be challenged through education and with a sense of purpose. The sheer brutality of what we keep seeing should wake us up to the urgency with which this needs to be addressed.
The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

title: The IMF loop
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
IF anything, the IMF reviews capture the paradox of Pakistan’s economic management. The numbers may be improving, but the economy itself remains largely unchanged.
The government is meeting some fiscal and monetary targets while missing reforms that would alter how the state and markets actually function. There is something increasingly tiring about watching these IMF reviews. The IMF mission arrives. The government presents its case. Officials hold meetings. Statements are issued. Then the Fund’s assessment comes out, identifying almost exactly the same strengths and weaknesses that were previously pointed out. The purpose of the reviews cannot simply be to pass successive tests. Yet much of the economic effort still appears organised around precisely that objective: meet the quantitative targets, secure the next tranche and move on to the next review.
    
The government has achieved an important degree of macroeconomic stability. Fiscal discipline has improved. Foreign exchange reserves have been rebuilt — even if they remain fragile. The external account is less precarious than it was. These are not small gains. But stability is supposed to create the space for reform and sustainable growth. It cannot become an end in itself. The more uncomfortable question is what has actually changed underneath the stabilisation numbers.
The IMF itself continues to point to delayed critical reforms, market interventions, weak governance and missed social-sector spending. The government has also yet to fully implement several legislative and institutional changes agreed under the programme. This suggests a bigger problem. The government, like its predecessors, may be trying to complete the programme without fundamentally changing the economic model that repeatedly produces the need for such programmes. Once the programme is completed and reserves rebuilt, it may loosen the fiscal and monetary brakes to accelerate growth before the election. The temptation will be to spend the gains of stabilisation on a short-term growth push and flaunt the resulting numbers as economic success. We have been there before — not once, not twice, but more than two dozen times. The danger is repeating this cycle after the current programme. Growth must come from structural reform, not spending the gains of stability and returning to the IMF yet again.
Published in Dawn, September 25th, 2026

title: Taxing traders
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE government’s much-publicised fixed tax scheme for traders is already showing signs of failure. Reportedly, with barely a week left to the Sept 30 tax filing deadline, only two previously unregistered shopkeepers have opted in. With 317 traders registered under the scheme, which is meant to bring shopkeepers into the tax net, only Rs26m has been generated against a budgeted target of Rs50bn. The Tajir Dost scheme introduced earlier had similarly failed to bring traders into the system. The government has again tried to make compliance attractive by offering traders a 1pc tax on turnover, exemption from routine audits and withholding obligations, as well as relief from installing digital payment systems. The lack of response to both schemes reveals a deeper problem: traders are unwilling to enter the formal tax regime even when the state offers concessions.
Many traders believe that their political influence and collective bargaining power offer greater protection than any incentive offered by the tax authorities. Their ability to shut shops, mobilise trader bodies and exert pressure has proved useful in resisting taxation and enforcement. It is easier, in their calculation, to oppose audits and documentation than to accept even a relatively modest fixed tax. The government cannot build a broad tax base on this basis. Nor can it continue compensating for the under-taxation of influential sectors by squeezing those within the system. The contrast with the salaried class is telling. Income tax collected from salaried taxpayers rose 7.5pc to Rs91bn in July-August, an increase of Rs6.3bn over the same period last year. Real estate, meanwhile, contributed Rs28bn, down 28pc, despite expectations of stronger property activity. This is precisely why the government must stop confusing incentives with tax reform. Incentives can facilitate compliance, but they cannot substitute for credible enforcement. If traders refuse even a highly concessional regime, the state must rethink its policy and ensure enforcement. A credible tax system requires equal treatment across sectors, reliable documentation, enforceable rules and the political will to apply them.
Published in Dawn, September 24th, 2026

This resistance creates an inequitable tax burden, with the salaried class bearing an increasing share of income tax while influential sectors like real estate show declining contributions.

The article argues that the government must shift its strategy from offering incentives to ensuring credible enforcement, establishing equal treatment across sectors, reliable documentation, and political will for effective tax reform.

title: Lack of planning
author: none@none.com (Ali Tauqeer Sheikh)
content:
THE Prime Minister’s Committee on Civil Service Reforms has finalised its core recommendations, yet omitted any clear roadmap for the Planning Commission. The latter is routinely described as dysfunctional. Whether or not that description is true is beside the point. The more useful question is whether Pakistan will do what India did when its own planning body stopped delivering, or take a different course altogether.
The two commissions began as near-twins. India’s was founded in 1950, Pakistan’s in 1953, both modelled on Soviet-style central planning and staffed by trained economists. Both were extra-constitutional bodies, created by executive order. Both were nominally chaired by the head of government and run day to day by a deputy chairman. Both produced Five-Year Plans as their central output and controlled how resources moved from the centre to the provinces or states. For roughly three decades, they were the same institution representing two flags.
The split started in the late 1980s with a fork in the road that both countries reached and only one of them took. India hit its own balance-of-payments crisis in 1991. It liberalised, and it grew out of the crisis rather than falling into a cycle of dependency. Pakistan entered IMF structural adjustment in 1988 and never left. It is now on its 25th programme. That single divergence did more to determine the two institutions’ fates than anything that followed. Since 1988, IMF adjustment programmes have taken precedence over what became, in Pakistan, the largely academic exercise of five-year planning. The Commission became just another ministry, concerned mainly with approving projects, and constrained even there by a development budget whose size the finance ministry set. India’s Commission kept setting the fiscal and growth framework that the finance ministry worked within. Pakistan’s relationship has flipped: the framework now comes from Washington, and the Commission works around it.
For a while, India’s Commission adapted. It absorbed the human development agenda from Mahbub ul Haq’s 1990 Human Development Report and embedded the eight National Missions of the 2008 National Action Plan on Climate Change into successive Five-Year Plans. It completed 12 plans across 65 years. But incremental change has a shelf life. By the early 2010s, India’s economy had become too large, too market-driven and too federally assertive for a centralised allocator to keep dictating terms to states that no longer needed its money. In 2014, the Modi government dissolved the Commission and replaced it with NITI Aayog, a leaner think tank with no power to allocate funds, built around advisory strategy, SDG tracking and competition between states. The point is not that India dissolved a failing institution. It dissolved a working one, because a model built for 1950 was not fit for 2015.
The civil service reform committee has left out crucial reform for planning institutions.
Pakistan never reached that fork, because it never adapted enough to outgrow the old model in the first place. Where India’s Commission built capacity and then had to be redesigned, Pakistan’s mostly stood still. The 18th Amendment in 2010 devolved 17 ministries to the provinces. But nobody redesigned what the federal Planning Commission should do once the subjects it used to plan for no longer belonged to it. It was recast into a full ministry in 2013-14, gaining nominal breadth, Vision documents, SDG coordination, CPEC planning, and losing whatever independence it once had. Four provincial planning and development departments expanded around it, each building its own project pipeline — and national development spending across federal and provincial channels now exceeds Rs3.5 trillion. The PSDP, the Commission’s one remaining function, amounts to just seven per cent of the federal budget, its ceiling fixed by the Finance Division, the IMF interlocutor.
This is where the comparison stops. NITI Aayog, for all its own gaps, has a claim: a 165pc increase in renewable capacity in a decade, an NDC (Nationally Determined Contributions) process it coordinated across ministries and industry, and the world’s first government-led subnational SDG index, lifting India’s national SDG score from 58 to 71 between 2018 and 2024 by making states compete on published rankings. It has real failures too. But it measures them. It tracks 113 indicators across every state and publishes the results. Pakistan has no institution that does either job for its own provinces. Nobody ranks them on outcomes. Nobody has evaluated whether the PSDP, after decades and trillions of rupees, has achieved what it was funded to achieve.
If we count what’s missing, nine separate failures emerge: a macro framework that has surrendered to the IMF since 1988; a series of launched and abandoned Vision documents; a collapse in human development that has left Pakistan’s HDI ranking 20 places behind India’s, with Bangladesh ahead of both; a PSDP process captured by political patronage rather than sustainable development logic; a think-tank function that atrophied while Mahbub ul Haq’s own institutional descendants scattered abroad; a climate and environmental blindspot in a country that ranks among the 10 most climate-vulnerable states; a federal role left undefined after the 18th Amendment; no subnational monitoring or evaluation framework; and, binding all of it together, an institution that has expanded in size while abandoning its function, producing the appearance of planning where substance no longer exists.
Put together, this is not one failure of implementation. It is three failures of obsolescence, layered on top of each other: 1) globally, the development agenda moved from GDP and infrastructure towards human capabilities, the SDGs and climate finance, and the Commission never followed, 2) domestically, four periods of military rule and an un-redesigned federal mandate after 2010 did separate, serious damage, and 3) functionally, what remains is a gatekeeping exercise inside a PSDP ceiling set in Washington, approving a backlog of projects, the so-called throwforward, worth several trillion rupees more than can ever be funded.
Pakistan does not lack planning institutions. It lacks a plan for its planning institutions. That is the reform the PM’s committee left out, and the one that was never optional.
The writer is a climate expert.

title: Dangerous border
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
WITH no let-up in terrorist attacks on Pakistan by elements finding refuge in Afghanistan, Islamabad has again launched kinetic action in the border area to target terrorist groups.
The actions have resulted in exchanges of fire with the Afghan Taliban regime. Pakistan seems to be trapped in a cycle of escalation for the simple reason that Kabul is unwilling to act against terrorist groups active on its soil, such as the banned TTP, that seek to harm this country.
Until this fundamental issue is addressed, bilateral ties will not improve. It was reported on Wednesday that the military had shot down drones apparently originating from Afghanistan as they attempted to violate Pakistani airspace. Earlier, Pakistan had launched air strikes in the border area, which killed a number of terrorists, after a spate of violent attacks, including the assault targeting the old Police Lines in Kohat last week. Pakistani forces also thwarted infiltration attempts in the Kurram area, which resulted in an exchange of fire with the Afghan Taliban.
Along with taking kinetic action, Pakistan has highlighted this grim situation on the world stage. The UN Security Council has condemned the Kohat terrorist attack, calling for the “perpetrators … and sponsors” of the atrocity to be brought to justice. Pakistan had earlier told the UNSC that it would respond to threats originating from Afghanistan in self-defence. Moreover, the deputy prime minister, while speaking at a meeting of the OIC contact group on Afghanistan on the sidelines of the ongoing UN General Assembly session, reiterated the need for a verifiable mechanism to prevent the use of Afghan soil for terrorism. China, as well as Muslim states such as Saudi Arabia and Qatar, has backed diplomatic efforts to resolve the differences between Kabul and Islamabad.
While hostilities are undesirable, if the Afghan Taliban take no action against those who spill innocent blood in this country, Pakistan will have no option but to take action to defend itself against terrorism.
Yet while immediate threats must be confronted, long-term peace can only come through dialogue, and a commitment by the Taliban to curb cross-border terrorism. As has been highlighted in these columns previously, a bevy of terrorist groups call Afghanistan home, and pose a threat to the whole region, not just Pakistan — although this country, owing to its physical proximity, has been hit the hardest.
Therefore, only a sustained and coordinated regional effort can succeed in eliminating the terrorist threat emanating from Afghanistan. It is clear that, ultimately, the Taliban must decide whether they want to integrate with the rest of the region, or remain a pariah regime because of their stubborn ideological attachment to their violent comrades.

title: Workplace order
author: none@none.com (Parvez Rahim)
content:
TO achieve both success and credibility in the market, an organisation should operate with transparency and fairness towards all its stakeholders. The employees, especially the lower cadres, should be comfortable in their interactions with the management; while the latter owes them a cordial work environment where contractual commitments are respected. At the same time, a company has the right to expect employees’ commitment towards improving productivity. When an organisation prioritises employee relations, the result is a disciplined workforce.
The Esso Standard Eastern, renamed Exxon Corporation, and an affiliate of Standard Oil in New Jersey, had established a fertiliser plant at Daharki in 1965. Both firms featured in Fortune 500. Besides Google, Salesforce, Adobe, and Southwest Airlines, Exxon Corporation retained a strong standing because of its work culture and employee relationship management.
The Standard Oil head had implemented an employee representative plan after the infamous industrial unrest of the early 20th century. This revolutionised the company’s approach towards human resources as industrial harmony was established through direct and cordial communication with workers. A few years after its Sindh chapter was set up, the worst industrial strife took place despite decent salaries and benefits. However, a competent labour leader managed to pacify the irate workers. The management responded by putting in extra effort, and more work to ensure that the plant’s output did not suffer. Ultimately, the union leaders were punished for their actions, and the plant continued to operate peacefully. During my tenure at this company, I noticed that thanks to strong employee relations at the plant, the workforce also prioritised their employer’s wellbeing.
Maintaining cordial relations with employees helps employers handle discipline-related problems smoothly and effectively. The sensitivity of such matters means employers must exercise more care in conducting inquiries regarding complaints, particularly when they are about harassment. Although over 12 acts and omissions constitute misconduct, significant importance is given to the implementation of Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010.
Cordial ties with employees ensure workplace discipline.
Despite the aforementioned facts, working women aggrieved by acts of harassment are reluctant to lodge complaints due to family pressure and direct interaction with the accused during proceedings — a situation that should not continue. Consequently, many harassment cases are not reported. This emboldens potential harassers to continue with their heinous acts.
There is a dire need to review Section 4 (C) of the Act, which states: “The inquiry committee shall inquire into the charge and may examine such oral or documentary evidence in support of the charge or in defence of the accused as the committee may consider necessary and each party shall be entitled to cross-examine the witnesses against him”.
In most cases, victims of harassment do not want to be cross-examined by the lawyers of the accused. Instead of subjecting the aggrieved party to cross-examination, the inquiry committee should be empowered to make recommendations based on its evaluation of the oral and documented evidence submitted during the probe. Allowing such interrogation discourages tormented victims from coming forward.
Besides, the punishment for an em­­ployee found guilty of misconduct should be commensurate with the gravity of the of­­fence committed. Ba­­sed on this principle, a division bench of the Supreme Court had, through its jud­gement on Aug 28, 2007, reduced the pe­­nalty imposed by the Federal Service Tribunal on the appellant who was a civil servant. The court had converted the penalty of compulsory retirement from service, prescribed by the tribunal, to a period of two years whereby the appellant would lose out on two increments.
The civil servant was removed from service on the two charges of non-compliance with the orders of his superiors, and absence from duty without prior permission. In the first charge, the court did not accept the plea of the appellant that the order given by the director-general to depute him to a special audit assignment was not conveyed to him in writing. But in the second charge, the Supreme Court had stated that “the mere fact that the appellant did not obtain permission before proceeding on medical leave on the advice of his doctor may not be considered an act of gross misconduct entailing the major penalty of dismissal from service”.
The writer is a consultant in human resources at the Aga Khan University Hospital, Karachi.

title: Filing season ends
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
AS tax-filing season draws to a close, for those innocent enough to be part of the exercise, it is perhaps worth taking stock of what has worked and what has not in the recent past. One thing that has clearly not worked is schemes designed to give retailers incentives to become filers. Another thing that has not worked is mounting penalties on non-filers, and ramping up the FBR’s powers to enforce such schemes.
Let me qualify what I said. When I say these have ‘not worked’ I mean something specific: they have not worked to break the barrier that keeps our tax-to-GDP ratio so dismally low that the structural fiscal deficit becomes the biggest ball and chain that holds the rest of the economy back. There is only one way to end this vicious cycle, and that is to come up with a tax reform programme that unlocks the significant tax potential locked up in those areas of the economy that see large-scale turnovers but contribute little to nothing by way of taxes. Not surprisingly, most of these areas are found inside the services sector, which accounts for more than 50 per cent of our GDP (in constant 2015 prices).
And within services one constant headache has been wholesalers and retailers, second only in size to communications, whose size and weight are inflated due to the sheer scale of mobile communications in Pakistan. Mobile communications are reasonably easy for the tax machinery to reach.
In his first year of power, Gen Pervez Musharraf targeted the retailers in a documentation drive, and the combined efforts of the FBR and the interior ministry, then headed by retired Gen Moinuddin Haider, were brought to bear on the problem. They used a raw power approach, demanding traders register themselves or face forcible closure of their business. And this ‘documentation drive’ faced its first big test in the sprawling Bara market of Peshawar, which was a major hub for undocumented frontier trade in those days.
Yet again, the authorities are trying to incentivise retailers to self-register using yet another fixed tax scheme.
It was the most dramatic showdown between the state and the retailers that we have probably ever seen. But eventually, the drive failed, and it turned out to be the last time the state ever used head-on collision as its strategy for bringing retailers into the net and documenting the economy.
The priority lay dormant after that. Once the 9/11 bonanza got going, nobody was too pushed with the documentation drive or widening the tax net. The next time the matter was taken up was as part of the 2008 IMF programme, which had only one structural reform criterion: implement the value added tax. They called it Reformed GST, or RGST, at the time, to underline the fact that this was not a new tax but simply an upgraded version of something that had already been under implementation since 1991. The idea under this strategy was to incentivise traders, suppliers and vendors and distributors and wholesalers and all parties that were part of the supply chains connected with manufacturing in this country to help document each other. Every party would only pay tax on the portion of value that they added to a good. So they had to declare how much they bought an item for and from whom, and how much they sold it for and to whom, and pay tax only on the difference between these two prices.
This also failed because the traders mounted enough of a protest against the tax for it to be defeated in parliament, mainly because the government’s own coalition partners opposed it. And after this defeat came a series of ad hoc attempts, organic, home-grown attempts, to try and net the retailers. The first of these was a combination of a set of penalties for the remaining non-compliant, coupled with an incentive to comply by declaring one’s assets and incomes via an amnesty scheme. This was in 2015. This was the first carrot-and-stick approach to this problem of rising undocumented incomes in the services sector. It sounded good at the time, especially since it was also coupled with large withholding taxes on bank transactions of non-filers of income tax returns.
But these measures also failed. And then came yet more subtle measures. In 2017, they created a category called Tier 1 retailers, covering chain-store outlets, shops in air-conditioned malls, retailers with an annual electricity bill over Rs600,000, and wholesaler-cum-retailers. A little earlier, they had started using information from electricity bills to assess tax liability and make the collection.
Much of the tax effort then focused on these Tier 1 retailers, expanding and contracting their definition over the years, adding and removing penalties, bringing in technology like point of sale (POS) machine integration, and running lottery schemes against the receipts issued through these machines. In 2022, they brought in a fixed tax of Rs3,000, 5,000 or 10,000, depending on the bill size, for non-Tier 1 retailers, to be collected through electricity bills.
None of it worked. And now they tried, one more time, in the latest finance act, to incentivise retailers once again to self-register using yet another fixed tax scheme. According to a news report by Shahbaz Rana, “[o]nly two new traders have so far opted for the 1pc fixed tax scheme while another 315 shopkeepers who have filed returns are already part of the tax regime”. This strongly suggests that the latest version of the same scheme is now headed towards failure. It was easy to see this coming, given how all previous incentives and fixed tax schemes have fared in the past one decade.
As the curtain prepares to drop on tax-filing season, it has become another ritual to observe the long and rather discouraging track record of the state’s failure to keep its fiscal effort up to date with the changes its economy has undergone over the years. And the innocent ones, like you and me, who file our taxes dutifully every year, pay the price.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

title: Debating transformation in the Global Order
author: Inam Ul Haque
content:
Last week, we discussed the salients of annual International Programme for Development and Stability (IPDS-26) conducted recently by Institute for Strategic Studies, Research and Analysis (ISSRA) at the National Defence University (NDU) Islamabad. We discussed the contours of 'Emerging Global Order (EGO)', the role and rise of China and the US/European dimension of the EGO. We continue.

Pakistan's former permanent representative at the UN, Munir Akram, identified three challenges and three opportunities for Islamabad under the EGO. Economy, Indian hostility and Afghanistan were challenges; whereas war in the ME, connectivity and balancing of ties with the US and China were exploitable opportunities. He emphasised 'developing' relations with the US and 'preserving' ties with China, and opined that the war in the ME will create regional security architectures with Pakistan as a security provider, as indicated through Makkah Agreement.

The second plenary of the Conference dealt with technology redefining power. Brig Gen Wharton of the US remained focused on the human dimension of technological development, emphasising technology's subservience to humanity. This, he posited, remains under stress due to 'potential' loss of human control over AI. He was appreciative of China's 'industrial capacity at scale' in the service of humanity at low cost, and as a critical element of national power.

On AI, South Korean speaker, Dr Park, emphasised expert control, while discussing AI development and AI risks. Unlike many countries ambivalent about AI regulation, Pakistan, she said, should have its own AI regulation. Russian panelist, Ms Oksana, also called for country-specific AI regulation and pressed for investing in people, emphasising humanity to be at the core of AI in its genesis, development and proliferation.

Panelists equated data security with national security, pointing out challenges of data centres – including hacking, uninterrupted electricity supply and water needed for cooling – warning about the perils of putting too much data online. On AI regulation, the dominant view gravitated towards the mechanics of doing so, defending 'human cognitive security' without controlling thought, and the dos and don'ts for governments.

The third plenary dealt with EGO-driven changing character of warfare and impacts on strategic stability. An eminent American scholar Dr Robert Pape, while enumerating the lessons of the US war with Iran, declared that the US was in an 'Escalation Trap'. The US dilemma was acute: conceding Iran's control of Hormuz emboldens states like China and encourages countries like India to undertake military unilateralism (against Pakistan). Recent Indian Navy incursion in Pakistan's EEZ is a case in point. While contesting Hormuz control risks escalation and is militarily untenable indefinitely for the US, as of now.

In his opinion, the Iran War is in many ways the 'inverse' of the 1991 War with Iraq. Since the Iraq War, there has been global diffusion of technology and 'democratisation' (inexpensive availability) of precision weapons, challenging the global powers. Prof Pape identified continued smuggling of Iranian oil through Pakistan as an ongoing challenge, and refugee influx and instability as the likely consequences of US ground invasion of Iran through Chahbahar beachhead, etc.

Brig Gen Kimmitt of the US Army theorised whether warfare was undergoing a 'Revolution in Military Affairs' (RMA) or an 'Evolution' (EMA). In his opinion (correctly), the conduct of warfare had changed with new tools at hand, while its nature (principles) remains unchanged. He, however, considered the 'principle of Mass' irrelevant without 'concentration'. He was reminded that 'technological mass' was the likely contemporary manifestation of 'Mass' as a cardinal principle of war; and that AI was the new RMA.

Gen Kimmitt suggested guardrails for AI regulation, postulating that 'unmanned platforms' were the new horizon in warfare, rendering pilots redundant, as machines could handle greater G Forces compared to humans. Swarming the battlefield with inexpensive weapons was the new normal, saturating adversary's response and raising his interception costs. Effective counter-drone capability was still away. And 'Internet of Things (IOT) was being replaced by 'AI of Things' (AIOT). Russian speaker, Dr Alexey, spoke about the 'Drone Revolution' contextual to the war in Ukraine.

Pakistan's Admiral Faisal discussed Iran's 'sea control' vis-à-vis America's 'sea denial'. Iran was employing 'compellence and deterrence' and the US was reacting to it. Iran, by default, decides shipping safety, insurance, freight costs, etc. He considered Hormuz control, Iran's Centre of Gravity and Tehran's political, diplomatic, economic and military leverage. He considered Hormuz critical, whether under Iranian control or under the world, and theorised the Iran war introducing 'strategies of choke points', making security more expansive and global trade more expensive.

The fourth plenary debated global competition and conflict prevention. Brazilian view was 'pro-hedging', as hedging provided more flexibility and strategic autonomy. Hedging by BRICS was beneficial, as BRICS participants shared the table simultaneously with myriad players, without dispensing with the UN/other forums. Platforms like BRICS provide low risk space for Middle Powers (MPs) to operate at universal, multilateral and bilateral levels. South African panelist described reform at the UN, and supported effective mediation, arbitration and facilitation under the UN's good offices. She identified 'middle power diplomacy' as multilateral tool for conflict prevention.

Pakistan's Dr Moeed Yusaf considered EGO another historic continuum. But this time around, the hegemon (US under Trump) had announced voluntary retirement without being displaced through historic decline, like in the past; leaving a fragmented Global Order, and vacuum/uncertainty. This allows MPs to formulate issue-based partnership as opposed to ideological camping; Brazil being a case in point. He suggested that MPs, sidelining NAM, will challenge Western hegemony. He defined MP as a country that cannot be ignored by either the US or China. He concluded that the future is likely to have a 'rule-based order', albeit with different set of rules, bringing together MPs under a resurgent UN.

As per Dr Moeed, Pakistan has a major opportunity under the EGO and it must become part of regional mechanisms. It should optimise its crucial geography like its location, mineral wealth, connectivity and transit potential. Islamabad needs to pursue internal cohesion, cheap energy and cooperative geoeconomics, shunning camp politics. He underscored good relations with both America and China and considered stable Pakistan critical for regional and global peace and stability. He suggested that Islamabad cannot and should not be a 'net security provider' regionally.

title: Process becomes punishment
author: none@none.com (Tahsin Shah)
content:
A STATE does not demonstrate its strength by the number of its critics it can imprison. Its strength is measured by its willingness to tolerate dissent, submit executive power to law and allow courts to protect even those whom the state considers troublesome. Pakistan today faces a troubling test on all three counts.
The cases of Baloch activist Dr Mahrang Baloch and lawyers Imaan Mazari Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha are different in their facts and legal foundations. Yet, taken together with the treatment of political opponents and other dissenting voices, they raise a larger question: is the criminal justice system increasingly being used not merely to prosecute alleged offences, but to manage dissent?
Mahrang Baloch emerged as a prominent voice against enforced disappearances and alleged ex­­t­rajudicial killings in Balochistan. In June, an antiterrorism court sentenced her and another activist to life imprisonment in a case arising from the death of a security official during the 2024 Ba­­loch Raji Machi. Amnesty International criticised the proceedings as an expedited secret trial, stating that no direct evidence linking her to the violence had been presented. Her case has consequently become emblematic of wider concerns about due process and the treatment of Baloch dissent.
    
The state is entitled — indeed obligated — to pro­­secute violence. Human rights advocacy or po­­litical activism cannot confer immunity from cri­minal law. But the converse is equally important: allegations of disloyalty or association with hostile organisations cannot substitute for evidence est­ablishing individual criminal responsibility. The graver the charge, the greater the need for transparent proceedings and scrupulous due process.
Exceptional powers created against today’s adversary may become tomorrow’s weapon against those who created them.
The experience of Imaan Mazari Hazir and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, raises another disturbing issue. Both lawyers and human rights activists, they were sentenced in January to 17 years’ imprisonment under multiple provisions of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act in relation to social media posts. On Sept 17, the Supreme Court suspended their sentences and ordered their release. Within hours, they were arrested in another case and sent back to jail.
Whatever the ultimate merits of that second case, the sequence raises a fundamental rule-of-law concern. If obtaining bail in one case merely opens the door to detention in another, judicial relief risks becoming theoretical. Liberty cannot meaningfully depend upon how many FIRs remain available after a court orders someone’s release. This phenomenon has implications far beyond individual defendants. Arrest becomes punishment before conviction; multiplicity of proceedings becomes a mechanism for prolonged detention; and appellate delay can make eventual acquittal an inadequate remedy. A person who spends years incarcerated before a conviction is overturned cannot be given those years back.
HRCP’s 2025 report described a severe contraction of civic space and raised concerns about erosion of judicial independence. It documented the increasing use of cybercrime, sedition and antiterrorism laws against journalists, political workers, activists and lawyers, alongside continuing repor­ts of enforced disappearances and restrictions on expression.
These developments occur against a persistent public perception that unelected institutions — par­ticularly the security establishment — exerci­­se influence over political and accountability processes. Both the establishment and government have rejected various allegations of political persecution. Such competing claims cannot be reso­l­ved by assertion. That is precisely why visibly in­­d­e­­pendent courts, transparent trials and faithful compliance with judicial orders are irreplaceable.
The controversy surrounding former prime mi­­nister Imran Khan’s medical treatment illustrates the institutional problem. On Aug 18, the Supreme Court ordered that he be shifted to Shifa Inter­national Hospital for examination and treatment, with his personal physician and sister. Instead, he was taken to the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences and returned to prison, prompting allegations of non-compliance.
The matter was fixed for Sept 16, but by then, the Federal Constitutional Court had requisitioned the record of the hospital transfer cases. The Supreme Court itself expressed reservations about the FCC’s intervention but, citing judicial comity, adjourned proceedings for three weeks while seeking the attorney general’s assistance on the jurisdictional question. What began as the straightforward issue of compliance with a prisoner’s medical treatment order thus became entangled in a dispute over the jurisdiction of Pakistan’s two apex courts — a development critics view as having shifted attention from the unanswered question: was the original order obeyed?
The issue need not be Imran Khan personally. Tomorrow it may be someone from an entirely different political camp. The constitutional question is whether an order of the highest court binds the executive in practice or merely begins another round of litigation. Montesquieu warned that “there is no liberty” where judicial power is not separated from the other powers of the state. The warning remains strikingly relevant. Courts cannot preserve liberty merely by issuing orders; those orders must command obedience. Pakistan does not need weaker security institutions. It needs stronger constitutional institutions.
Allegations of terrorism, violence and incitem­e­­nt should be prosecuted where evidence exists, but antiterrorism and cybercrime legislation must not become convenient substitutes for ordinary criminal process. Trials involving political activists should be transparent. Appeals involving inc­a­­rcerated defendants require genuinely expedited hearings. Bail and release orders must be im­­plemented in substance, not defeated through serial detention.
Most importantly, enforced disappearance can have no place in a constitutional state. Every person detained by the state must be produced before a court, informed of the accusation and afforded access to counsel.
The government, opposition and establishment should all understand the same principle: exceptional powers created against today’s adversary may become tomorrow’s weapon against those who created them. Pakistan’s crisis, therefore, is larger than Mahrang Baloch, Imaan Mazari Hazir, Hadi Ali Chattha or Imran Khan. It concerns the boundary between the citizen and the state. A criminal justice system earns legitimacy not when it efficiently imprisons the unpopular, but when it protects due process precisely when doing so is politically inconvenient. The ultimate test of the rule of law is simple: whether law restrains power — or power determines what the law will mean. n
The writer is a retired inspector general of police and former DG FIA.
Published in Dawn, September 23rd, 2026

The criminal justice system in Pakistan appears to be increasingly used to manage dissent, rather than solely to prosecute alleged offenses, as exemplified by cases like Mahrang Baloch and Imaan Mazari Hazir.

Serial detention, non-compliance with judicial orders, and jurisdictional disputes between apex courts undermine the substantive meaning of liberty and legal relief, turning judicial orders into mere theoretical pronouncements.

Persistent public perception of unelected institutions influencing political processes necessitates visibly independent courts, transparent trials, and faithful compliance with judicial directives to establish legitimacy and resolve competing claims.

Exceptional powers, like anti-terrorism and cybercrime laws, risk becoming instruments against those who created them, underscoring the vital need for robust constitutional institutions and strict adherence to due process for all citizens.
