title: Urban air pollution
author: none@none.com (Umair Ahmad Ghumman)
content:
ACCORDING to IQAir’s World Air Quality Report 2025, Pakistan recorded the worst air quality among 143 monitored countries, with an annual average PM2.5 concentration more than 13 times the WHO guideline. The Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26 confirms that around 22,000 deaths each year are linked to air pollution. Four of the world’s 10 most polluted cities are in Pakistan. Lahore is the worst, followed by Faisalabad, Multan and Peshawar. This insight argues that Pakistan’s urban air pollution crisis stems mainly from local factors, with transport being the largest contributor. Long-term improvements will come from consistent, city-specific reforms rather than temporary emergency measures that emerge each smog season.
Pakistan’s National Clean Air Policy, approved by the federal cabinet in 2023, attributes 235,000 premature deaths annually to air pollution exposure. Similarly, the University of Chicago’s Air Quality Life Index suggests that complying with the WHO guideline could extend average life expectancy by 3.3 years, and by more than five in Lahore and Peshawar. Punjab took the serious step of declaring a health emergency. At the same time, provincial records showed nearly 1.93 million respiratory cases in just one month. Unicef warned that 11m children under five breathe toxic air each day.
The Pakistan Air Quality Initiative’s national landscape report from December 2025, which is the country’s first comprehensive inventory that looks at each city individually, helps clear up a lot of the confusion. In Lahore, transport makes up 35 per cent of PM2.5 levels. Rawalpindi-Islamabad sees transport as the main source at 53pc; Peshawar is at 51pc, and Karachi stands out as being predominantly industrial, with 49pc from industry and port operations. Since each city faces different pollution sources, the situation calls for tailored solutions.
Cleaner fuel is most effective when paired with cleaner engines.
With Pakistan’s heavy reliance on roads, transport has emerged as the top urban issue. In Lahore, studies link about 36pc of fine-particle pollution to diesel and two-stroke exhaust, with two- and three-wheelers being particularly high emitters. Peshawar’s problem is compounded by over 50,000 unregistered two-stroke engine rickshaws, a vehicle class that emits more particulate matter per kilometre than any other on the road. After the decline caused by the 2022 floods, sales bounced back in 2024, making Pakistan one of the fastest-growing two-wheeler markets globally. Many cities have faced similar choices between making long-term structural changes and applying temporary solutions.
Peshawar’s TransPeshawar bus rapid transit system, which uses hybrid-electric buses, moves over 345,000 passengers daily, making it the busiest BRT in the country. Lahore’s Metrobus and Orange Line together transport more than 250,000 people each day. The Rawalpindi-Islamabad Metrobus system serves around 135,000 commuters daily, now supported by 160 electric buses imported from China. Expanding and linking these systems is a powerful step, offering the greatest benefits.
Cleaner fuel is most effective when paired with cleaner engines. Pakistan is now providing Euro-5 fuel nationwide and aims to reach Euro-6 standards by 2030. However, the impact is limited because there is no strict enforcement of vehicle-emission standards; for example, Punjab has only 32 inspection stations to serve over 24m vehicles. Implementing mandatory emission testing and fitness certification could be a simple yet significant step forward.
Improving rail freight and the ML-1 corridor can help red­uce heavy diesel trucking on urban roads, which in turn can help lower city pollution. That’s a great reason to support the Rail­w­ays’ goal of increasing its passenger modal share from around 4pc to 20pc.
Renewing the fleet is the next positive step. A trustworthy scrappage scheme for the oldest and most polluting vehicles would be an effective follow-up. Electrification then directly tackles the most harmful segment. The National Electric Vehicle Policy 2025-30 aims for 30pc of new vehicle sales to be electric by 2030, supported by over Rs100 billion in incentives. Focusing on two- and three-wheelers offers the fastest path to cleaner city air.
The response should match the problem: a city-specific programme built on mass transit, cleaner fuels and fleet electrification. Paid parking to discourage private vehicle use, organised parking facilities, and a congestion charge in major urban centres would reduce traffic and increase dem­and for mass transit. Development of public transport infrastructure should be prioritised over the construction of new flyovers and underpasses. Clean air is a strategic priority rather than a seasonal concern. 
The writer is an assistant research associate at the Institute for Strategic Studies, Research and Analysis, National Defence University.
Published in Dawn, September 19th, 2026

title: Why isn’t the economy growing?
author: none@none.com (Syed Sardar Ali)
content:
DURING the roughly 150-year period between 1760 and World War I, England, the countries of northwest Europe, and the US went through the economic transformation of the Industrial Revolution. Real per capita GDP, which had remained stagnant at $2-3 per day, started to rise. Real wages that had historically remained slightly above subsistence level doubled. The percentage of labour force employed in agriculture plummeted. The West’s share of global manufacturing — around 25 per cent before the Industrial Revolution — jumped to more than 80pc by 1914. Some economic historians have labelled this shift as humanity’s ‘great escape’ from poverty, disease, and squalor.
In the past 200 years, Japan, South Korea, and China stand as the only non-European nations to have bridged the economic divide with the West. These countries accomplished in decades what the West achieved in centuries by sustaining long periods of nearly double-digit economic growth.
    
After the destruction wreaked by World War II, Japan grew at an average annual rate of nearly 10pc from 1955 to 1973. In 1968, it surpassed Germany to become the second largest economy. Starting in the early 1960s, South Korea entered a period of sustained economic growth, described as the ‘Miracle on the Han River’. Real GDP increased 25-fold in three decades. In 1996, South Korea became a member of the OECD. In the 40 years following the ‘reform and opening up’ of 1978, China’s economy grew at an average annual rate of about 9.5pc, increasing the size of its GDP roughly 35- to 40-fold in real terms. In the process, China lifted nearly 800 million people out of poverty and became the world’s largest economy in PPP terms in 2014.
The high-speed economic growth of the East Asian economies displayed three characteristics. First, the period of rapid economic growth was preceded by fundamental restructuring of society’s political and cultural institutions. Second, the shift from an agricultural to industrial economy was spearheaded by the state. Third, during the transformation period, the attainment of econo­m­­ic goals was prioritised over political freedoms.
For Pakistanis to live better, the economy must grow at near double-digit rates for decades.
From 1945 until 1951, Gen Douglas MacArthur presided over Japan’s post-World War II transformation as supreme commander of the allied powers. He had Emperor Hirohito issue a rescript denouncing his divinity, promulgated a new constitution, carried out land reforms, changed the education system, and introduced American cultural elements to Japanese life. In South Korea, before Gen Park seized power in 1961, land reforms had already been accomplished through the initiative of the United States Army Military Government in Korea. Gen Park launched the New Community Movement, promoted traditional ethno-nationalism, and strictly regulated social life. During the first 30 years after the revolution of 1949, the Communist Party of China dismantled the 2,000-year-old imperial system, gave land title to nearly 300m peasants, and laid the foundations of a modern state.
The post-World War II reconstruction in Japan was led by the ‘iron triangle’ of bureaucrats from the trade and industry ministry, Liberal Democratic Party politicians, and the captains of Japan’s leading industrial conglomerates. In South Korea, Gen Park adopted the policy of export-led economic growth by providing subsidised credit to chaebols, suppressing domestic demand, and quashing labour unions. In China, the state laid the foundations of basic and heavy industry through financial and technical Soviet assistance. Even after Deng Xiaoping’s liberalisation, the state still controls strategic sectors of the economy and takes the lead in pioneering new technologies.
    
Nominally, Japan was a parliamentary democracy during the post-World War II economic tra­n­s­­formation, but the Liberal Democratic Party re­­mained in power for 38 years in what is described as a ‘one-and-a-half party system’. Following a coup in 1961, Gen Park first ruled South Korea as a military dictator and then adopted a constitution giving him near absolute powers without term limits. China has remained a one-party-led state since its founding in 1949. Deng Xiaoping, who launched the economic ‘reform and opening up’ in 1978, rejected dem­ands for Western-style democracy and suppressed the 1989 demonstrations in Tiananmen Square.
In varying degrees, these conditions were present in all countries that successfully transformed into industrialised nations. Pakistan experienced something similar during its first two decades, when it attempted land reforms, passed the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, and adopted the five-year planning system, with input from the Harvard Advisory Group. All the economic and social gains of these early decades were lost starting in the 1970s. In 1998, Pakistan discontinued the practice of drawing five-year plans and began transitioning to a medium-term development framework. Slow growth in the last two decades has caused Pakistan to fall behind its South Asian neighbours in living standards. The manufacturing sector represents less than 13pc of GDP, and the country runs an average annual trade deficit of around $30 billion.
Harsh policy measures have stabilised Pakistan’s economy. During FY2024-2025, Pakistan recorded a current account surplus because of import restrictions and robust remittances. Fiscal deficit dropped to a multi-decade low of 2.6pc of GDP in 2025-26. Record-high inflation has come down to more manageable levels. Pakistan’s sovereign credit rating has improved because of lower external risks. However, growth has remained stagnant at around 3.5pc per annum for the last decade. The IMF projects an annual growth rate of 3.5pc for 2026-27, which is barely sufficient to offset the depreciation of the capital stock and compensate for population growth.
For Pakistanis to experience any meaningful improvement in living standards, the economy needs to grow at near double-digit rates for several decades. Our current subsistence level agricultural economy with a rudimentary level of industrialisation has reached the limits of its productive capacity. Transformative growth can only come by making the quantum leap to industry. However, industrialisation requires us to fundamentally restructure the political and social order of society, and the state should lead the industrialisation process, with political differences subordinated to the pursuit of economic goals. The poverty trap will not be broken by incremental policy reforms. It requires restructuring the entire system of society.
The writer has a background in public administration. He has worked with international financial institutions, including the World Bank.
Published in Dawn, September 18th, 2026

title: Beyond the dollar
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S plan to seek a larger currency-swap facility with China while pursuing a similar arrangement with the US is a prudent financial diversification effort. Despite improvements, our foreign exchange reserves remain vulnerable to debt repayments, import costs and external shocks. More liquidity backstops can ease that pressure. A currency swap lets central banks temporarily exchange their respective currencies, giving the liquidity-constrained country access to foreign exchange for payments and easing pressure during shortages. Pakistan has drawn China’s 30bn yuan facility, due for renewal in 2027 when Islamabad seeks an increase, while awaiting America’s approval for $10bn.
Pursuing both arrangements would give Pakistan more options when external financing comes under pressure. The Chinese facility can also support trade and payments with China in renminbi, reducing the immediate need for dollars for some transactions. A dollar facility would provide more direct support for dollar-denominated obligations and foreign-exchange market pressures. But the limits of these facilities must be clear. A drawn facility creates a liability that must be repaid. The State Bank reserve figures should therefore disclose and distinguish between freely available reserves and funds with repayment obligations. That said, these facilities are not a substitute for economic reform. They can provide breathing space, but cannot permanently strengthen the external account. The risk would be to use easier access to liquidity to postpone the difficult work of raising productivity, expanding exports and reducing dependence on external borrowing. For now, however, the strategy is useful. Pakistan needs stronger buffers against oil-price spikes, debt-service pressures and other external shocks. A wider network of bilateral liquidity facilities can reduce the risk of a temporary shock turning into another protracted balance-of-payment crisis. The aim should be simple. Build credible external buffers and use them sparingly. More importantly, increase exports, attract stable FDI and boost the economy’s capacity to earn foreign exchange.
Published in Dawn, September 19th, 2026

title: The forgotten NSP
author: none@none.com (Khurram Abbas)
content:
WHEN the PTI government introduced Pakis­tan’s first-ever National Security Policy (NSP) in 2022, the framework placed its primary emphasis on geo-economics and the pursuit of economic security. However, as this five-year policy nears expiration, it seems that the geo-economic vision and citizen-centric approach envisioned under the NSP have failed to achieve their objectives. This lack of success stems from three major reasons.
The foremost reason is the curse of political discontinuity. When prime minister Imran Khan unveiled Pakistan’s first-ever NSP in January 2022, it was hailed as a revolutionary pivot towards a citizen-centric geo-economic future. Yet, just months later, the predictable wheel of Pakistani political instability turned, and with the ouster of the PTI government, the strategic document was promptly relegated to bureaucratic limbo. It seems that in Pakistan’s deeply polarised political landscape, structural continuity is a luxury. Successive administrations traditionally suffer from a profound ‘ownership gap’, and view the policy blueprints of their predecessors with suspicion. This does not mean that the incoming coalition government ripped up the NSP. Rather, the subsequent administrations of the PDM alliance and then the PML-N-led coalition found itself completely consumed by the base instincts of political survival and immediate fiscal fires. These priorities diluted institutional focus and shifted the national priority from long-term economic integration to immediate to short-term emergency bailouts.
Secondly, a viable geo-economic vision cannot survive in a fortress state. Rather, it demands liberalised trade policies, open borders, and a hyper-competitive export sector. But Islamabad remains wedded to an inward-looking protective regime, that maintains high tariffs on intermediate inputs averaging eight per cent, which is twice as high as Indian and Bangladeshi standards, effectively cutting off Pakistan’s industries from global value chains. This protectionism has pushed Pakistan’s export capacity against a hard structural ceiling, rendering regional competitive advantage remarkably weak. When the NSP was introduced, Pakistan’s total exports had reached a record $39.52 billion. Yet, while the policy promised a geo-economic turnaround to boost these numbers, subsequent years brought severe political instability and soaring energy tariffs that caused total exports to contract.
Third, for Pakistan, a fractured and hostile neighbourhood is a major constraint in realising its geo-economic strategy. Even the most robust economic policies are ultimately at the mercy of geography. The regional assumptions that underpinned Pakistan’s first-ever NSP collapsed almost as soon as the ink dried. At the time of the NSP’s release, there was cautious optimism in the strategic community of Islamabad. Backchannel diplomacy with India had successfully culminated in a 2021 understanding to ‘strictly observe’ a ceasefire along the Line of Control. This development indicated a slow path towards normalisation despite the scar of the 2019 Pulwama-Balakot crisis. However, New Delhi’s uncompromising policy of refusing any structural dialogue effectively froze the eastern front for Pakistan. Furthermore, New Delhi’s subsequent decision to hold the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, coupled with the intense four-day armed hostilities of May 2025, has effectively slammed the door on any lingering hopes for normalisation in the foreseeable future.
A viable geo-economic vision cannot survive in a fortress state.
Simultaneously, Islamabad’s grand calculations on its western border have turned to dust. The initial hope that the Afghan Taliban regime in Kabul would secure transit corridors to Central Asia was quickly shattered. Instead of acting as a cooperative partner, Kabul chose to prioritise its ideological fraternity with the TTP over its relationship with Islamabad. This policy decision of the Taliban regime plunged the Pak-Afghan border into a volatile cycle of skirmishes, trade closures, and a sev­ere domestic security crisis that completely derai­led the NSP’s transit-hub ambitions. Resultantly, bilateral commerce between Pakistan and Afghanistan, Afghan transit trade volume via Pakistan, and third-country exports through Pakistan contracted sharply. Adding to this paralysis, Pakistan’s southwestern frontier remains structurally locked. While the diplomatic relationship with Iran has managed to be stable and progressive, the pervasive American sanctions regime has severely strangled any realistic potential to further enhance economic ties with Tehran. 
Pakistan’s geo-economic vision cannot be realised until Islamabad radically restructures its domestic priorities and foreign policy architecture on three major fronts. First and foremost, Islamabad must insulate its core economic strategy from the volatile swings of its political cycles. This demands a rare moment of political maturity, where cross-party consensus elevates econo­mic diplomacy to a non-partisan national objecti­­ve and ensures that a change at the Prime Minister’s Office doesn’t translate into abandonment of the country’s long-term economic roadmap.
Second, Islamabad must formally divorce its economy from its security apparatus, and treat them as separate, independent domains so that trade channels are never again sacrificed to the knee-jerk impulses of geopolitical friction. Instead of attempting a grand, macro-level regional integration that is easily checked by state-level hostility, Islamabad must pivot towards a bottom-up approach that maximises its leverage by creating dedicated border economic zones and automated, high-tech transit terminals with its eastern and western neighbours. 
Third, to transition from a security state to a true citizen-centric development state, Pakistan must boldly address its structural bottlenecks. This means dismantling the protectionist tariff walls that stifle innovation, aggressively diversifying the low-tech export basket beyond textiles, and creating a stable, predictable regulatory environment capable of attracting genuine foreign direct investment. Regionally, while the geopolitical landscape remains treacherous, Islamabad cannot afford to be economically isolated. It must leverage its strategic partnership with Beijing to optimise the next phase of CPEC, while simultaneously utilising creative, localised trade arrangements with Kabul and Delhi, where formal diplomatic breakthroughs remain stalled. 
Islamabad must realise that, while it has regained significant strategic importance in the Middle East, and beyond to some extent, it finds itself increasingly isolated within its own region. To fix this, Pakistan must fundamentally rethink its regional and domestic policies so it can truly benefit from its renewed global influence and turn its geo-economic objectives into lasting economic growth. 
The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.

title: Sugar threat
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE sugar industry has renewed pressure on the government for permission to export 1m tonnes of sugar. Millers say they may delay the next crushing season unless the government complies. It is not a request or demand; it is a threat. The Pakistan Sugar Mills Association projects a 1.25m tonne surplus. That number needs independent verification. Sugar millers do not have a clean record on stock reporting. They have been accused repeatedly of inflating surpluses to obtain export permission. Past inquiries have flagged manipulation and coordination among them. None of that makes industry estimates a reliable basis for policy.
The export track record itself is the strongest argument for caution. Each time exports have been approved, shortages have followed, with the government importing sugar to fix the mess it created by exporting the commodity. Selling a ‘surplus’ abroad only to buy it back later at a higher price is not trade policy. It is a subsidy for politically influential sugar producers. The government should avoid extremes. It should refrain from imposing an outright export ban or greenlighting the export of 1m tonnes on the industry’s pressure. If independent verification confirms a surplus, it can be exported in tranches. More exports can be approved only if the data shows that the local supply is holding up. That said, deregulation of the sugar sector is the real, long-term fix — not case-by-case export permissions but a supply chain that is freed end to end. The market should set the price of cane and sugar, while imports and exports must be run according to fixed rules and not at political discretion. For this, the industry must open its books for independent checks to verify stock claims, and be exposed to real competition, instead of operating as a tight-knit cartel. In such a scenario, millers will not need to issue threats; a functioning market would give them what they want. And farmers would no longer find themselves in the crossfire.
Published in Dawn, September 18th, 2026

title: Restructuring lessons
author: none@none.com (Ghazan Jamal)
content:
INTERIOR Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s proposal for more provinces wasn’t the first time someone close to the establishment made the suggestion. However, this time a stated motivation was also provided: namely, the complete collapse of the existing governance system. While much has been written about this issue, it has largely been theoretical and speculative, with the closest real-world examples coming from other countries. The problem with those examples is that, while informative, they mostly exist in a context very different to Pakistan’s, making it difficult to draw parallels. But an example closer to home can help us predict better. The last time Pakistan’s internal borders were redrawn was in 2018 with Fata’s merger with KP through the 25th Amendment.
    
A similarly stated motivation for the merger was given at the time — the utter collapse of the old Fata governance system. That system has been blamed for the militant takeover in many parts of Fata (now called the merged districts). Many also hold it responsible for erstwhile Fata’s extremely poor human development indices compared to the Pakistani average. The merger with KP, and thus the extension of KP’s institutional structures, laws, and systems, was deemed necessary to resolve Fata’s problems. Another proclaimed benefit was that the merger would bring the government closer to the public. The state believed that the militants had filled the void created by an unresponsive government. So, in many ways, the motivation to merge rested on two beliefs: first, to replace an old, collapsed system with one offering better governance; and second, to involve communities in decision-making by bringing government closer to them. Similar justifications are now being touted to support the idea of new provinces.
Eight years after the merger, the question is: how effectively has the change improved both aspects for residents of the merged areas? The question of whether decision-making has been brought closer to the people and thereby made government institutions more responsive to the public’s needs is perhaps the easier one to answer: there’s no evidence that matters have improved; if anything, the opposite appears to be true. The merged areas still have no share in the NFC and continue to depend on discretionary federal funding. In fact, they are a step removed from that planning process, as it must come through KP rather than directly to them. Similarly, the tribal system is, by definition, participatory and community-led. Replacing it with a more centralised, institutional state structure has decreased community involvement and the power of the local people to run their own affairs.
    
The question of governance is more complex, but even here, there is not much improvement. First, the new system is less participatory even in governance, further alienating people from their government. Second, the administrative system is now far too bureaucratic to respond promptly. It is increasingly bloated — current administrative expenditures for the merged areas have more than doubled, from about Rs50 billion at the time of the merger to over Rs100bn now. Similarly, the judicial process, like elsewhere in the country, is painfully slow, making locals increasingly likely to turn to traditional jirgas rather than the courts. The creation of alternative dispute resolution me­­chanisms and dispute resolution councils, aligned with traditional jirgas and under the guise of the district administration and district police respectively, acknowledges the delay in dispensing justice. Worse, there has been no marked improvement in any human development indicator; apart from isolated instances, no real examples of systemic improvement in service delivery exist. Where security is concerned, there is a surge in militant activity in the region, with terrorist incidents and casualty figures worse than in the years before the merger. Clearly, the merger is not preventing the resurgence of militancy in the area.
What insights does the Fata merger offer into the recently proposed move to create new administrative units?
The merger failed to achieve the improvements that proponents vowed it would bring, even though it had backing at the national level, unlike the idea of new provinces, especially from the three major national political parties (the PML-N, PTI and PPP), establishment experts and development partners. It was a rare moment in Pakistan’s recent political history in which all three major national parties came together to pass the 25th Constitutional Amendment and then saw it passed in the KP Assembly by consensus. The idea of new provinces has no such national consensus at the moment; it would look more like arm-twisting if the political parties go ahead with it. However, even in the case of the merger, locals were excluded from the decision-making process, and a majority of Fata’s elected parliamentarians at the time favoured reforms, though they raised serious reservations about how these reforms were being pursued. This was cause for concern. Regrettably, their alarm was disregarded; in fact, it was termed a vain effort by locals to save an archaic system.
One might argue that the merger was, in many ways, a different reform than creating new provinces. Yet both reforms ignore the same basic issue of structure and approach, which must be addressed before there is any redrawing of internal provincial borders or creation of new administrative units. To have a responsive government, communities need more involvement through a regularly functioning, well-resourced local government system. Helping communities decide the policies they want is essential for a successful transition to new systems. Whether this happens in a larger administrative unit or a smaller one matters less.
Most importantly, Pakistan needs a mindset shift in how it pursues policy and reforms. We need an approach that replaces preconceived notions and unsubstantiated beliefs that dictate policy. We must move away from a mindset that envisions the state as a mere administrative entity; instead, the state must assume the role of a citizen-empowering force that serves the people. Without this, even the most logical ‘reforms’ will prove cosmetic and do little to address systemic failures.
The writer is a development practitioner and a former parliamentarian.

title: For Ishmal
author: none@none.com (Rafia Zakaria)
content:
IN Pakistan fatherless daughters walk with a target pinned to their backs. No male guardian leaves them unprotected from the eyes of the men who surround them. In a recent heart-breaking case of the cruelty of this truth, a nine-year-old girl named Ishmal was shot dead.
Ishmal lived in upper Swat. She was the youngest of six children who were all left orphans when their father passed away. According to family accounts and police reports, Ishmal went to school as usual on Sept 9, 2026. When she came home, she changed out of her school uniform and went to a neighbour’s house (she reportedly often did this). According to media reports citing the police complaint, not long after she had left her home, her sister heard screams and then gunshots. When the sister rushed to the neighbour’s house, she saw Ishmal lying on the floor covered in blood. The man who would turn out to be the accused in this case was seen going into a room.
Family members and neighbours rushed to help, and Ishmal was taken to the hospital. Ishmal died on the way to the hospital or shortly after getting there. The investigation revealed that she had been allegedly sexually assaulted, shot twice and left to die. Such was the alarming cruelty perpetrated on her. She was simply a child, a fatherless girl, who was adjudged to be worthless except to fulfil the lust and will of a man. 
The suspect, a man identified as Sultan, has been arrested. The suspect had a government job as a watchman. He is the father of six children, some of whom were Ishmal’s friends and the reason why she would go to his house in the afternoons after school. His wife was also taken into custody — possibly because she was present during the assault and murder. The accused has been booked on murder charges under the Pakistan Penal Code.
Once media attention ends, no one pursues cases of assault and murder.
On Sept 11, 2026, a huge protest was held in Madyan in Swat, where women came out to protest against the murder and what they saw as the unlikelihood of the culprit (who is reportedly seen by the locals as having government contacts) being brought to justice.
The answer to that question is unlikely to be known soon. Swat has been the site of some alarming violence against minor girls of late. On June 24, 2026, a 17-year-old girl Ayesha was found missing from her home in Abbottabad. According to the FIR, the girl had been abducted by two men who took her to a hotel, where she was sexually assaulted. She was allegedly given a poisonous or intoxicating substance afterwards. She was left abandoned at Saidu Sharif Teaching Hospital in critical condition and died during treatment.
In that case, too, there were arrests, including of a man named Muzammil who was identified as the chief suspect in an FIR registered in Mingora. Cases for murder, rape, kidnapping and administering a poisonous substance have all been registered against him. There was initial outrage, but as soon as it died down, it was unclear what became of the prosecution and how many more suspects had been arrested.
Cases are registered; suspects are caught and even charged and put in prison. The court process begins, but after that it becomes increasingly unclear as to what happens to the men who commit these crimes with such impunity. While it seems that the government and law enforcement in Pakistan believe they should give the impression that ‘something is being done’, once the media attention dissipates, no one bo­­thers to find out whether those who are caught, charged and jai­led are ever real­­-ly punished.
So, in the wake of the ever-growing numbers of dead Pakistani girls, one can only make a plea to the government to demand that all provinces and all police stations start providing end-of-year reports on the status of various convictions for the murder and sexual assaults of girls within their jurisdiction. 
While the numbers of actual cases will always be low because the vast majority of them are never reported, at least there would be some accountability for what happens to the accused in the year or two years following. 
Once the relevant institutions start to take some responsibility and are made to feel accountable for any lack of action, and when the conviction of femicidal maniacs who abduct and sexually assault women becomes a priority, a cultural change might ensue, in which women and girls are not seen as worthless and expendable — lesser citizens who can be raped and murdered at the whim of a man. 
The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.

title: Court vs court
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
A SUPREME Court order directing the hospitalisation of former prime minister Imran Khan for medical tests and treatment has now turned into a much bigger crisis than anyone anticipated.
After the court’s original order was disregarded by the government, like so many others before it, the matter landed before the Federal Constitutional Court via a separate case filed by three other Adiala inmates seeking similar treatment. The FCC has since taken control of the Imran Khan hospitalisation case as well, much to the SC’s chagrin.
To observers, the FCC’s move directly challenges a May ruling issued by Chief Justice of Pakistan Yahya Afridi, in which he had described the SC and FCC as “coordinate courts exercising clearly demarcated jurisdictions over distinct matters”. However, the current dispute underlines a clear jurisdictional collision between the two courts, which still seem rather uncertain regarding what each is supposed to be doing since the 27th Amendment.
    
At the heart of the crisis is the 27th Amendment, which had substantially rearranged constitutional jurisdiction by creating a completely new judicial forum, the FCC, and placing major constitutional questions and fundamental rights matters within its domain. The FCC invoked that same jurisdiction days ago to summon the complete records of cases concerning Mr Khan’s hospital transfer from the SC, indicating that it intended to frame the matter as a question of determining whether prisoners are constitutionally entitled to such treatment.
However, it then went a step further and also fixed the case before itself. To its credit, the SC has responded with restraint. The three-member bench hearing the case merely remarked that the FCC’s order had raised “considerable legal and constitutional significance” and then adjourned for three weeks while seeking comment from the attorney general over whether the FCC’s order was, indeed, binding on the SC. Mr Khan’s hospitalisation, of course, seems moot at this point.
    
Perhaps matters were bound to arrive at this juncture thanks to the undue haste with which the 27th Amendment was foisted upon the nation. It appears that its text never settled the matter of what happens when a constitutional question arises in an ongoing SC case, especially when such a case pertains to the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Contempt of Court Ordinance, which are very much within the SC’s remit.
It is even more remarkable that a crisis of this nature has erupted at the highest level of the judiciary over what was otherwise a rather straightforward order to transfer an ailing prisoner to a hospital and get them the treatment required. It is certainly not a good look for the current dispensation that the fragility of the architecture that props it up keeps being exposed, and over matters that ought to be minor in perspective.

title: Ties with UAE
author: none@none.com (Dr Raashid Wali Janjua)
content:
PAKISTAN-UAE relations have stood the test of time despite geopolitical upheavals. The current souring of relations does not reflect the true potential of ties between the two countries. Bilateral ties are rooted in shared faith, cultural affinity, and enduring people-to-people bonds. Pakistan was among the first countries to recognise and establish diplomatic relations with the UAE after the country’s founding in 1971. Since then, ties have continued to expand.
Pakistan’s contribution to the UAE’s development remains an important glue that still binds the two states together. Pakistani military personnel, engineers, teachers, professionals and skilled workers have contributed to defence, aviation, education, and engineering. A 2.2 million-strong Pakistani diaspora remains an important pillar of the UAE economy, contributing $8 billion in remittances, while also providing demographic balance vis-à-vis 4.2m Indian expatriates. The UAE is Pakistan’s third-largest trading partner.
There is steady progress towards investment-led partnerships in logistics, technology, agriculture and food security. This is supported by the Pakistan-UAE Compre­hensive Economic Partnership Agreement, which is expected to raise trade volume to $16-20bn. Pakistan’s 240m consumer market, young, tech-savvy workforce, 2.3m freelancers, and 26,000 registered IT/ITeS companies offer significant opportunities for UAE investment in Pakistan’s IT parks, fintech, and e-commerce.
Pakistan’s defence ties with the UAE date back to 1974, when 115 Pakistani defence personnel laid the foundations of an enduring partnership by training Emirati pilots and military personnel, and establishing the Armour Training School. The extent of cooperation is evident in the fact that the first five chiefs of air staff of the UAE Air Force were Pakistan Air Force officers. Pakistan offers joint special forces training exercises for counterterrorism and co-production of defence hardware, on account of its advanced defence industry, along with prospects for future cooperation in AI, cyberspace, electronic warfare, and advanced defence systems.
Ties between Pakistan and the UAE have continued to expand.
Agriculture and food security is another area of convergence due to Pakistan’s fertile land and the UAE’s demand for agricultural products. Pakistan’s climatic conditions, agricultural workforce and production capacity can contribute to UAE food security. Conversely, UAE capital, technology, and logistics can make Pakistan’s supply chains more resilient through cold-chain storage, marketing, and value addition.
Minerals are another area of cooperation. Pakistan possesses immense mineral wealth. Already, Pakistan’s Mari Energies is collaborating with the UAE’s International Resource Holding to explore copper and gold reserves in Chagai, as well as opportunities in antimony, aluminium ore, and rare earth elements. A few UAE companies are also exploring the possibility of establishing an ore-refining industry in Punjab.
Geopolitical challenges like the UAE’s joining of the Abraham Accords and its economic rivalry with Saudi Arabia have resulted in political cleavages that have widened during the Iran-US conflict. Israel’s expansionist policies have not helped; the UAE’s quest for regional peace has foundered on the rocks of Israeli militarism. The UAE’s policies in Somaliland, Algeria, Libya, Yemen and Sudan have often placed it in Saudi Arabia’s rival camp.
Israel and the UAE are increasingly collaborating in some fields, and India’s influence is also growing because of its close ties with the former. However, Pakistan understands each country’s choices and does not have a di­­rect cla­sh of interest with any of the I2U2 (India, Isra­­el, the USA, UAE) sta­tes. Pakistan wants to play the role of re­­gional stabiliser in West Asia through alliances like the Makkah defence alliance. Pakistan’s mediatory role in the Iran-US conflict has also created space for the UAE’s rapprochement with Iran.
Pakistan and the UAE face a common threat in transnational terrorism and organised crime. As a global trade and transshipment hub, the UAE faces direct threats from the narco-trade emanating from Afgha­nis­tan. Pakistan’s ports like Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar complement rather than compete with UAE ports, lessening their burden and relieving congestion in Hormuz.
The scope for counterterrorism cooperation is broad. The two can combine Pakistan’s CT intelligence experience with the UAE’s capabilities in financial monitoring, border and aviation security, cybersecurity, etc to disrupt threats. Pakistan and the UAE should take advantage of the full range of economic, defence and CT cooperation opportunities, since their common interests far outweigh any geopolitical differences.
The writer has a PhD from NUST.

title: Managing the shock
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE energy shock Pakistan faces calls for immediate demand management. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and shipping have strained an already fragile supply chain by disrupting oil and gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
Global oil prices have been pushed to their highest level since May. A net energy importer, Pakistan has felt the impact directly: petrol has risen to Rs384.34 per litre and high-speed diesel to Rs415.83. Pain at the pump is pushing people to the edge. Moreover, higher global oil prices are feeding into the import bill, transport costs and inflation, adding further pressure on financially strained families.
RLNG prices have also risen. The government says greater use of domestic energy sources has helped keep power plants running. Domestic resources accounted for 72pc of electricity generation in August. Without more domestic gas for power generation, we could have faced another hour of loadshedding and an additional Rs10.6bn in consumer tariffs. That may provide some respite but is not a reason for complacency.
    
Energy conservation must start now. That does not mean shutting the country down. A nationwide lockdown would cost businesses working hours, deplete workers’ income, and hit daily-wage earners hard — a burden that an economy already struggling to generate growth and jobs cannot easily absorb. What the government should pursue, instead — at least for now — is targeted conservation: measures that cut avoidable consumption without halting productive activity. Schools could shorten operating days to ease transport and electricity demand. Government offices and private employers can be encouraged to work from home where practical. Markets, especially in major cities, could close earlier to cut late-night transport and commercial power use. Malls, offices and commercial buildings should face reasonable limits on unnecessary lighting and cooling.
Government departments need to lead by example rather than leave conservation to households alone. Provinces must follow suit so that the effort is not fragmented. The prime minister’s fuel relief package for motorcycle and small car owners may cushion a small part of the population, but subsidies cannot fix a supply shock, and protecting fuel consumption through the budget only gets costlier as global prices climb. The priority now is to protect incomes and essential economic activity while cutting non-essential demand.
    
The larger point is that Pakistan cannot keep meeting every external energy shock by either subsidising the cost or shutting down activity. Building domestic solar energy availability, grid efficiency, storage capacity and public transport is what actually reduces this vulnerability over time. Meanwhile, the choice is not between business as usual and a lockdown. There is a lot of room between the two. And the government needs to use it: conserve early, cut waste, keep the economy running.

title: Bab al-Mandeb closure
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
AS the pro-Iran Houthis battle both the Saudis and the Riyadh-backed Yemeni government, alarm bells are ringing across the world over the economic shockwave the long-term closure of the Bab al-Mandeb strait would send across the globe. The militia, which controls significant territory in Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, has, over the past few days of fighting, consolidated its gains around the strait. The Houthis say that passage through the channel is open for all except Saudi vessels — against whom they have vowed to enforce a “blockade for blockade”. Yet this will do little to reassure crews, as few vessels will want to pass through an active war zone. The Strait of Hormuz — that other major regional chokepoint — is already practically closed due to the US war on Iran. If shipping traffic through Bab al-Mandeb also grinds to a halt, the global economy will be in very dangerous territory. The government has said Pakistan faces an energy crunch. But Pakistan is not alone; disruption in the strait or the Red Sea will have an impact far and wide. Protests have been reported from as far afield as Syria and Indonesia, and if the situation worsens, more public unrest is likely as fuel pumps run dry.
Therefore, the Houthis — whatever their differences with the Saudis or the Yemeni government — must reconsider closure of Bab al-Mandeb, and pledge to keep it open for all vessels. As the Pakistani representative told the UN Security Council the other day, any attempt to “threaten, obstruct, or weaponise” vital waterways will have negative effects on international trade and shipping, as well as energy security. He added that “diplomacy must assume urgency”. The need for talks cannot be emphasised enough. The region cannot afford more violence; the Yemeni people have already suffered for over a decade, while the global economy is on tenterhooks due to the situation in Yemen. As the Saudis have enforced a blockade of Houthi-held territory since 2015, Riyadh could offer to lift the blockade if the militia stopped their attacks on the kingdom’s territory. Furthermore, a Yemeni-led, Yemeni-owned peace process is essential domestically. All belligerents need to step back and give talks a chance, as an escalation in violence would be catastrophic for the region.
Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026

title: Some critical questions
author: none@none.com (Shahab Usto)
content:
TRUE to tradition, a ‘plan’ to ‘reset’ the country’s entire structure has come down like an epiphany from apparently ‘non-political’ quarters. The plan envisages creating multiple provinces and changing the country’s very tapestry — its geography, topography, demography, ethnic relations, resource distribution, power sharing, and broader political calculus. The situation raises critical questions.
Why new provinces? The interior minister, who announced the plan, hasn’t held forth on the reasoning or offered an acceptable justification for adopting such an extreme and hazardous course. However, he has mentioned bad governance, population implosion, and systemic failures as some of the causes. Nor are there any official authoritative studies proposing a close nexus between good governance and smaller administrative structures. In fact, the global landscape reveals a mixed pattern. Some countries have fewer or territorially larger constituent units, and yet they are stable, functional, even enviable. Others have multiple small units/ provinces, but are perennially afflicted with broken, inept and even failed political systems.
    
The factors that generally determine the performance and vitality of a state are the legitimacy and efficacy of its political system, the character and ability of its leadership, and the maturity and capacity of its institutions — not only to deliver better governance, but also to meet the continuing challenges thrown up by ever-changing societal and state imperatives. In revitalising the ‘failed’ political systems, we don’t know if the so-called plan contemplates these factors.
Who is demanding them? Interestingly, most of these ideas have originated outside regular political processes, whether as One Unit, Basic Democracy, ‘Islamisation’, enlightened moderation, or hybrid governance. People have always been on the receiving end of new-fangled ideas and their pernicious consequences. The call for a structural ‘reset’, too, appears to have similar origins. So far, none of the governments — federal, provincial or even local — or the mainstream political leaderships have called for restructuring the provinces. However, there is near-consensus across the political spectrum on creating provinces in south Punjab, and KP’s Hazara belt. In fact, the Punjab and KP assemblies passed resolutions for these provinces, but they went nowhere.
Instead of new units, the country needs softer options to heal societal wounds.
Reorganising the state structures would be an extremely risky exercise. India’s Congress party had included the ‘linguistic’ provinces in its manifesto as early as 1917. Yet, after Partition, both prime minister Jawaharlal Nehru and home minister Vallabhbhai Patel were reluctant to reorganise the states, fearing balkanisation of the fledgling country. It was many months of intense political agitations across the country, expert studies, judicial commissions, and a much-mourned fast unto death by Telugu nationalist Potti Sriramulu that finally brought the government around. Still, the Reorganisation Act of 1955 was not passed to improve governance but to group various linguistic communities in their own separate states. In other words, distinctive ethno-cultural identities were recognised and restored, rather than brutally denied and suppressed as would have been the case if the states had been broken up in a manner that dispersed the historically located ethno-cultural communities — something that is being contemplated here.
    
Is referendum feasible? Perhaps encouraged by the smooth passage of the controversial 26th and 27th constitutional amendments, and not expecting a large section of the political establishment to oppose the proposed move, some elements here had appeared confident of securing the required numbers to ensure restructuring. However, the JUI-F, ANP, PTI, and even the ruling party’s major coalition partner have dug in their heels. In fact, even the prime minister and his party seem reluctant to support the restructuring, though some government ministers are backing it, albeit without the cabinet’s approval. Likewise, the Sindh Assembly has also rejected the break-up of the province.
As a result, other means are being sought — preferably, a referendum to execute the plan. But a referendum would not validate the wholesale reorganisation of the state. It lacks legitimacy and credibility. It cannot be used to circumvent or be a substitute for the mandatory constitutional amendment. People will not accept it because every military dictator has used it to legitimise their rule. Instead, a referendum will be seen as farcical and incite public anger, triggering a maelstrom of pushback.
Will the ‘plan’ succeed? Any idea, policy, or law that is imposed on the people has miserably failed to achieve its objectives; in fact, it has often led to disasters. Steamrolling the restructuring of provinces — against the will of the people — will further aggravate identity-driven politics across a fragile multiethnic landscape. It may even ignite the tinderbox the country has become, particularly for poor and disgruntled youth who have endured the harrowing realities of failed systems. The numbers are dreadful. Half the population lives in poverty, around 28 million children are out of school, four out of 10 children suffer from stunted growth, three-fourths of the populace is consuming contaminated water, and the increasingly murky security environment scares away local and foreign investors.
In these dire circumstances, the country desperately needs softer options to heal societal wounds — options that recompense the people through justice, equity, peace, opportunity, and development, which are democracy’s tested tools. The yawning fault lines — ethnic, social, political, inter-provincial and centre-province — must be mended, and federal democracy, which remains buried under the hybrid regime, restored.
The system does need a ‘reset’. But the reset should mean building efficient and accountable institutions, strengthening rules-based governance, and allowing legitimate and representative leadership to run political and public offices. That requires a continuous process of fair, free elections held on time, so that dead wood can be replaced with a fresher, cleaner leadership at the federal, provincial, and local levels.
Finally, a ‘reset’ would be fatal if it ignored the emotional, even spiritual, bonding of the various ethno-cultural communities with their respective provinces. This bonding goes beyond ideology or politics. It is the product of the centuries-long interplay between these communities and their distinctive land, history, culture, language, literature and art. This bonding leads many in Sindh to conceive their province as an indivisible historical entity — a firmer federalised version of Scotland or Quebec.
The writer is a lawyer.

title: Schools and smog
author: none@none.com (Alefia T. Hussain)
content:
AFTER a three-month summer break, Lahore’s school gates officially reopened on Aug 24, bringing back the hurried footsteps of children racing to beat the morning bell and bursts of laughter as they spill through the school gates in the afternoon. With them have come pickups and rickshaws, bulging with children and their oversized schoolbags, motorcycles weaving through traffic, often carrying three or more students at a time, and cars — so many cars — streaming across the city, sometimes carrying just one child. Buses carrying 20 or more children, meanwhile, are a rare sight.
Undoubtedly, beneath the bustle of the daily school run lies the palpable innocence of childhood — as well as the uneasy reality of the world they are growing up in. The cars, motorcycles and rickshaws ferrying children to and from school add to smoke that, come autumn, will mingle with dust, and turn the skies grey with smog.
To mitigate the harm of the annual smog, the Punjab government announced the Pre-Smog Action Plan 2026 (July-September 2026), to “ensure timely preparedness, prevention and mitigation of smog during the upcoming smog season”. Broadly, and rightly, the action plan calls for stronger Environment Protection Agency monitoring, drone surveillance and activation of district anti-smog committees, alongside weekly coordination among relevant departments. It requires calibration of air quality monitors and emission testing stations, inspections of industries and brick kilns, and checks on construction sites and stone crushers. Transport measures include vehicle testing and action against vehicles emitting black smoke, among other critical measures.
The plan largely carries forward the 10-year smog policy launched in 2024. To be fair, Lahore’s pollution levels were lower in 2025 than before — although favourable weather conditions had a hand in that improvement. But it is time to discuss measures that have escaped the smog plan’s purview so far — starting with the school traffic system.
Lahore must revamp its school transport system.
Lahore needs a transport system that puts hundreds of thousands of schoolchildren on far fewer vehicles. The government has attempted this, at its familiar slow pace, but only after pressure from the courts.
In an Aug 13, 2026, judgement, Justice Shahid Karim of the Lahore High Court (LHC) noted that vehicular emissions account for 45 per cent of Lahore’s pollution, thus getting children into buses is about cutting emissions that contribute to dangerous smog. Justice Karim described the order as the “last judgement in the trilogy”, which arose from a petition filed in 2018 regarding environmental degradation in Punjab.
Over eight years of proceedings, school transport became one strand of the case. The provincial government was directed to press schoolsto shift children from private vehicles to buses, to ensure buses for at least half the students, and to make transport compliance a condition of school registration.
All these years, the government’s response to the court’s order has largely consisted of meetings with school administrations and associations, followed by letters urging compliance. It has been a token effort — for, the government has not pushed hard enough to persuade private schools to set aside their claims of limited resources and invest in buses. Off the record, private school officials say the government sends letters and raises school transport in meetings, but no one seriously expects anything to come of it.
Lahore has hardly been a city of school buses. Since the mid-2000s, school transport has been shadowed by security concerns. During the years of the ‘war on terror’, when schools were conspicuous targets, parents saw buses carrying many children as a security risk. Then, in 2016, came a spate of reported child abductions across Punjab. In August that year, the then LHC chief justice Mansoor Ali Shah ordered schools to deploy security guards in pick-and-drop vans and directed the police to monitor school transport.
The fear was not confined to kidnapping. The rape and murder of Zainab Ansari in Kasur in 2018 intensified a wider anxiety about children’s vulnerability — and about the adults entrusted with their care. Then there was the danger posed by the vehicles themselves, with children often sharing space with unsafe gas cylinders.
To say that those fears have disappeared would be incorrect. They persist. And the urgency to overcome them has grown. The number of vehicles making the journey twice a day must be reduced. The stress on educating children rings hollow if the air they inhale is dangerous to their health. The best solution, of course, is a public school bus system — unless schools are brought within walking distance of every child.
The writer is a freelance journalist based in Lahore.
alefiath@gmail.com
Published in Dawn, September 16th, 2026

title: Dangerous escalation
author: none@none.com (Zahid Hussain)
content:
JUST weeks after its formation, the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement faces its first challenge: the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi militia. The rebel group has struck Saudi air bases and key oil facilities with missiles and drones, while the kingdom has intensified air strikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen. The Houthis have also targeted Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea.
The escalation began in mid-July, when the Houthis formally declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting Saudi-flagged shipping, after Yemeni government forces attacked a flight from Iran at Sana’a airport. The Houthis have been fighting Yemen’s internationally recognised government since 2014. The violence subsided after the warring sides reached an internationally brokered ceasefire in 2022, but flared up again after the July incident when the militia broke the truce, declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and began attacking Saudi vessels. Its ultimate aim is to drive Saudi Arabia out of Yemen and take full control of the territory.
This latest escalation has widened the conflict in West Asia, even as America’s war with Iran grinds on with no end in sight. With the fighting now threatening Saudi Arabia directly, will the kingdom invoke the alliance’s mutual defence clause — the one that treats an attack on one member as an attack on all members? The danger of a wider conflagration engulfing the entire region carries serious implications for the rest of the world.
The Houthis, who already hold much of Yemen, have seized a strategic island in a lightning offensive against government forces, giving them complete control of Bab al-Mandeb — the key marine chokepoint through which 12 per cent of the world’s trade passes. They now control 90 per cent of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline. The Houthi leadership says it is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea, only Saudi-linked vessels.
But the heightening tension is likely to keep other ships away. With the Strait of Hormuz virtually blocked, the situation is explosive. Global energy markets, already reeling from the six-month conflict between US-Israel and Iran, are bracing for further shock.
Saudi Arabia, which had stayed out of the Iran war, now risks being drawn into a wider conflict.
These actions by a militia widely seen as aligned with Iran have opened a new front in the conflict. They have coincided with a drone attack, apparently launched from Iraq by allegedly another Iran-linked militia, that forced temporary closure of the East-West oil pipeline crossing Saudi Arabia. Together, the attacks have disrupted Saudi oil exports. It is widely accepted that Iran backs the Houthis, though the group also operates independently of Tehran. The attacks on Saudi Arabia are certainly not in Iran’s interest while it is engaged in an existential war with the US — the fallout is already visible.
Saudi Arabia, which had so far kept itself out of the Iran war, is now in danger of being drawn into a wider regional conflict. Although Iran has distanced itself from the attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure by the two militias, the incidents have heightened tensions between Riyadh and Tehran. Following the attacks, talks between Iran and the Gulf states aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz were postponed. It would have been the first meeting between Iran and the main GCC member states in two years; the meeting, to be held in Oman, was part of an effort to find a regional solution allowing free passage through the critical waterway. The latest flare-up has thwarted that effort.
As the fighting spreads, Saudi Arabia finds itself on the front line. In the latest turn, the kingdom reportedly sought American military help, only to be turned down by President Donald Trump, who said the Houthis had assured him they did not want to expand the conflict. The development has given an intriguing twist to the conflict. Trump’s response is said to be driven by his frustration with the kingdom for failing to actively support his war against Iran.
America and Israel have carried out missile strikes against the Houthis in the past over their support for the Palestinian resistance. But there is also the question of whether US intervention in the Saudi-Houthi conflict will help stabilise a situation for which Washington is itself responsible. The growing tension between Iran and Saudi Ara­bia will only serve the US agenda in the region.
So far, Saudi Arabia has not formally invoked the Makkah defence alliance clause, which would require Pakistan and Turkiye to come to its def­ence if it is attacked. But consultations are under way as the conflict spreads. Diplomatic efforts to halt the Houthis’ escalatory moves are still continuing. Reportedly, Pakistan’s military chief and the Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan both spoke to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Pakistan is also believed to have conveyed a Saudi message urging Iran to rein in the Houthis, and reminded Tehran of Islamabad’s own pact commitment to Riyadh.
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif recently said that unprovoked aggression against the kingdom, or a spillover into it, would make the pact operational — “there should be no doubt about that”. Earlier, in April 2026, Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry announced that a Pakistani military contingent had arrived at King Abdulaziz Air Base, with fighter and support aircraft, under a bilateral defence pact signed in September 2025. Following Khawaja Asif’s remarks, however, the Foreign Office spokesperson said, “I don’t think we should be discussing this topic in the context of its operationalisation”.
The situation remains dangerous for both Pakistan and the larger region, and the widening conflict could suck in even those countries that have kept out of the Iran war and have been trying to help broker a negotiated end to it. Pakistan needs to tread a more cautious path in a conflict that could prove disastrous for the country. It’s a perilous escalation that needs to be resolved through negotiations rather than war.
The writer is an author and journalist.

title: Prudent move
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE State Bank’s decision to hold the policy rate at 11.5pc is the right one. With seven of the 10 members voting for the status quo, the Monetary Policy Committee has, with reason, resisted the wider business pressure — and temptation — to revert to monetary policy easing in an uncertain global economic environment exacerbated by the war in the Middle East. The case for a pause is even stronger today than it was a few months ago despite external sector stability and improved macroeconomic fundamentals. These are encouraging developments for an economy that has repeatedly been constrained by its external account. But the improvement should not be mistaken for the end of the crisis. The regional situation that appeared to be moving towards resolution a few weeks ago now looks uncertain. Oil supplies remain vulnerable to disruptions while uncertainty over shipping, energy routes and regional security continues. For an import-dependent economy such as Pakistan, a renewed oil shock could quickly widen the import bill, push inflation higher and put pressure on the rupee.
The latest inflation numbers underline that risk. Headline inflation accelerated sharply to 11.1pc in August from 9.2pc in July, showing how quickly supply-side pressures can return. The SBP acknowledges that inflation risks have risen significantly. This makes monetary policy particularly difficult. Cutting rates now would hardly provide any support to investment and domestic demand. Rather, it would risk adding to external and inflationary pressures if the regional shock intensifies. How inflation and interest rates move in the coming months will largely be determined by energy prices and the duration of the regional disruption. A premature rate cut is not necessary to achieve the modest growth recovery of 3.5-4.5pc, particularly when monetary conditions have already eased substantially from their previous punishing levels. For now, therefore, the continuation of the pause is desirable. The economy has gained some breathing space, but the external environment remains too uncertain for a rate cut. The central bank should preserve its room to respond if the regional crisis produces another oil or balance-of-payment shock. Instead of demanding lower rates at this moment, the business community should be calling for real reforms: the ones required to broaden the tax net, fix the energy sector, ensure policy predictability and improve export competitiveness.

title: Divide and rule?
author: none@none.com (Dr Niaz Murtaza)
content:
LEWIS Carroll set a daunting bar in Through the Looking-Glass: one must run to stay in the same place; to get somewhere one must run twice as fast. How far will our one step forward, two steps back gait take us then? Nations once behind us now run twice as fast to perform 21st-century miracles; our rulers still plod after 19th-century mirages.
The mirage now being sold to end misrule to entice a nation sick of it is creating many provinces. What they will fix is unclear: low growth or poor services? I dug deep into global research to test this idea but got a blunt rebuke from reform sages: more provinces fix neither; adopt sound policies for growth; devolve, not divide, for better public services. But our rulers avoid such steps. Provinces must ideally focus on policy and large projects; however, ours also control local services. Division will create new patronage layers and fragment policy across small areas; it will keep services poor. Devolving power and purse locally will ensure better services and policy coherence. If research evoked rebuke, global practice evokes alarm. The bottom 15 states on the Fragile States Index average five times more first-tier units than us but have populations only one-fifth of ours. Many created new units in one go. Yet, they are the most fragile and misruled states. Needless division may multiply misrule.
Provinces created politically for federal balance and ethnic equity make sense if viable. Punjab comprises over half the federation. The Baloch who form around six per cent of the population have a province; the Seraiki-speaking people, numbering nearly three times as many, do not. A Seraiki unit would improve balance, cutting Punjab’s share to about one-third and being about as big as KP itself.
    
In terms of development, reports rank Seraiki districts far behind Punjab’s dominant ones. But the main minority districts are at par with majority ones in Balochistan and far ahead in Sindh and KP. They would contain nearly 40 million people, big cities like Multan and Bahawalpur, a large agrarian base and be strategically located. A rough review of the net fiscal impact of its NFC share, provincial revenues and Punjab funds lost reveals a small surplus. So, it meets all three tests prima facie. But those based on other minority demands or administrative logic may fail at least two.
What more provinces will fix is unclear.
New provinces require two-thirds votes in parliament and the provincial assembly. A referendum can’t override the Constitution. This makes Sindh’s division hardest given its valid political, fiscal and historical concerns. Bulldozing it via rigged referendums and pliant courts may backfire as, unlike other smaller units, it straddles key trade routes. It rightly said no to the Kalabagh dam and canals project; both remain stalled. The Sindhi-speaking population especially are likely to resist any division. Karachi has huge issues but paradoxical rankings — near-bottom globally among cities; near-top nationally among districts. It exhibits relative individual prosperity and collective adversity. Strong local bodies nationwide will benefit everyone.
    
An Islamabad province would fail at least two tests as a rich region with under 1pc of our population. National capitals globally are usually not made full provinces, more so small ones. Also, a province is just the first step in ensuring equity. So, it is not an ethnicity demanding a province but one that already has one — the Baloch — that is the most aggrieved. Another huge risk is low state capacity for such big changes, evide­­nt even in the much simpler Fata mer­g­­er. New units may emerge on paper but lack capacity, es­­­­pe­­­cially in milita­n­cy-hit regions where terrorists may exploit the void. Lastly, this set-up’s debatable mandate and hybrid status make such changes contentious.
Why do our rulers avoid such systematic analysis and the right policies and sell us only dodgy ideas? Has any set-up ever presented rational policies for public debate, and adopted and implemented them? Only the 18th Amendment and the 1973 Constitution come to mind, both with significant provisos. Nations using top analysts to devise smart policies zoom ahead; we use glib pundits to peddle controversial ideas, and are left trailing behind. Our misrule stems from foundational gaps: lack of legitimate and empowered set-ups. But those blocking them distract us with banal design fixes. Dividing provinces smacks of colonial divide-and-rule ploys. The 26th and 27th Amendments undercut the horizontal balance of power in their favour. A new one may now do so vertically.
The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.

title: Shiny new toys
author: none@none.com (Danyal Adam Khan)
content:
LAST week, an MNA from Islamabad expressed his gratitude to the interior minister for proposing that the capital be given provincial status. The MNA fully backed the minister’s statement, terming this a “long-standing demand of residents of the capital”.
This is intriguing for several reasons, not least of which is that in the list of priorities of the capital’s residents one encounters daily, the ‘long-standing demand’ for a new province is not one that features anywhere, let alone prominently. What Islamabad’s residents have categorically demanded, on the other hand, is not being evicted from their land and having their homes bulldozed, access to affordable housing, piped water connections, a functioning solid and liquid waste management system, and a fully integrated public transport network.
As far as governance architecture goes, the most tangible demand Islamabad has made for years is having an elected local government — not just a tick-box of procedural democracy, but one that is politically, administratively, and fiscally empowered to deliver its mandate too. Ironically, the MNA referencing the democratic aspirations of his constituency belongs to the ruling party which has delayed LG elections in Islamabad four times over the past four years. Each time, this is done ostensibly to strengthen the structure of a system the residents never actually get to experience.
The latest round in this carousel was meant to end in October, when the Election Commission would conclude delimitation and issue an election schedule. However, it is now likely that this will be kicked further down the road as the ruling coalition gears up to introduce a new governance model for Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT). Unlike previous tweaks, this one aims to overhaul the entire system.
Provincial status isn’t a priority for Islamabad’s residents.
For the uninitiated, the proposed ICT governance model creates a ‘province-like’ status for Islamabad by establishing a 27-member elected legislative assembly, including reserved seats. It provides for a chief executive — likely in the form of a chief minister — and probably a governor. There’s a chief secretary, four secretaries, 26 departments, six specialised authorities.
To be fair to this proposal, it has both merits and demerits. Meaningful engagement with the capital’s governance model is long overdue, and this recognition of the need to remedy a fractured system is welcome. There is also much to critique, including the retention of basic powers such as master planning and law and order with the federal government, ambiguities in the executive structure, federal secretaries continuing to govern ICT authorities, and the lack of thought towards reforming fiscal architecture.
Since the proposal is still in the works, much may yet be remedied. However, the fatal flaw is not hidden in the details but buried at the foundations. The model creates an effectively bloated structure at the top, while the decay at the grassroots union councils remains unaddressed. It establishes a legislative assembly, without empowering the LGs whose job it is to provide essential service delivery. It may give political leaders a ribbon to cut and a tangible reform package to point towards, but will it make for better results for the 
residents? Instead of an elaborate new scheme, could more have been achieved by simply extending basic legislative powers to the now-dismembered Metropolitan Corporation of Islamabad?
This aspiration to give Islamabad a ‘province-like’ structure has found support in the nationwide frenzy of new provinces, and an al­­ready bloated pro-
posal may now be pursued beyond its limits. Perhaps the biggest red flag is the confirmation of the earlier perception that this newfound interest in Islamabad’s gover­nance model has something to do with securing an extra NFC share at the centre.
This demand is both half-baked and dangerous. The federal government is responsible for Islamabad in the same way that KP is for Peshawar. If the latter is not demanding a separate slice of the NFC to govern its metropolis, then the former’s 42.5 per cent share should also be sufficient. In case it isn’t, it may finally be time to consider meaningful urban fiscal reform that allows cities like Islamabad to raise own-source revenue, particularly through its overpriced real estate. But that will also require political leaders to take on a state-backed property mafia, and we don’t seem ready for that kind of conversation.
We’ve heard a lot recently about how the devolution of power is inevitable. Instead of carving up the country into new provinces just to see where it may take us, perhaps we might take the obvious route and try empowering LGs first. Perhaps we might try to work with what we already have instead of chasing shiny new toys. 
The writer is a governance specialist working on devolution, cities, and climate.
Published in Dawn, September 15th, 2026
