title: Rethinking relief
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE prime minister’s decision to subsidise petrol purchases for motorcycle and small-car owners is understandable amid consumer outcry against high fuel rates. But it is unlikely to offer much relief.
The Rs75bn package may sound substantial but is barely a fraction of annual petrol sales. Its reach will be narrower because eligibility depends on conditions such as vehicle and SIM ownership. A monthly subsidy of Rs2,000 for motorcycles and Rs3,000 for small cars may help households, but cannot shield them from sustained global oil price increases. Nor does it assist those who rely on public transport. The question that arises is whether the government is trying to soften the political impact of another fuel price shock.
    
The government must rethink the relief architecture. The BISP National Socio-Economic Registry already has a mechanism to target assistance by household income. Additional support through this system would be more equitable than subsidising a particular fuel purchase. Cash transfers are preferable because recipients can decide whether they need petrol, bus fare, food or another essential. Fuel subsidies make that choice for them and risk encouraging consumption of an imported commodity when foreign exchange pressures are rising.
The demand is for a cut in the petroleum levy for broader relief. But the government has little fiscal space for that. Slashing it would create another fiscal hole. Islamabad should, instead, work with the provinces to support public transport users through targeted — and transparent — assistance.
The other problem that subsidies cannot solve concerns rising prices of food and other essentials. Fuel price hikes are passed on by transporters and traders to consumers through higher fares and commodity prices; reductions rarely produce equivalent decreases. Provincial and district administrations must monitor this asymmetric pricing more seriously. The global oil market outlook offers little comfort due to the uncertainty caused by the Middle East conflict. Petrol was around $135 a barrel at the end of last week, against the $120-122 benchmark underlying domestic calculations. Every $1 increase in the global benchmark is estimated to add around Rs1.80 per litre to domestic petrol prices. A sustained $10 rise in annual average oil prices could add $1bn-$1.25bn to Pakistan’s import bill, further draining scarce foreign exchange.
The pressure could intensify in winter as lower hydropower generation increases reliance on imported fuels and raises electricity costs. The government’s dilemma is clear: higher fuel prices fuel inflation and hurt households, while subsidies put pressure on imports and the fiscal deficit. It has no painless option. Relief must therefore follow need, not vehicle ownership. A poor household using public transport deserves no less consideration than a relatively better-off motorcycle or a small car owner.
Published in Dawn, September 15th, 2026

title: Burdens of politicians
author: none@none.com (Arifa Noor)
content:
IT was a humid Sunday afternoon in Islamabad. The small pharmacy was empty with just one man behind the cash counter. A woman approached him, prescription and medicines in hand. She was simply but not shabbily dressed. But she still returned a quarter of the medication once the bill was generated. The man behind the counter explained the bill was around Rs4,000, and she returned about Rs1,000 worth of medication. This took place at a pharmacy in the heart of Islamabad, where real estate sells or rents at eye-watering prices. There was no doctor nearby or a hospital. The woman, chances are, lived close by.
It is not a dramatic story or one that really shocks. Tell it to a group of people and they will nod, and, in fact, recount similar stories. Of people’s difficulties. The loans they have taken. How someone got a utility bill higher than their salary. How a colleague had switched from his car to a motorbike. How another had begun shopping for lower-quality food.
Conversations such as these abound. And this is before the past week when petrol hikes — even those of a daily kind — had begun to hit the headlines. People are now taking bets on when the price of petrol will hit 400 — a far more probable prospect than the cricket team managing a respectable score.
    
That the government realises the impact of the petrol hikes is evident from its announcement to relaunch its subsidy scheme. There is little clarity on how effective the last one had been and how long it lasted, but it’s now back with some tweaks. Ask the government to reduce the petrol levy, and suddenly the big bad IMF enters the conversation; the same IMF which can’t get the government to impose a proper tax on traders or agriculture income or even stop it from giving relief to real estate. Apparently, the petrol levy is the red line.
There is little conversation about what inflationary impact this petrol hike will have.
And of course, there is little conversation about what inflationary impact this petrol hike will have on food, transport and more — what will happen to the electricity bills, and what this new cycle of inflation will do to already weakened purchasing power.
Before the reader rolls her eyes at my audacity to write a piece on the economy, let me clarify that I am about to do no such thing. This is simply going to be a clutch-my-pearls piece on the callousness of the ruling elite. It doesn’t get simpler than that.
    
Long before the Iran war and its impact on the global economy, Pakistan’s human story was already a matter of shame. Our infant mortality rate (46 to 58 deaths per 1,000 births) is higher than the rest of the region and comparable to Afghanistan and Yemen. Nearly 20 per cent of the population has an insufficient caloric intake, and around 40pc of children under five years are malnourished and suffer from stunting — in this, Pakistan is comparable to countries hit by conflict and civil war. The numbers are not recent so as to be linked to the economic mess of the past few years.
This is the real story, with facts and figures, along with our own experiences and the anecdotes we all hear of the suffering of the people. But for those ruling us, there is little empathy or awareness of the crisis. This may seem a bit harsh but what else does one say when governments are incapable of curbing even their own lavish personal lifestyles in the face of human misery?
The prime minister and his deputy, it seems, spend more time abroad than in the country. Newly born babies recently died in a hospital fire in the heart of the capital, petrol is going up faster than pollution, and we already know he is off to New York on the 20th to tell the world about Pakistan’s efforts in mediation. When one’s home is on fire, shouldn’t saving it be more important? A rhetorical question — for soon we will be subjected to a bunch of ministers and advisers walking on the tarmac and entering a plane.
The rest are not far behind. Just recently both the president and the chief minister of Punjab travelled to Europe on personal visits on private planes. And only widespread criticism forced them both to make public the information that the trips were paid for personally. As if anyone needed any more proof of such disconnect from the lives of ordinary Pakistanis.
The president was on a personal visit while the party and the government he heads was announcing war on proposals to divide Sindh. If the situation was that dire politically, shouldn’t he have been in Pakistan and in the province? And the Punjab CM — two-and-a-half years later — does not seem to realise that a display of wealth in these times is just poor judgement. Despite the widespread criticism of the aircraft purchased by the Punjab government, it was used for a personal trip.
However, this criticism is simply water off a duck’s back. The display of a lavish wedding followed all of this. This is not to say that politicians should not be allowed private lives; they have every right to it. However, extensive footage and images displaying the grandeur of an event is simply a poor decision.
No one expects Pakistan’s ruling elite to behave like their counterparts in the West where ministers carry their own baggage and fly economy. We are far too realistic to expect miracles here but a little discretion can do no harm. And for once, it is not enough to argue that there are powerful people in Pakistan who perhaps enjoy even more perks than politicians but are not spoken about.
Indeed, those who take part in electoral exercise and claim to be popular have different burdens than those who simply wield power. And the people in government need to understand this difference.
The writer is a journalist.
Published in Dawn, September 15th, 2026

title: To heal a divided family
author: none@none.com (Jawed Naqvi)
content:
CENTURIES before Charles Darwin theorised our shared human evolution from the fish, multiple traditions linked humanity to a single common fold. The 18th BRICS summit in Delhi saw Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi as the host leaning on the Sanskrit phrase ‘Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam’ — the world is a family — to underpin the spirit of unity, which unfortunately eludes much of mankind. The ancient aphorism is a good but an overstretched reminder of seeing everybody as an equal human being. Some would say that there was perhaps a greater need to find a phrase that frames all Indians as one family before stretching it to include the world. A problem with citing one’s ancient aphorisms at international conferences is that it begins to resemble the Sadda Mian complex.
Sadda Mian was a roundly admired elderly Afghan member of Bhopal’s royal family. He wou­­ld walk along the promenade abutting Bhopal’s vast lake called Bhadbhada, which, he decided, was the largest water body in the world. Another characteristic unique to Sadda Mian was that he fed his domesticated quails with his mouth, tucking the tiny grains of food behind the lower lip. The late thespian Dilip Kumar told me about his invitation to Sadda Mian to visit Bombay where the actor took the genial Pathan to watch the Arabian Sea from the city’s Marine Drive. Sadda Mian, his sherwani unbuttoned and fluttering in the breeze, was so awestruck by the sea’s expanse that he exclai­med gently: “Kya haqeeqat hai Bhadbhade ki!” Sadda Mian’s dumbfounded response translates as: ‘Where does any Bhadbhada hold a chance!’
    
I looked up a few random traditions from across the lands and seas that don’t seem too different in the spirit of acknowledging the world as a family. But few among them, if any, would be found jumping ecstatically as Newton did watching an apple fall from a tree. There was a time in the early days of Narendra Modi’s rule that the foreign ministry printed and distributed copies of the Bhagavad Gita to foreign dignitaries. In the bargain, the ministry displaced coffee-table books of the Taj, Ajanta caves and Madurai temples. I am not aware of Israel handing out the Torah, or the Vatican presenting the Bible to esteemed visitors, nor does Saudi Arabia or Iran make it a point to offer return gifts of the Holy Quran to visiting dignitaries. Or for that matter, would a privileged guest, returning from China, come home with an officially gifted copy of Mao Zedong Thoughts, or more recently Xi Jinping Thoughts? I bought the Xi book on Amazon.
If the world is a family, which it is, talking to the neighbour and sorting out the problem bilaterally is mature.
So yes, the world is a family, but what kind of a family? The BRICS summit sought to address some aspects of the troubling question but, by all accounts, it’s going to be a long trudge. Modi said BRICS has come of age — in the sense that the leaders of the UAE and Iran agreeing to meet and not pressing their case too hard to enable a summit statement was an achievement. One could have accepted the condemnation of the terror attack in Pahalgam and reference to cross-border terrorism as a victory for India. But Pakistan had condemned the attack too. Actually, the BRICS summit in Xiamen in 2017 had gone several steps further when under President Xi’s stewardship it named some extremist outfits allegedly based in Pakistan together with Taliban groups and local security elements for censure.
If the world is a family, which it is, talking to the neighbour and sorting out the problem bilaterally is mature. The world brotherhood will applaud. And, yes, the word ‘family’ loses its meaning when someone is seen standing with an aggressor like Israel and visits the country on the eve of Israel’s assassination of a revered supreme leader of a far friendlier country. Also, if the world is a family, let’s stop patronising lynch mobs against fellow humans everywhere. It’s not unlikely that the BRICS summit’s statement slamming Israel’s occupation of Lebanon was a sign of the coming of age.
Xi Jinping dominated the show. He said BRICS should become a peacemaker. There needs to be peace within the family. Looking objectively at the idea of global brotherhood with all its warts and wrinkles, the Nehruvian ideal of non-alignment was quite representative of the quest. But Xi, too, has made a forceful intervention to make BRICS more proactive in its quest for global brotherhood. And he stated that BRICS must be a “pioneer in upholding peace and stability”, emphasising that the group needs to actively manage global hotspot issues by addressing both their symptoms and root causes. He clearly outlined a four-point plan for West Asia, focusing on peaceful coexistence, respect for national sovereignty, adhering to international law, and regional development. It was Xi who reiterated the necessity of pushing for an immediate ceasefire at all the hotspots in West Asia to establish a lasting two-state solution for Palestine to resolve the nub of the crisis.
Unlike the Sanskrit phrase cited by Modi, which seems ornamental and ill-fitting given India’s domestic and foreign entanglements with strife, the ancient South African ideal of Ubuntu very crucially was at play when apartheid was dismantled in the country. Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu leaned on the Zulu phrase ‘Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu’. Strikingly similar to the Sanskrit worldview, Ubuntu assured every race and community in the country of equity and equality. The phrase literally means: ‘A person is a person through other persons’ or ‘I am because we are’. The Abrahamic scriptures carry similar messages of a united mankind. The Galatians 3:28 in the Bible says: “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” This isn’t dissimilar to India’s Maha Upanishad defining narrow-mindedness as calculating ‘this person is a relative, that one is a stranger’. A tricky proposition for Modi to grasp.
The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.

title: Showing empathy
author: none@none.com (Huma Yusuf)
content:
ON the 100-day anniversary of the Oct 7, 2023, attack by Hamas against Israel, and after 25,000 Palestinians had been killed by Israel’s retaliatory strikes, then US president Joe Biden made a shocking statement: “I will never forget the grief and the suffering I have heard in my meetings with the families of the American hostages. No one should have to endure even one day of what they have gone through, much less 100.”
His statement did not reference the thousands of slaughtered Palestinians, including women and children, or the intentional targeting of hospitals and journalists. Nor did it acknowledge the International Court of Justice hearings that had begun days prior to investigate allegations of Israeli war crimes. The statement was derided as “shameful” by Barnett Rubin, a US foreign policy expert who knew Biden from their time in the Obama administration.
Biden’s one-sided statement is flagged in a new book, Crossing the Red Line, by award-winning Pakistani journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed, which documents how the Biden administration enabled Israeli atrocities in Gaza, and set the stage for the widening of the Middle East conflict during the current Trump administration.
In a book filled with examples of US negligence and complicity in breaches of international law in Gaza, this example resonates. Speaking last week at a book launch event, Ahmed used the example to illustrate Biden’s tunnel vision when it came to the Israel-Palestine conflict, specifically his inability to acknowledge the plight of Palestinians. In Biden’s and his administration’s perspective, all Palestinian children killed were the children of Hamas fighters; reports of famine in Gaza were exaggerated; schools and hospitals were Hamas hideouts; and intelligence or humanitarian reports suggesting otherwise were forced to caveat findings or report selectively.
The need for engagement is too often simplified.
The president’s inability to humanise Palestinians or empathise with their predicament was, Ahmed argued, a determinant of the US’s Israel policy and its failure to curtail Israeli transgressions. He highlighted a key reason for this lack of empathy: the US administration barely had any interaction with Palestinians. Although there was robust engagement with Israelis, Ahmed reports there were only five State Department officials in direct contact with Palestinians.
Of all the avoidable tragedies Ahmed’s work highlights, the fact that you need to talk to people on the other side of a conflict to remember that they are human, truly resonates. That recognition of humanity is then enshrined in policy and decision-making.
This need for engagement is too often simplified and understood as the need for backchannels during a crisis. No doubt, informal, person-to-person contact is invaluable when de-escalation is required. Recall the secret meetings that avoided nuclear war during the Cuban Missile Crisis or — closer to home — the DGMO hotline that prevented the May 2025 Pakistan-India conflict from escalating further.
But backchannels cannot substitute for broader diplomatic and societal engagement, the type that goes past mere coordination to empathic connection; the type the Americans have in place with Israel, but did not bother to develop with Palestine, even at the height of humanitarian crisis during the darkest days of the Gaza war. It is a point that should be emphasised in the context of mainstream diplomacy at a time when most Western governments are reducing global diplomatic staff and closing embassies, usually as a cost-cutting measure, leaving them with few personal touch points in regions in perma-crisis.
But these lessons also apply domestically. The political polarisation of Western countries is increasingly attributed to a breakdown of engagement between urban and rural residents, the rich and the poor, and between different racial and ethnic communities. This, in turn, is blamed on everything from the isolation wrought by social media to the claw-back of government funding for community spaces.
We are not absolved from complicity closer to home. It is difficult to imagine Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz making the divisive comments she did about threats to Punjab primarily emanating from regional provinces without years of political suppression and polarised rhetoric between provinces, particularly with Balochistan and KP.
Without more access and engagement, compatriots cannot empathise with each other’s challenges. That engagement should be encouraged across all levels of provincial governments, but equally across society, whether in the form of more scholarships, economic ties, tourism, arts engagement or the lifting of media censorship. Without engaging, we’re in danger of forgetting each other’s humanity, and so exacerbating rather than allaying tensions. 
The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.

title: Extraction and delivery
author: none@none.com (Umair Javed)
content:
AS the debate on changing provincial boundaries and decentralisation rages on, it is worth taking a step back to see what is at stake here. What are the main problems that require attention and which have made several people, including entrenched insiders, declare that the current system is ‘broken’?
The biggest issue being sidestepped by everyone involved (except opposition parties) remains constitutional rule and legitimacy of the state. The current discourse chooses to ignore this, considering it either taboo or a foregone conclusion. Bringing it up seems particularly futile in this discussion given how little it bears on those making decisions and increasingly with those tasked with interrogating these decisions.
    
The second issue is macroeconomic growth, or the absence thereof. What changes are needed to the form of the state that can help kickstart broad-based and sustained capital accumulation? What needs to be done to make the state fiscally more viable?
The third issue is social development, and the slowdown in improvement of basic education, health, and other human capability-related indicators. What strategy or approach will help break through the current plateau, marked by a slowdown in literacy rate improvement, a persistently large number of out-of-school children, poor learning outcomes, and no considerable progress on health indicators?
When the interior minister talks about a system collapse, the primary subject of this collapse is the state. The Pakistani state, like every other modern state, is engaged in a variety of tasks, none of which it seems to be doing too well. Broadly these tasks can be clubbed under two domains — extraction (getting something from its population) and delivery (doing something for or to the population). There is a third domain — regulation (setting boundaries or implementing rules for various things that private actors may be doing) — as well but we’ll keep that to one side for now.
There is no one-size-fits-all approach for the many developmental challenges confronting Pakistan today.
The historical record on extraction and delivery is generally poor. Extracting taxes from anyone other than a captive population has proven to be a challenge. Regulating private behaviour, from polluting emissions to urban sprawl to inter-gender interactions, has been difficult as well. And delivering basic services — law and order, education, health — remains highly uneven across rural-urban and provincial lines.
If one thinks about the state as the core of a governing system, the track record so far provides ample grounds for a complete overhaul. But a key question to ask is: do all of these functions require an overhaul of the same type?
It is possible to look at the exceedingly few examples of success on part of the state in each domain as a blueprint of sorts for what works, especially when thinking about administrative changes.
What type of extraction has the state done well and where has it failed? In recent years, the state has done a ‘good’ job of getting people to pay for expensive electricity at cost, rather than delay tariff revisions or provide blanket subsidies. This is an example of a reform that is not really productivity enhancing, but it is certainly something that the state was not doing a decade and a half ago.
    
Similarly, the state has been successful at extracting more taxes from the formal sector and the salaried segment of the population in recent years. This is both by raising the tax rate and by making it ever difficult for the formal sector to avoid its share through an entrenched withholding tax regime. This has happened even while the state has failed to bring many sections of the population into the tax net.
When we review the evidence on what enables some types of extraction over others, the absence of discretion and fragmentation of functions comes out as a possible factor. In the case of electricity bills and withholding taxes, the state has centralised collection and removed discretion from its own functions. Local state functionaries have some leeway, sure, but by and large people have no option but to comply and pay directly to the state. In contrast, where economic activity has to be documented by state functionaries themselves (ie, a situation of increased discretion) local politics and influence come into play.
On the other hand, the evidence on delivery points in the opposite direction. The biggest gains in social development took place during times of greater decentralisation. When schools were being managed at the school council/local level, improvements in literacy rates and enrolment happened at a faster rate. Similarly, greater autonomy for basic health units and hospitals (with requisite oversight) allowed them to respond to actual patient-level challenges more effectively.
Even in delivering basic municipal infrastructure — sanitation and sewage, roadworks — decentralised decision-making and expenditure (between 2002-2008) proved to be more effective.
Since province-level centralisation took hold in 2011, gains in key delivery areas of health and education have slowed down. In some parts of the country, outcomes have stagnated altogether. The challenge of delivering to hard-to-access populations has become far more acute.
Given this admittedly speculative review of patterns in both extraction and delivery, it is clear there is no one-size-fits-all approach for the many developmental challenges confronting Pakistan today. In domains of extraction, there is an urgent need to reduce discretion and fragmentation of state authority, perhaps even with the use of automated structures in whatever form.
In delivery related domains, we likely need even more discretion and fragmentation of the state, via substantive decentralisation that devolves decision-making and accountability down to the level where delivery is supposed to take place.
The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums.

title: Political disconnect
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
THE disconnect between the government and public concerns could not be starker. While people worry about their economic situation the government is focused on altering the country’s provincial structure. According to the latest Ipsos poll, three in four people believe the country is headed in the wrong direction. The economy and especially inflation are their top concerns. A majority of respondents also said they do not view the economy as strong.
It is this low public confidence and pessimism about the future that should concern the government rather than seeking to redraw the provincial map for ill-defined objectives. So far it hasn’t offered any coherent rationale for carving out more provinces. It has also not conducted any study on an issue of such consequence.
    
Although speculation had long been rife about the hybrid government’s intentions it was Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi who made a public pitch for new provinces in July. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal went further, calling for 15 additional provinces. Each province, he said, should be subdivided into three. As an alternative, he proposed 160 district governments. He argued that establishing more administrative units would deliver effective governance and better social outcomes.
The proposal provoked a furious response from the ruling party’s ally, PPP, which opposed any plan to divide Sindh. The party got the Sindh Assembly to adopt a resolution rejecting the division of the province or creation of new administrative units. The MQM, which has long wanted Karachi as a separate province, boycotted the session. It said its proposals were not incorporated in the resolution, including establishing new administrative units. The resolution declared “Sindh is one and shall remain one” and “unequivocally rejected any proposal, plan, scheme or constitutional arrangement … which sought to divide Sindh … or create any new province out of its territory”.
Technical fixes are no panacea that will miraculously solve the country’s problems.
The government’s attempt to start a debate seemed to flounder and spin out of control after its key coalition partner came out in strong opposition. A senior PPP leader questioned Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s silence and asked him to state his position publicly. Another PPP leader accused federal ministers pushing for new provinces of having a “fake mandate”. Meanwhile, PML-N ministers themselves issued contradictory statements. Rather than clarifying matters, this compounded the confusion and exposed divisions within the party. Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz is also said to be opposed to any division of her province.
    
The joint parliamentary opposition comprising PTI, JUI-F and other smaller parties rejected any plan to divide provinces at its inaugural meeting in late August. Earlier, JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman argued this was not the time to divide provinces given the country’s troubled economic and security situation. PTI is now planning a multiparty conference of the opposition on the issue. The party itself has yet to enunciate a clear public position. In the past, it advocated creating a new province in south Punjab. Some PTI leaders say the party opposes changes under “an illegitimate and fraudulent set-up”. The party chairman, however, has urged consultations and said any hasty decision would “harm the federation”. Meanwhile, the leader of the National Party in Balochistan has said creating new provinces would only exacerbate present tensions.
None of this has deterred federal ministers from continuing to insist on administrative restructuring. Mohsin Naqvi declared this was essential and no one can stop it. But he added it will only happen with the “will of the people”. He wasn’t walking back from his proposal. His statement implied a referendum might be held to ascertain the ‘will of the people’. Such a move would be deeply controversial and divisive. It would also lack credibility given the history of dubious referendums conducted by past military governments. Questions have also been raised about whether a referendum can constitutionally be used to create new provinces.
Proponents of ‘reform’ in the hybrid government ignore the fact that their proposal has already divided the country. It is clear that there is no political consensus on the issue. Consensus cannot be manufactured or coerced. While the government has rammed controversial constitutional amendments and other laws through parliament, using the same method to reorder the provincial structure carries much greater risks. Given the far-reaching consequences of the change and the opposition it faces across the country, the implications would be serious. If pursued, it would further undermine national cohesion and deepen polarisation.
    
There is a clear constitutional procedure to change provincial boundaries. A referendum cannot override that. Any change requires two steps. First a resolution passed by a two-thirds majority in the relevant provincial assembly. Second a constitutional amendment adopted by a two-thirds majority in both the National Assembly and Senate. This effectively gives affected provinces a veto over any change. This requirement cannot be bypassed. Any political manoeuvre to circumvent this will be a disaster.
There is no doubt that the governance system needs to be improved. Government should be brought closer to the people to ensure their voices are heard and for better service delivery. But this goal can be realised by empowering local government. It is the third tier of government that needs to be strengthened through functional local bodies as mandated by the Constitution.
Improving governance requires more than a technical fix. Above all, it demands an environment grounded in the rule of law. It needs accountability of both leaders and institutions. Administrative changes cannot substitute for competent leadership — with a clear vision and sense of purpose — who are legitimately elected. Good governance also requires prudent policies and much-needed economic reforms shaped and overseen by capable professionals.
This is not an argument against administrative change. It is an effort to emphasise three points. First, drawing new provincial lines is not a panacea that will miraculously solve the country’s problems. As noted above, other aspects of governance matter far more. Map-drawing and not fixing fundamentals is meaningless. Second, such changes do not figure among the public’s governance concerns, which are very different. Ignoring those priorities and focusing just on technical fixes will only show how out of touch the government is with people. Third, without broad national consensus, imposing administrative changes will make a mockery of democracy and serve to divide the country.
The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.

title: Road to dignity
author: none@none.com (Zafar U. Ahmed)
content:
IN Pakistan’s recent history, billionaire bankers and former staff of multilateral institutions, among others, have led national development. After assuming office as finance minister, one was alleged to have declared that he empathised with ordinary people and then promptly imposed a tax on baby food in a country where, due to malnutrition, 40 per cent of children are stunted. The results are hardly what we had hoped for.
How, then, should national development policy be made? Let us take a hypothetical case of a recently formed country, its borders determined by departing colonialists. It is not a ‘civilisational state’ with thousands of years of shared history, so the allegiance and love of its people should now be earned.
There must be a clear rationale for forming the new country. A civilised society might agree that its rationale is the welfare of its citizens: people come together to improve their standard of living, to have equal opportunity to reach their full potential, and to live by their values. The citizens are to pay a share of their income to a common fund, from which the state would administer services to all, such as education, healthcare, support for economic endeavour and security. The country must be sovereign and independent.
If the former colonialists offered to guide and direct the new country’s development, surely they would be spurned: after 200 years of ruthless exploitation, they could hardly be trusted. While the people’s priorities are likely to be efficient agriculture and affordable food, quality education and skills training, healthcare and economic development, outsiders might want to prioritise gender issues and preparedness for future disasters.
Policy must be made by those who represent the people.
Conventionally, to pay for imports such as oil, gas and advanced machinery, a country has to earn international currency through exports. If imports were double the exports, that would be untenable. The country would then have to take loans from foreign sources on conditions that absolutely compromise its sovereignty. Even multilateral institutions have voting systems firmly controlled by the West. At the IMF, for instance, Pakistan has 0.43pc of the vote, Russia 2.59pc, China 6.08pc, and the US 16.5pc, besides the votes of all its ‘loyal allies’.
To be sovereign, the country would focus its exports on markets where its products — including new ones beyond traditional leather goods, towels and the like — were more likely to find acceptance. A developing country’s products are more likely to be accepted in the Global South, among other developing countries that are more price-sensitive and less demanding about quality. It should try to exchange goods in national currencies or through a swap arrangement. The country would not implore its former colonial masters to grant it limited market access — as a great favour — that could be rescinded over any supposed breach, with sanctions imposed.
The country would encourage innovative, efficient and cost-effective production. Open and fair competition would bring forward businesspeople capable of competing internationally. Surely, ‘crony’ business groups with no merit beyond maintaining relationships with decision-makers would not be tolerated. Nor would rules be made or changed to benefit particular businesspeople, or unjustified subsidies and concessions be granted to them. Where a subsidy was justified, proportionate shares and profits would go to the state.
Taking full advantage of its border with a great power — the world’s manufacturing centre — the developing country would offer every facility to serve as a goods-processing hub, especially in its coastal regions.
The key lessons are clear: policy ought to be made by people who understand and represent the people, not by narrowly focused technical specialists. A country’s national development policy must be predicated on an agreed direction — its rationale, and the people’s priorities, needs and values. Not foreign donor agendas. The country’s economic transformation requires open and fair business competition. ‘Cronyism’ sabotages it. Focus exports on the Global South and make every effort to exchange goods in national currencies or through similar arrangements. Especially in the coastal zones, offer every facility for goods processing from the bordering great power. Incentivise officials by aligning promotions with the performance of the areas they serve.
This is a time of great opportunity for the Global South. The global power balance and systems are changing — a change so fundamental that nothing comparable has happened in hundreds of years. Pakistan must tailor its public policy to the changing environment to achieve its national development goals and pursue national sovereignty and dignity. 
The writer is the author of Pakistan: Principles of Public Policy Redefined.
Published in Dawn, September 14th, 2026

title: Britain’s liberal establishment
author: none@none.com (Nadir Cheema)
content:
THE opera Die Entführung aus dem Serail (The Abduction from the Seraglio) by Mozart composed in 1782, was superbly produced at Glyndebourne this summer. One reviewer noted that, since the opera embodies the late 18th-century fascination with “all things Oriental”, the director sets it in the period of its composition, “largely discounting historical anachronisms and showing less interest in cultural value judgements”.
This remark is revealing of how British conservative — with a small ‘c’ — intellectuals view what they describe as the hegemony of liberals across public spheres and institutions, labelling them the ‘liberal British establishment’. For them, political correctness has gone too far; conformity with liberal values is ‘woke’. Pakistani intellectuals tend to socialise largely with their liberal-left British peers.
The terms ‘liberal elite’ and ‘cosmopolitan eli­te’ increasingly serve as metaphors for groups that have prospered from globalisation, the Euro­pean Union project, and the post-Second World War global liberal order. Brexit and the rise of the far-right Reform Party have epitomised resentment towards this established ‘liberal’ political class. Institutions such as the BBC, elite universities including Oxford and Cambridge, and even the British civil service are often perceived as standard-bearers of the domestic liberal establishment.
One also encounters claims that PhD humanities funding for work on straight, white men has become harder to secure; that young academics researching conservative themes face limited prospects because of liberal-left dominance in academia.
Criticising liberal cultural values as ‘woke’ whilst divorcing them from the economic consequences of neoliberalism offers no answers.
Conservative critics see ‘woke’ culture as a pendulum that has swung too far. There is also an argument that Britain has failed the white working class. This was reflected in the fall of the so-called Labour Party ‘Red Wall’ in the formerly industrial British Midlands, as sections of the white working class deserted Labour for Reform in recent local elections. The Conservatives have also lost heavily to Reform.
Far-right parties such as Reform, however, offer few solutions to the real economic causes of this political rupture. Instead, they capitalise on working-class grievances, galvanising support around issues such as migration. The white working class lagging behind is perhaps the only valid strand of the far-right argument. This is because the proverbial trickle-down effect of the neoliberal economic model did not reach the working classes, regardless of race, resulting in the unevenly distributed proceeds of economic growth.
Margaret Thatcher, portrayed as an apostle of neoliberalism, was convinced that Milton Fried­man’s monetarism was a “scientific doctrine”. Yet in 2003, Friedman himself admitted to the Financial Times that “the use of quantity of money as a target has not been a success”. Neoliberals failed to fulfil their promise that working classes would catch up after the initial inequalities, a claim that is central to the idea of economic progress under capitalism.
Yet neoliberalism survived the 2008 Great Financial Crisis. Conservative prime minister Liz Truss was punished by financial markets for her unfunded tax cuts in 2022. Andy Burnham became prime minister promising to address regional inequalities, but he had to calm the bond markets even before entering parliament after his previous statement that “this country should not be in hock to the bond markets” sent jitters through the markets.
In the US, the rise of Zohran Mamdani, the New York mayor, and President Donald Trump reflects a similar disconnect between cosmopolitans and the country. While Mamdani’s victory is celebrated by liberals and progressives, they need to reckon with the fact that it is also a symptom of the widening gulf.
Academics and public intellectuals are trying to grapple with the rise of right-wing populism, particularly in the West. Some draw analogies with Europe’s mid-14th-century social and political crises, in the aftermath of Black Death, the Hundred Years’ War between England and France, and peasant revolts in both countries.
Other writers draw on Hugh Trevor-Roper’s 1959 essay, The General Crisis of the 17th Century. As Alan Wooldridge argues, Brexit Britain resembles Oliver Cromwell’s Roundhead Britain: small towns and the countryside resenting elite institutions. Contemporary populists rail against elites much as Cromwell and his supporters opposed the court, believing that elites embrace global rather than national values. Anglo-Catholicism was once a marker of sophistication, while university degrees serve a similar function today to court connections in the 17th century.
Some draw parallels with 1930s populism, which contributed to the rise of Hitler and Mussolini, and was fomented by the economic crisis that ensued from the Great Depression of 1929.
But the problem with neoliberalism is deeper. Criticising liberal cultural values as ‘woke’ whilst divorcing them from the economic consequences of neoliberalism offers no answers; it merely reinforces the far-right narrative against ‘woke’ culture. The attack on liberalism and the Enlighten­ment project has been mounted by postmodernists, structuralists and poststructuralists, conser­vatives, socialists, nationalists, multiculturalists, communitarians and even libertarians, who share ancestry with classical liberalism.
While historical populism analogies and critiques of liberalism may have merit, revisiting liberalism’s evolution over the past two centuries may better explain today’s political rupture. As I previously wrote in these pages, the rise of a mass working class during the late 19th and early 20th centuries — a product of the Industrial Revolution — brought profound socioeconomic shifts and heightened inequality. Modern liberals recognised that classical principles of mere physical freedom were no longer sufficient. They began advocating state-provided social welfare to enable individuals to realise their potential — a modern understanding of ‘freedom’. Figures such as John Stuart Mill can be seen as transitional figures bridging classical liberalism and modern social liberalism. Neoliberals would do well to revisit how earlier liberals embraced social welfare in response to rising inequality.
The English upper classes who gather at the opera may have a point: centuries-old traditions deserve to be preserved and experienced within the cultural worlds that gave them meaning. Yet they must also confront an uncomfortable irony — that they have prospered from economic liberalism, and that liberalism, taken as a whole, carries cultural values that may strike its conservative critics as distinctly ‘woke’.
The writer teaches economics at SOAS, University of London, and is associated with Bloomsbury Pakistan.

title: Terrible 9/11
author: none@none.com (Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry)
content:
THE 11th day of September, 2001 (9/11), started out as an ordinary day in bustling New York. As residents headed to work, the first plane struck one of the twin towers of the World Trade Centre at 8.46 am. Minutes later, another plane hit the second one. A third plane hit the Pentagon building while a fourth was downed in Pennsylvania. This was a massive terrorist attack against what was then the world’s sole superpower. An ordinary day had turned into a watershed moment for global geopolitics. So much changed so rapidly.
First, transnational terrorism emerged on top of the global priority list. Prompted by the US, the UN Security Council ado­p­ted on Sept 28, 2001, Resolution 1373, which bound all member states to prevent, suppress, and criminalise the financing of terrorism. A few years later, Resolution 1540 was adopted by the UNSC, obliging member states to prevent non-state actors from acquiring weapons of mass destruction. Thus evolved a comprehensive global ecosystem against non-state actors carrying out terrorist attacks anywhere in the world.
Second, the US and Nato countries launched a ferocious attack against Taliban-led Afghanistan, which had given refuge to Al Qaeda, the group the US held responsible for 9/11. This embroiled Washington in a war that became its longest since the end of World War II. With Pakistan’s help, the US was able to eliminate the Al Qaeda leadership, except for Osama bin Laden, who was killed later in 2011. However, the US war against the Taliban dragged on with no success. The US tried to blame Pakistan for its military defeat in Afghanistan because of the support that the Taliban had allegedly received. Pakistan’s view all along was that this issue should be resolved via political means.
    
The US later took Pakistan’s advice and concluded a peace deal with the Taliban in February 2020, but did not take the second piece of advice regarding a responsible withdrawal. Instead, it abruptly withdrew its troops from Afghanistan in August 2021, creating a vacuum that was filled by the Taliban rather than an interim government comprising all Afghan factions. Further, the US left behind massive arms and ammunition, which have since been used for terrorism by entities like the TTP and BLA. Sadly, 25 years after 9/11, Afghanistan is once again a sanctuary for global terrorists.
Third, barely two years after 9/11, the US decided to invade Iraq to destroy alleged weapons of mass destruction. This attack set a dangerous precedent of using force illegally (not sanctioned by the UNSC) and pre-emptively, ie, merely on suspicion. This precedent has since been followed by other powers against their adversaries, as seen in the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2014 and 2022 and India’s aggression against Pakistan in 2016, 2019, and 2025. Armed conflicts have now expanded to every corner of the world. According to the ICRC, there are 130 active armed conflicts worldwide.
The events of 9/11 changed so much so rapidly.
Fourth, Pakistan became the front-line state in the US-led global war against terrorism, mainly because America needed Pakistan’s help in fighting Al Qaeda based in neighbouring Afghanistan. Pakistan ended up not only having to deal with infiltrating terrorists and extremists from Afghanistan but also prosecuting extremist outfits that had taken root in the country ever since the days of the so-called Afghan jihad of the 1980s. Pakistan thus found itself “in the line of fire” — the title of Gen Musharraf’s book.
    
Fifth, the events of 9/11 provided India a self-serving opportunity to team up with the West against so-called radical Islam and project itself as a victim of what New Delhi alleged was Pakistan-sponsored terrorism in Indian-occupied Kashmir. India also used the occasion to cast the Kashmiri struggle for the right to self-determination as transnational terrorism.
Sixth, the new concept ‘responsibility to protect’ was born, with powerful countries arguing that if a state’s leadership was unable or unwilling to protect its own people, then it became the responsibility of the international community to protect them. Using this concept, the West intervened in several Arab countries to bring about regime change. This was described as ‘Arab Spring’, but, as time showed, the events destabilised the entire Middle East and turned out to be an ‘Arab autumn’.
The terrorist incidents of 9/11 profoundly changed global and regional geopolitics. The era of globalisation became the first casualty. The use of force emerged as the main arbiter of international disputes.
The definition between freedom struggle and terrorism was blurred. Multilateralism was marginalised and international law violated with impunity. The world disorder that one sees today is rooted in what happened on 9/11 — that fateful September day.
The writer is chairman Sanober Institute and former foreign secretary of Pakistan.
Published in Dawn, September 13th, 2026

title: Pakistan: 25 years post-2001
author: none@none.com (Muhammad Amir Rana)
content:
THE terrorist events of Sept 11, 2001, changed the world and brought about a new security order. Social engineering took place on a large scale, especially within Muslim societies. Conflict erupted across Africa and Asia, often linked to terrorism. These developments triggered large-scale migration towards the West and strengthened the far right in Western societies. Populism took multiple forms.
In short, the world changed course, and an era of increasingly controlled societies emerged, affecting technology, the economy, mobility and politics.
The 25th anniversary of the tragic incident has triggered a debate: what has the world gained and lost since these events, and what kind of world em­­erged in their aftermath? This question is equally important for Pakistan, as it became a front-line state in the global war against terrorism.
Pakistan’s 25-year experience can perhaps be summarised in one sentence: the country has fai­led to defeat terrorism completely, lost Afgha­nis­tan, witnessed weakened internal cohesion, experienced the rise of authoritarianism, and its economy remains in disarray.
    
The return of the Taliban to power in Afghanistan in 2021 contributed to renewed challenges, particularly from the banned TTP. Meanwhile, Balochistan remains another major security theatre, with separatist groups targeting security forces, infrastructure, and Chinese interests.
Economically, Pakistan received billions of dollars in US assistance and Coalition Support Funds but failed to convert this geopolitical opportunity into lasting economic transformation. Terrorism imposed enormous costs through loss of life, reduced investment, damaged infrastructure, and increased security expenditure.
However, Pakistan has also achieved significant strategic successes. Before 9/11, Pakistan was under sanctions because of its nuclear tests. The Kargil conflict had contributed to political instability and military rule, and Pakistan experienced some global isolation. After September 2001, however, Pakistan emerged from isolation to become a front-line ally of the US in its global ‘war on terror’. Pakistan was later designated a major non-Nato ally. However, this partnership came to be characterised by mistrust, particular­ly over Afghanistan, terrorist sanctuaries, drone strikes, and the 2011 Abbottabad operation.
The country’s biggest achievements and major failures have been in counterterrorism.
Pakistan’s biggest achievements and major failures have been in counterterrorism. Through operations including Rah-i-Raast, Rah-i-Nijaat, Zarb-i-Azb, and Raddul Fasaad, Pakistan dismantled major terrorist sanctuaries. It ended the ability of terrorist groups to exercise territorial control in areas such as Swat and the former tribal districts.
In foreign relations, Pakistan strengthened its strategic partnership with China and expanded ties with the Gulf countries and Türkiye, but its relations with Afghanistan have remained deeply problematic.
While it took nearly two decades to fully abandon the use of radical and militant proxies on the external and internal political fronts, two factors played an important role. First, international pressure forced the establishment to take measures against militant groups such as Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed. Second, many members of such groups became disillusioned and joined the TTP, Al Qaeda, and IS-K, making it increasingly difficult for security operators to treat and manage these networks separately.
Although these groups are no longer openly active in militancy, they still shoulder political and diplomatic baggage. India frequently exploits this issue to confront Pakistan at the diplomatic level and has used it to build pressure against Pakistan, contributing directly to the military confrontation last year.
However, the international community increasingly recognises Pakistan’s efforts to overcome its terrorism problem, and India’s terrorism narrative against Pakistan appears to be losing some of its effectiveness internationally.
Over the last 25 years, terrorism has emerged as a core problem for the country, while counterterrorism has become one of its key strengths.
Pakistan remains among the countries most affected by terrorism. Security concerns have negatively impacted Pakistan-China relations, especially CPEC. At the same time, counterterrorism has provided an avenue for cooperation between the US and Pakistan, and since President Donald Trump took office, the two have developed greater synergy against IS-K and in dealing with the Taliban, apart from their multilevel engagement in the Gulf region. In this re-engagement, Pakistan has lost the strategic vision for Afghanistan that Gen Ziaul Haq and his predecessors had crafted.
Terrorism and counterterrorism have changed the country’s structure. Counterterrorism has created an imbalance of power, as civilian governments gradually handed over internal and external security affairs to the establishment and re­­frained from interfering in order to avoid friction. As a result, political engineering became more convenient for the establishment. Social and political engineering have also changed society and left it without direction. Terrorism remai­­ns a major obstacle to attracting foreign investment into the country, yet Pakistan’s counterterrorism capabilities have become a strength that allows it to engage with Western and Asian countries.
    
From Gen Pervez Musharraf onwards, military leaders have tried to take credit for the counterterrorism efforts. Yet it is paradoxical that very few acknowledged terrorism as an indigenous problem rooted partly in previous state policies of nurturing militant proxies. In alliance with the clergy, these policies created an infrastructure of extremism in the country. Religious groups were used for multiple purposes — from advancing nationalist projects to acting as pressure groups. Their perception of terrorism was simplistic, and simplistic approaches produced poor policies and flawed strategies.
During these years, Pakistan lost 75,366 people, including 3,189 soldiers, 2,598 FC personnel, 3,599 police officers, and 26,547 civilians, apart from casualties in other security institutions. Pakistan launched 2,961 military operations, both medium- and large-scale, against terrorists, in addition to several other types of military operations against terrorism.
The country has established dedicated counterterrorism institutions, including Nacta (lately in the news for another reason), counter-extremism centres, NFTIC, and others. Pakistan has also produced 13 policy documents, ranging from the National Action Plan and National Security Policy to Paigham-i-Pakistan.
After all these sacrifices, operations, institutions, and policy documents, is Pakistan still searching for a new counterterrorism policy?
The writer is a security analyst.
Published in Dawn, September 13th, 2026

title: Smog response
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PUNJAB’S decision to begin fighting smog before the air turns poisonous deserves support. For years, the province’s response to winter pollution has too often appeared reactive: schools close, outdoor activity is restricted and emergency measures follow once Lahore’s air becomes hazardous. The latest “pre-smog crackdown”, targeting construction dust, dry sweeping, crop-residue and waste burning, brick kilns, and vehicle emissions, is therefore a sensible change in approach. Some of the new steps are practical: ending dry sweeping, requiring wet or mechanical cleaning, covering construction material, checking vehicle emissions and using technology to identify violations can reduce avoidable pollution. Making dust-control compliance at construction sites a condition of project approval would be useful, provided penalties apply equally to public and private projects. Likewise, farmers should be helped to dispose of crop residue through modern machinery rather than simply punished for burning it; enforcement without affordable alternatives will invite evasion. The real test, however, is implementation. Punjab already has rules against waste burning, emissions standards and dust-control protocols, yet the EPA itself says inspections in Lahore found poor compliance at several development projects despite SOPs issued last year. That should temper official claims of progress.
Punjab must resist treating smog as a three-month problem. Transport, industry, waste management and urban construction pollute throughout the year. Winter weather merely traps these emissions closer to the ground and makes the consequences harder to ignore. Cleaner public transport, stricter vehicle fitness regimes, better fuel quality, modernised industry, proper waste collection and continuous air-quality monitoring matter as much as raids and fines. Authorities should publish emissions data, inspection results and penalties so the public can judge whether enforcement is sustained and whether repeat offenders are being deterred. Greater coordination among provincial departments and city authorities is important. Citizens, too, have a role, but official appeals for cooperation cannot replace governance. Individuals cannot regulate kilns, redesign transport systems or police construction sites. Those are state responsibilities. Punjab is right to act before October, but the crackdown will only count as progress if it becomes routine.

title: Flawed NEV incentive
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE draft New Energy Vehicle policy gets its destination right. Electrifying transport, cutting the oil import bill and building an export-oriented auto industry are worthwhile goals.
But the incentive structure chosen to achieve them rewards the wrong technology. The main flaw is treating plug-in hybrid and battery electric vehicles as interchangeable.
Both qualify for the same 1pc sales tax on CKD units and NEV inputs — as if a PHEV running mostly on petrol delivers the same environmental pay-off as a BEV. It does not. Pretending otherwise weakens the policy’s stated purpose.
Weak charging infrastructure and real range anxiety discourage Pakistani consumers from buying BEVs. Subsidising PHEVs just as heavily hands them an easier option, which will show up as progress on paper while doing little to build the charging network or battery-vehicle demand the transition actually needs.
    
PHEV assemblers received generous concessions under the last auto policy but never delivered localisation or built charging infrastructure. Repeating that arrangement will invite the same outcome: subsidised assembly with no real technology transfer.
Taxing conventional hybrids at 25pc, up from 8.5pc, while cutting PHEV tax to 1pc, amounts to picking a winner through the tax code rather than market competition. That stalls transition towards genuine transport electrification while penalising Japanese manufacturers who built much of Pakistan’s auto parts ecosystem.
A more coherent policy would reserve the sharpest incentives for BEVs, and let others compete on their actual emissions and fuel-savings performance. Consumers, not tax brackets, should decide which of these technologies wins as charging infrastructure improves and prices come down.
    
The rest of the draft holds up. Export targets, tighter localisation rules and incentives tied to auto-parts exports could finally push manufacturers to build for international markets, instead of just assembling for domestic buyers.
But those incentives need to reward genuine export growth and local value addition, not simply subsidise the same low-localisation assembly model that has defined the industry for decades.

title: Bank domination
author: none@none.com (Shahid Kardar)
content:
PAKISTAN’S financial system is heavily bank-centric. Commercial banks account for over 80 per cent of total financial-sector assets. In a ma­­t­u­­re financial system, household and corporate savings flow through multiple competing channels — capital markets, pension funds, insurance companies, asset managers and private equity. But in Pakistan, many of the institutions that should compete with banks are themselves economically and financially connected to them. What appears to be institutional diversity is, to a large extent, concentration masquerading as diversification.

Banks dominate for many reasons. They possess advantages their competitors cannot easily replicate: large capital bases, extensive branch and distribution networks, long-standing ties with government, customer trust built through decades of deposit-taking, and access to millions of small deposits through everyday transaction accounts. This gives them balance-sheet strength, scale and a low-cost funding advantage. Their established relationships with borrowers, ability to demand collateral and capacity to monitor credit also make them natural intermediaries. These advantages are barriers to entry for competing financial institutions.

But the most important explanation is the government’s persistent financing needs. Commercial banks have become the easiest channel through which government finances its fiscal deficit. Today, some 62pc of banking assets comprise government securities, while lending to the private sector accounts for a mere 22pc. Banks have become primary financiers of the state rather than intermediaries channelling savings into productive private investment.

The incentives are obvious. Government securities offer double-digit, effectively risk-free retu­rns. Lending to private businesses requires assessment of credit risk, documentation, collateral, monitoring. Why create capability to underwrite bonds, financial instruments or support new equi­­ty listings when there is an attractive return on financing government with little effort? As long as government continues to rely on banks to finance its deficit, banks will remain the dominant and highly profitable powerhouses in the financial architecture. The state reinforces this dominance. It borrows heavily from banks, operates National Savings, owns financial institutions, influences development finance, etc. An independent financial institution is not only competing against banks, it is competing against the state itself.

Commercial banks have become the easiest channel through which government finances its fiscal deficit.

The weakness of capital markets reinforces this structure. Stock-market participation is low — account holders represent less than 0.5pc of the population. Households prefer cash, bank deposits, real estate and physical gold, reflecting limited financial literacy as well as a historical mistrust of market volatility.

Corporate sector listing on the PSX or issuing corporate bonds requires compliance of SECP regulations involving extensive disclosure, auditing, corporate-governance requirements, credit ratings, which is time-consuming and expensive. Corporate debt consequently accounts for less than 3pc of Pakistan’s debt market. For most businesses, borrowing from a bank is faster and easier — secured through a bilateral relationship with a banker — than raising capital from the market. For large corporates that tend to be family-controlled businesses there is little incentive to list. A bank loan only requires a discussion with a bank official, while listing also brings exposure to tax and regulatory authorities. Retained earnings and bank borrowing therefore remain the preferred sources of corporate finance.

Institutional investors that could provide an alternative source of long-term capital are underdeveloped. Pakistan lacks a mandatory, broad-based pension system. Existing pension arrangements revolve largely around government employees and are predominantly unfunded and pay-as-you-go. Pension and insurance assets therefore remain minuscule relative to GDP. Investment restrictions further constrain them, with public-sector pension and insurance institutions required to place much of their funds in government securities or bank deposits.

Pakistan’s regulators have been reasonably successful in ensuring that banks remain solvent, liquid and systemically safe. But the same regulatory architecture has not succeeded in creating institutions capable of competing with them.

Large capital requirements may be justified for institutions taking substantial risks with other people’s money. But applying requirements designed for banks to specialist institutions creates prohibitive fixed costs. Mutual funds illustrate the problem. Non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) are legally prohibited from taking demand or retail deposits. They must, instead, persuade savers to voluntarily invest with them or raise capital through equity or borrow from banks at commercial interest rates.

Products connecting banking and capital markets require clearances from both SBP and SECP, creating regulatory silos and slowing innovation in financial products. A process intended to protect consumers can, if poorly crafted, protect incumbents instead. Good regulation must distinguish between prudential requirements that protect customers and systemic stability, and high fixed regulatory costs that prevent new institutions from entering the market. Also, SBP’s discount window and emergency liquidity facilities are exclusively available to banks, while NBFIs operate within a fragmented and evolving framework without comparable institutional support. Banking regulation has enjoyed greater stability and predictability over decades, whereas the regulatory framework for NBFIs has been repeatedly redrafted.

Unsurprisingly, banks have responded rationally. Rather than compete with NBFIs, they have established or acquired them. The largest asset-management companies and mutual funds are not extensions of the bank’s balance sheet, they are overwhelmingly owned or controlled by banks. Their apparent independence hides their integration into the banking system. These institutions will, in the absence of sufficiently deep corporate bond markets, take corporate or household savings, invest them in Treasury bills, government-sponsored Sukuks or bank deposits-instruments that already exist — and channel much of that money back into the banking system. Ownership, distribution, funding and investment decisions remain concentrated within the same financial groups.

Pakistan’s financial system is therefore bank-dominated not simply because banks are efficient or because savers prefer them. It is bank-dominated because the state’s financing needs, corporate structures and the regulatory architecture have prevented alternative channels of financial intermediation from acquiring scale and independence.

The challenge is not to license more NBFIs while leaving these structural incentives unscat­hed. We require a function-based, competitively neutral financial system in which regulation protects risks of financial activities rather than the institutional boundaries between banks and NBFIs. Until then, Pakistan will continue to have many financial institutions but essentially one dominant player in the financial system — the banks.

The writer is a former governor of the State Bank.

title: Double standard
author: none@none.com (Maria Ahmad)
content:
THE Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan has published, in collaboration with UN Women, a Gender Fair Language Framework for the judiciary. It is a 20-page document containing vocabulary premised on promoting equality in law. ‘Chairman’ is replaced with ‘chairperson’. The ‘reasonable man’ of tort becomes the ‘reasonable person’. Passages quoted from older judgements are even permitted to be marked with a [sic] to disown the original phrasing.

This is thoughtful and commendable work. Courts are, at last, being taught how to speak about women. It is unfortunate then that they still aren’t allowed to fully listen to them.

The Law and Justice Commission is asking the judiciary not to refer to women as the ‘weaker sex’. However, Pakistan’s law of evidence (Qanun-i-Shahadat Order, 1984) still says, in Article 17(2)(a), that any matter relating to financial or future obligations that is reduced to writing must be witnessed by “two men, or one man and two women, so that one may remind the other, if necessary”.

In practice, this means a woman in Pakistan cannot get a loan for business, rent a house, settle a debt, or give a guarantee without at least one man to witness her signature. It makes no difference that she has four women standing by to attest for her. The contract might even refer to her properly as ‘she’ instead of ‘he’. None of that survives the signing page: where every national and international commitment made for women’s equality is discarded. Embarrassingly, it is also where foreign counterparties discover the Pakistani state’s arithmetic and go looking for witnesses to match: two women to one man.

Courts may use more equal language, but laws haven’t changed.

The State Bank should be troubled by this the most. Millions are spent on financial inclusion — targets for women’s accounts, women’s credit, support desks. All to bring women to the table and then hand them a contract with signature blocks for two witnesses only. Two, because it is easier to opt for two men than one man and two women. Not just banks, but companies, law firms, real estate agents, anybody who needs a contract witnessed takes the shortcut and pulls two men from the next desk. By default then, contracts and templates carry two witness spaces, never three. This isn’t prejudice, which requires actual thought and action. It is something far duller. It’s saving lines on a page, avoiding all mental effort. You would be forgiven for thinking this is, perhaps, one of Pakistan’s most efficient ways of making women disappear: not by deliberation, but disuse.

The defence of Article 17(2)(a) has always been theological. That is not a debate I would delve into here. But notice how the Federal Shariat Court argued to keep Article 17(2)(a) on the books. In 2012, three male judges analysed its religious basis, with no advocate, state counsel or amicus curiae to assist. Litigation is a hardship, they decided, from which women have been spared. In no period of history or any society should a woman have to face the “irritating and imposing male-majority environs” of a court alone, that too with thirst, hunger and unanswered “biological and natural calls”. It is equally unfair to ask a pregnant or nursing mother to give evidence. And then the court’s other problem: women find it much harder than men to recall “unpalatable and objectionable descriptions” repeatedly.

Financial matters, it seems, are where the real unpleasantness lies. The same Article 17(2)(a) shows no concern for fraught nerves while accepting one woman’s word in a murder trial.

The courtroom part, at least, holds true. But it would be foolish to see that as anything other than a scathing indictment of the state. No person of any sex should have to suffer in court without water or a bathroom, but no one’s ever asked a man to bring a friend along to testify. If a second woman is required because Pakistan has not, in 79 years, made its courts fit for half its population, that is not theology. It’s plain neglect.

Worse still is how out of tune Article 17(2)(a) is from everything else the law says about women and money. Just this year, the Supreme Court ruled at length to uphold women’s right to inheritance. It is unlawful for a woman’s husband or in-laws to lay claim to her gold. For the first time in Pakistan’s history, a woman’s right to a share in matrimonial property was recognised. Yet, the same legal system that is fighting for her right to be financially independent does not trust her to witness a signature without a chaperone. There’s also the judge who can decide a million-dollar lawsuit but can’t attest a lease alone.

Irony and humiliation, another one of the state’s compulsory pairings for women.

title: Flu: a public health crisis
author: none@none.com (Faisal Bari)
content:
LAST fall, after many years, my wife, our daughter and I decided to get flu shots. The decision wasn’t popular with our nine-year-old, who doesn’t like having her skin punctured, but we thought that, given the smog season and the health disruptions we faced every winter in Lahore, it was worth the trouble and expense. And it was. Last winter, we had far fewer bouts of illness, despite the smog highs; when we did have symptoms, they were much milder and recovery much faster. My wife and I lost fewer days at work, and our daughter was able to go to school most days. We also relied much less on cough syrups, antibiotics, and similar medications.

It is almost that time of the year again. Flu shots should be available soon, if they aren’t already. Since influenza mutates significantly, the flu vaccine has to be updated often, and shots have to be taken every year. Despite this inconvenience, they are worth it. But it seems they are not very popular or widely available in Pakistan. We had to ask around and find clinics where we could get a flu shot. A muscular injection, they should be available at most, if not all, pharmacies.

Last year, our shot cost around Rs3,000 per head. So, they can be expensive for many households, but, given the cost-benefit, the state should make them available to vulnerable populations free of charge. It is very much a public health issue. The evidence from other countries is clear. The return on investment is indeed significant. Flu shots save the lives of vulnerable people: children, older populations, and people with compromised health and co-morbidities. Hospitalisations are fewer, and symptoms are less severe and more manageable when people fall sick. Even for the healthy, flu shots can collectively save millions of work hours. Children miss school less. And flu shots also create herd immunity. For the cost, could one ask for more?

In the UK, all children are given flu vaccines free of charge. These are administered in September. Since most or all children are in school in the UK, schools administer the vaccine, which is efficient and effective. For children, there is even a version that can be squirted up the nose, so an injection is not the only option. I am sure children are quite happy with that.

It is a story of neglect. There is no public effort to promote flu vaccination.

The elderly also have access to free shots, as do any adults whose health systems might be compromised: diabetes, immune disorders, etc. The National Health Service administers the shots. This is a large campaign and can have significant waiting times, but it gets done. For other adults, shots are available at most pharmacies for £10 to £25 per shot. Given the protection the shot offers, many adults do get them every year. This helps the UK build significant herd immunity.

Given Pakistan’s higher smog levels, elevated child malnutrition, and the fact that about one-third of the adult population is diabetic, one would think that flu shots would be even more important for us and treated as a public health issue. Of course, if we had national campaigns for flu shots, they would be organised differently from those in other countries. Not all of our children are in schools, and we do not have a comprehensive national health service. So, we will need to have a network involving public health institutions (basic health and above) and Lady Health Workers and Visitors.

Availability through private clinics, hospitals, and pharmacies would also need to be ensured. Some mechanism would have to be designed to ensure that vulnerable and deserving populations have easy access to the vaccine at low or no cost (BISP and similar programmes with large outreach). This won’t be easy for our health authorities. But maybe the lessons from Covid vaccinations can be useful here.

Sadly, as usual, it is a story of neglect. There is no public effort to promote flu vaccination. It does not even seem to be on the agenda. Even with visible rising health costs from increasing smog, office and school closures, and other disruptions, there has been no effort to address the issue. Individuals and families largely bear the cost of ill health. If a child falls ill, the child bears the health cost, and the family pays for care. If flu spreads through an infected child, the increased cost is now borne by other children and households. If an adult falls ill and misses work, the cost is again mostly borne by the person, his or her family, and the individual business or workplace. The state does not bear any costs.

There is no realisation of how much this costs society and the economy as a whole. This is something the state should worry about, but since it is not an explicit cost, it does not. If costs rise for businesses, revenues and profits decline; households bear higher costs — all of this is reflected in national output and performance figures. The impact on health, longevity and morbidity is separate from this. Sadly, the state does not care much about them either.

With smog expectations the way they are, we are likely to experience another tough winter. Considering the impact on children and adults, and keeping in view the days missed at school because of ill health, and even school closures, a large campaign to vaccinate schoolchildren and vulnerable populations makes sense. Sadly, since this requires significant preparation, we are likely to miss this season again. Maybe, next year it will be different.

The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
