title: More than a single day
author: none@none.com (Ayesha Irshad Mian)
content:
“No man is an island, entire of itself; ... any man’s death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind; and therefore, never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.”

JOHN Donne wrote these words four centuries ago, and Ernest Hemingway later used a part of the quote as the title of his novel. The quote describes a principle that modern epidemiology has since validated with data: that no death by suicide is a purely private event. Each death reverberates through a family, a workplace, a community, and, in aggregate, through the statistical and narrative record of a nation’s health.

Every year, on Sept 10, the world observes International Suicide Prevention Day, and every year I find myself uneasy with the framing of this ‘observance’. In practice, it so often slides towards something that resembles a commemoration where panels are convened, experts invited, and statistics projected onto screens. The day then passes and is folded back into the calendar — until it comes around again the following year.

I do not begrudge any of this; awareness, conversations, panels and specifically data, matter. My unease is narrower and rests in the belief that suicide is not a subject that can be adequately held by a single day, however earnestly it is marked. It is a chronic and distributed public health problem that requires sustained clinical, social, and policy attention throughout the year.

The task is to find and reinforce the one thread that tethers the struggling individual to hope.

As a physician, I practise under an oath that obliges me to preserve life and relieve suffering, grounded in the biological premise that human beings possess an innate desire to survive. This means that if you are a living creature, you must want to live. This is not simply an ethical assumption; it is observable at a physiological level, in the autonomic responses that mobilise the body against threat and injury. When a patient reaches the point of ending their own life, the clinical interpretation is not that they have uncovered some previously hidden preference for non-existence. Suicidal ideation is clinically read as evidence that they have reached the outer edge of despair, a point at which an underlying and usually treatable condition, often a brain illness like depression, psychoses, substance abuse or something else, has temporarily overwhelmed that baseline instinct to live. Our task, in that moment, is not to argue someone out of their pain, but to identify and reinforce that one thread, however thin, that tethers them to hope and life — long enough for treatment to take effect.

Within medicine we often draw an analogy between suicidal crisis and other acute, potentially fatal medical events, such as cardiac arrest, an ischemic stroke, or pulmonary embolism. This comparison is not made lightly. It reflects a genuine clinical understanding that such crises are frequently time-limited, and that patients who receive timely and appropriate care — whether hospitalisation, medication, psychotherapy, or structured follow-up — very often go on to recover and to build lives they later describe as worth living. Understood this way, suicide prevention is less a philosophical argument against a person’s stated wish to die and more a form of emergency medicine: stabilise the acute crisis first, and treat the underlying condition once the immediate danger has passed.

And yet, even while holding that conviction firmly, the framework does not fully resolve a question I continue to face in clinical practice. When a terminally ill patient signs a do-not-resuscitate order, declining further intervention as their body finally fails, it is generally regarded as a legitimate exercise of patient autonomy. The ethical basis for distinguishing that decision though, from a decision to end one’s life in the context of prolonged, treatment-resistant psychological suffering is less clear than clinical convention often assumes. At what point does a physician’s judgement that a patient ‘lacks the capacity’ to make such a decision become a form of paternalism rather than clinical care? I do not raise this to suggest that suicide should be approached with anything other than urgent clinical concern; the evidence for the treatability of most suicidal crises is strong, and that evidence should govern practice. I raise it because intellectual honesty requires acknowledging the limits of our current ethical frameworks, and enduring the discomfort of the question, rather than rushing to resolve the tension to avoid facing it.

Even so, the clinical and philosophical dimensions of this issue address only part of the picture, because suicide is not solely an individual pathology; it is also a measurable outcome of the socioeconomic conditions in which individuals live. This is particularly relevant to the population now coming of age, and which is confronting a convergence of structural pressures with limited precedent: climate instability, economic contraction, political volatility, widening income inequality, and, more recently, uncertainty about labour market disruption from automation and artificial intelligence. These conditions have not been matched by a corresponding adjustment in social expectations. Academic achievement, career stability, and conventional markers of success remain the default benchmarks, even as the institutional infrastructure that once made those benchmarks attainable has weakened. This mismatch between expectation and structural opportunity is a documented risk factor and a significant contributor to the hopelessness that so often precedes suicidal thinking.

Given all of this, a more honest and accurate framing of the annual suicide prevention day is to treat it as an invitation to structured, sustained and evidence-based reflection, individually, clinically, and at the level of policy, on why a species biologically oriented towards survival and social connection continues, in significant and rising numbers, to arrive at a decision to end its own life. That question cannot be resolved within a single day, a single panel discussion, or a single article. It is a question owed, on a continuing basis, to every person currently at risk. Donne’s observation that the bell tolls for all of us remains, four centuries later, an accurate description of what’s at stake.

The writer is a consultant child, adolescent and adult psychiatrist and founder & CEO at Synapse Pakistan Neuroscience Institute.

title: Questions around CPEC 2.0
author: Imtiaz Gul
content:
A public-welfare SMS message that appeared across the Chinese mobile network on September 10 read: "The rule of law to escort the new journey of the 15th Five-Year Plan and work together to build a solid electromagnetic space safety network. Let us join hands, cherish spectrum resources, and set frequencies in accordance with laws and regulations."

The unambiguous emphasis on the rule of law in a public message was striking. It reflects an important feature of China's political economy: an emphasis on governance anchored in law, public interest and a sustained pursuit of institutional and economic capacity.

This theme also resonated during a Sino-Pakistan roundtable involving Pakistani diplomats and Chinese scholars at the Fudan University in Shanghai. Beyond the customary pleasantries and positive references to bilateral ties, several Chinese participants raised some pointed questions about Pakistan's development priorities and the future of the relationship.

Most of the Chinese conversation revolved around the rule of law, investment in education and skills and Pakistan's own priorities and commitment. One participant noted that effective absorption of technology required a sound business environment, protection of contracts and intellectual property, and adequate human capital.

Does Pakistan have a long-term development plan? Does it want to prioritise development at all or eager for a strategic role abroad? Can Pakistan convert its strategic relationship with China into sustained economic growth?

"CPEC 2.0 is very important, but in my understanding the first step is to establish national consensus and internal stability," one professor observed. "No matter how much support comes from outside, absence of consensus among political parties and provinces will fail it," he cautioned.

A female professor stressed that CPEC 2.0 should reflect the needs and aspirations of people on the ground. According to her, if Pakistan and China want to build on their cooperation, they should listen to the legitimate demands and aspirations of the Baloch people.

Without referring directly to Pakistan's current political circumstances, another scholar emphasised that "state capacity does not necessarily mean a stronger state, its ability to coordinate policies, translate decisions into results and create a predictable business environment makes it strong."

Another professor was more direct: "We would like to ask our Pakistani friends about their goals. Is the priority economic development at home or excellence in foreign relations? Do you want to play a leading role in the Islamic world, or educate your own people and build the foundations for development?"

She also raised the implications of Pakistan's emerging strategic commitments. "You may become militarily involved abroad in the event of a war between Saudi Arabia and Iran, but would that contribute to the goal of peace? How can you pursue peace by joining an alliance perceived as anti-Iran," she asked.

Recalling Defence Minister Khawaja Asif's earlier television statement that Pakistan's nuclear capabilities "will absolutely be available" to Saudi Arabia under the bilateral Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement - although he subsequently walked back the statement - the Chinese scholar asked whether Pakistan wanted "more wars and influence abroad or development and prosperity for its own people."

Pointing to China's own experience, another participant said, four decades of planning and sustained investment in education, skills and economic planning got the country to its current standing. Pakistan, too, needed to strengthen its human capital and technological base before expecting significantly greater investment and technology transfers from China, he said.

Pakistan's ability to absorb advanced technologies, including AI-based technologies, remains low; hi-tech transfers can generate broader economic and social benefits only when the recipient country has the skills, institutions and infrastructure needed to integrate and deploy them effectively.

One scholar also suggested that Pakistan and China should first consolidate their bilateral relationship and then look more systematically at multilateral cooperation and regional development. The broader objective should be to promote economic integration and improve living standards across the region.

The Chinese participants recognised that Pakistan wants greater investment, technology and economic opportunities from CPEC. But they stressed the need for well-thought-out and consistent planning as requisites.

"China got here on the back of focused economic planning. India is also planning," one participant observed. "But do Pakistani leaders have a long-term plan for development and modernisation?"

According to him, infrastructure investment remains important, but projects should have practical economic utility and contribute directly to people's development.

Military-to-military coordination between China and Pakistan remains an important component of the relationship. But, the discussion suggested, cooperation should increasingly extend to economic development, industry, technology and business. The objective should be to turn projects into industries and Chinese capabilities into Pakistani capacity.

The central challenge is therefore how to convert decades of strategic investment in friendship into growth-led and sustainable development. The recurring message was that solutions to Pakistan's economic and political challenges ultimately have to begin at home.

All eleven Chinese scholars agreed that the "iron brotherhood" between China and Pakistan was built over decades of mutual support, particularly during difficult periods, but believed that preserving the friendship also required updating its economic strategic content.

For Pakistan, the challenge is to convert the considerable strategic capital accumulated through decades of bilateral cooperation into productive capacity, industrial development, technological capability and sustained economic growth.

That is ultimately what CPEC 2.0 should seek to achieve: turning a longstanding strategic friendship into a foundation for sustainable development.

title: The end of 9/11
author: none@none.com (Rafia Zakaria)
content:
TWENTY-FIVE years can change anything. This Friday when the US marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, it was a remarkably different country from when the attacks took place. For much of the quarter century following the attack, the occasion was used to showcase patriotic zealotry, renew calls for attacking yet another Muslim country and spew the usual variety of slurs and insults against American Muslims. While the last persists, the former two have all but disappeared.

In its September/October 2026 issue, Foreign Affairs, the leading journal in Washington’s foreign policy circles, notes: “After 25 years, the United States may finally be closing a chapter that began with the attacks on September 11, 2001, and President George W. Bush’s declaration of a ‘war on terror’ days later.” Authors contributing to the issue sound a similar note, a remarkable departure from the war-mongering diatribes that featured in the magazine over the decades.

These included essays by former defence secretary William Perry who argued in 2001 that the US should fight terrorism with a global campaign rather than just a single military effort directed at one country. Similarly, former secretary of state Colin Powell in 2004 defended the Bush administration’s policies — which included torture and the deadly bombing of tens of thousands of innocent Iraqis — while pursuing non-existent weapons of mass destruction.

For these reasons, it is no small thing to see Foreign Affairs author Audrey Kurth Cronin argue that if Al Qaeda perished, it was owing to its own dysfunctions and follies rather than the multi-trillion-dollar global wars that the US unleashed on the rest of the world.

The years since 9/11 have done their damage.

There are many reasons for this shift in US foreign policy. President Donald Trump’s ill-advised war on Iran does not use the same rhetoric as that deployed by neoconservative Republicans for much of the so-called war on terror. There are political calculations behind this. A huge section of the ‘new right’ (isolationist, nationalist Republicans) is far more interested in shutting down borders than in the war on terror, whose ‘foreign war’ expenditures they see as directly responsible for the lack of resources at home.

One example of this shifting political view can be seen in the positions of Tucker Carlson —a far-right former Fox TV personality who now runs his own media network and has millions of subscribers and loyal fans. In his 9/11 documentary series, which is available on YouTube, Carlson says the ‘official account’ is a lie and the 9/11 Commission was a cover-up. He questions aspects of the established account that 19 Al Qaeda hijackers carried out the attacks planned by figures including Osama bin Laden and Khalid Sheikh Mohammad, and raises allegations that the CIA knew more about some of the hijackers before the attacks. He further questions why Israeli intelligence knew about the possibility of the attacks and whether it warned the US, pointing to how the wars in the Middle East have benefited that country.

All this is to say that whether it is foreign policy establishment journals like Foreign Affairs or far right commentators like Tucker Carlson, the possibility that the war on terror was motivated by incentives other than those stated for decades is becoming an increasingly common perspective. The far left, which was a small bastion of American political thought that opposed the global war, cannot help but be smug about these de­­velopments. The Nation, for instance, used the occasion to publish an article that noted how, after 25 years,

it became alright to ma­­­ke jokes about 9/11. More than 100 million Americans alive to­­day were born after the attacks, which it notes cynically, helped the shift.

Sadly, realising that bombing Muslim countries in pursuit of terrorists does not add up is not the same as realising that demonising religion is similarly self-serving and misinformed.

The two and a half decades in which ‘Islamic’ and ‘terror’ were said as one word have done their damage. Indeed, the chunk of diehards that support the war on Iran are mostly happy that the bombing ensures Muslims are being killed.

Nothing is a bigger face-palm to the neoconservative Islamophobes who oversaw the torture and killing of Muslims and the destruction of countless homes than the fact that the city that saw the attacks now has a Muslim mayor. This 9/11, Zohran Mamdani attended a memorial to the victims — his presence and leadership becoming the best testimony against the American-led war on terror and the delusions that promoted it.

The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.

title: After Sept 11
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
A QUARTER of a century since the Sept 11 terrorist attacks, the world continues to feel the effects of that epochal event. The US response to the attacks on its soil went beyond a counterterrorism operation. It metastasised into a sprawling imperial ‘crusade’ that laid to waste countries that had nothing to do with the terrorists who had hijacked the American airliners.
In fact, the US misadventure in Iran is a continuation of these flawed policies. Today, the world is no safer from religiously inspired terrorism than it was 25 years ago, reflecting the futility of the American-led ‘global war on terror’ and its modern-day iterations.
    
Soon after the attacks, Muslims, including Arabs, in the US faced intense discrimination. Matters may have improved in some respects; after all, New York City, which was the epicentre of the terrorist attacks, today has elected a Muslim mayor. But conversely, Islamophobia in the US is currently at historic levels, spiking after the launch of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in 2023. The current US administration has contributed to this bias, with many of President Donald Trump’s close confidantes spewing reprehensible views. Big Tech, too, has played a significant role in mainstreaming anti-Muslim hate across the larger West.
In the field of foreign policy, little has changed. Post-Sept 11, Washington launched invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq. In the first instance, after a two-decade nation-building experiment, the Americans beat a hasty retreat, leaving Kabul to the Afghan Taliban who returned to power. In Iraq, the US occupation resulted in a vicious sectarian war, which paved the way for the rise of the self-styled Islamic State group. IS was arguably even more brutal than Al Qaeda, the outfit the Americans had sought to crush for carrying out the Sept 11 attacks. Though its abilities stand diminished today, IS continues to threaten global security, putting a question mark over America’s transnational counterterrorism campaign.
    
Following George W. Bush, even ‘liberal’ presidents, such as the Nobel Peace Prize-winning Barack Obama, backed regime-change operations in Libya and Syria. Today, both remain broken states. Despite some bitter lessons, the current US president champions American exceptionalism, and violates the sovereignty of other nations in pursuit of his nebulous goals.
Where the Iranian misadventure is concerned, the reasons cited for Washington’s aggression have kept changing. America’s ‘war on terror’, in fact, spawned even more lethal terrorist groups, while leaving in its wake gulags such as Guantánamo Bay and Abu Ghraib, alongside populations in several Muslim countries grappling with the residue of collapsed states. The post-Sept 11 period offers lessons in imperial overreach, and how not to fight terrorism. But as its actions continue to show, the US has learnt no lessons at all.

title: Political order
author: none@none.com (Ghulam Shabbir)
content:
MAN’S superiority over creation lies in his faculty of creative knowledge, ie, the capacity to discover the laws of, and thus achieve mastery over, nature, or, in Quranic terminology, “to know the names of all things”, and then use this mastery under the human initiative to create a just political world order. Endowed with choice and charged with responsibility, man is a bearer of ‘Trust’ under whose weight the entire universe chafed. He assumed the task which the heavens, despite their heights, the earth despite its vastness, and the mountains, despite their firmness, shrank from undertaking.
This task involves fulfilling the primordial covenant: to establish a just world order, since the challenge God gave man at creation was to create a sociopolitical order that reflects the equality all people share in the eyes of God. It was to orient the forces of history towards a just social order rather than to compromise with them under the cover of secularism. Hence, for Islam, politics is through and through a moral endeavour to accomplish the task. The Quranic idea of ‘fauz’ (success) or ‘khusran’ (failure) is rooted in executing the same task, since it is the quality of the political process through which civilisations rise and fall.
The Quran, in its coherent unity, shows that it is a troika of religious, political, and mercantile elites that manoeuvres the materials of history towards their vested interests. And when exploitation reaches its critical point, the whole of society or civilisation is mowed down. When the Quran talks about the death of individuals like Pharaoh, Qarun and Haman, it is showing the self-destructiveness of the way of life of a society or civilisation. The remedy lies in building a just sociopolitical order, since societies built on unbelief may survive, but unjust ones may not.
Now, because injustice is often rooted in socioeconomic disequilibrium and grave fiscal malpractices can lead to socioeconomic suicide (4:29-32), the Quran makes monotheism-based socioeconomic reforms the linchpin of its moral programme. Therefore, Islam, since its very inception, was socio-politically geared to uproot the corrupt socioeconomic structures of Persia and Byzantium and to build anew, to inject fresh blood into the veins of a decrepit and decadent humanity.
In Islam politics is through and through a moral endeavour.
Islam views power as a means to an end, not an end in itself, as prayer and zakat are instruments of socioeconomic equality. Implementing them in letter and spirit required political power, so the Prophet (PBUH) felt duty-bound to build a state based on an ethical sociopolitical order.
Hence, man is a moral political being with ibada as his purpose of creation — which means to know the will of God and implement it in life, and to restore moral order in individual and social life to redeem the balance of history.
The Quran constituted an egalitarian community, with equal rights for all to participate in or lead the execution of the task through shura, or mutual consultation. The community’s internal conduct was based on active goodwill and cooperation with no trace of elitism. Externally, it kept inviting the religious others to share the burden of building a world moral order. It fared well and was blessed with political control of Arabia, eventually expanding into parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe.
However, later, with the onset and patronage of dictatorship, Sufism Hellenised almost every bit of the faith. In the long run, this development resulted in the colonisation of Mus­lim Asia and Afri­­ca by Western po­­­­­-wers. At this critical juncture, Syed Jamal al-Din Af­­gh­ani rediscovered the Quran’s moral political vision. He proposed building an Islamic republic across a wide region of Central Asia and the Muslim-majority areas of northwest India to realise Islam’s sociopolitical ideals. He amply fired the imagination of Iqbal and Ali Shariati. The former conceived the idea of Pakistan, and the latter paved the way for the Islamic Revolution in Iran.
Today, the Muslim world has either succumbed to secular structures or theocratic modes. The realisation of the Quran’s moral political vision that seeks just socioeconomic and democratic organisation of society seems like a distant dream.
The Quran hardly demands military conquests which could stand in the way of the prospects of the socio-democratic organisation of society. What the vision needs is a tract of land with a just political order whose fragrance may be smelt in the world around and which, in the long run, is destined to create a just world order. Does such a realisation prevail anywhere in the Muslim world?
The writer is an academic.
Published in Dawn, September 11th, 2026
topic: Islamic Political Philosophy, Just World Order, and Societal Decline

It offers a critical analysis of historical societal decline and proposes an ideal for a just socio-political order, highly relevant for essays on governance and religious philosophy.
summary: Humanity's core 'Trust' is to establish a just world order reflecting divine equality, viewing politics as a moral task to orient history towards justice, not compromise with secularism.
The Quran attributes societal and civilizational collapse to the exploitative actions of a 'troika' of religious, political, and mercantile elites driven by vested interests.
Injustice, often stemming from socioeconomic disequilibrium and fiscal malpractices, necessitates monotheism-based socioeconomic reforms as the linchpin of Islam's moral program.

The article critiques the Muslim world's current succumbing to secular or theocratic structures, advocating for a just political order on a tract of land whose fragrance can inspire a global just order, echoing the vision of reformers like Afghani and Iqbal.

The Quran uses figures like Pharaoh, Qarun, and Haman to illustrate the self-destructiveness of exploitative societal ways of life.
Key reformist thinkers mentioned are Syed Jamal al-Din Afghani (who proposed an Islamic republic), Iqbal (who conceived Pakistan), and Ali Shariati (who paved the way for Iran's Islamic Revolution).
Historically, the Hellenization of Sufism under dictatorship contributed to the colonization of Muslim Asia and Africa by Western powers.

title: Terror forever
author: none@none.com (Aasim Sajjad Akhtar)
content:
THE 9/11 attacks happened 25 years ago, ushering in a new epoch. The so-called global war on terror was launched by the Bush administration a few days later, and Washington has wreaked havoc across the globe ever since.

The majority of the world’s states have followed the US lead by making the prosecution and hunting down of ‘terrorists’ their primary raison d’être. Ideological apparatuses, including the culture industry, have indoctrinated generations of young and old alike into believing that ‘terror’ is ubiquitous and that the state must be endlessly empowered to snuff it out, even at the cost of basic liberties.

Pakistan was one of the major staging grounds of the ‘war on terror’, facilitating both the US invasion and occupation of Afghanistan whilst also launching innumerable military operations on its own soil. A plethora of ‘anti-terrorist’ laws have been promulgated since 2001, the scope of which is growing wider. While these instruments are deployed to clamp down on all forms of dissent and popular political mobilisation, the insurgencies and other forms of political violence that ostensibly should have been curbed by the state’s various ‘counterterrorist’ initiatives have only become more intense.

Beneath the surface, a global military-industrial complex profits endlessly from the West’s totalitarian regime. Washington has thrown $8 trillion at various wars since 2001, a significant chunk of which has been pocketed by private defence contractors integrated with the deep state. In Pakistan, too, the ‘war on terror’ inaugurated a host of opportunities for state functionaries and private contractors to mint money.

The policing of dissent is paralleled by Big Tech’s power.

Today, we are at another crossroads. With the rise of Big Tech to the apex of global capitalism, the nexus of state and private capital has morphed into a behemoth without historical precedent. The discourse around ‘terrorism’ expanded some years ago in conjunction with the dramatic transformations of cultural, economic and political life provoked by digitalisation. Terms like ‘cyberterrorism/‘cybersecurity’ and ‘fifth-generation war’ reflect the evolution of a political idiom that both incorporates the logics of the war on terror and extends well beyond it.

The policing of dissent by the state and aligned propagandists in the digital lifeworld is paralleled by the immense power of Big Tech companies to access, share and manipulate data. Earlier this week, a whistleblower resigned from Anthropic, warning that AI development is being allowed to spiral into an existential threat to humanity. Anthropic’s Claude tool has already shown its destructive capabilities at the outset of the war on Iran. Edward Snowden told us what was coming as early as 2013.

Despite their claims of being pro-market libertarians, billionaires like Peter Thiel and Elon Musk are buttressing the state’s immense coercive and surveillance capacities. They view humanity as a plaything that is, at best, ‘saved’ and, at worst, sacrificed in the interests of landing on Mars or crafting more ‘intelligent’ species. Quite aside from hyperbolic claims that an AI-triggered extinction event is around the corner, the unbridled pursuit of power and profit by Big Tech alongside the contemporary state’s unlimited quest for social control must surely trouble anyone concerned with the age-old quest for human emancipation.

Even non-human life is at stake. At a time when climate breakdown events are playing out with ever greater frequency and intensity, states everywhere are bending over backwards to build huge data centres to serve Big Tech’s interests by guaranteeing eno­rmous and unint­errupted supplies of electricity and water. The US st­­a­te and Silicon Val­ley billionaires are the primary protagonists of the contemporary militarised capitalist order. But we cannot be seduced by blind-faith arguments that there are ‘good’ states — not least of them our own — and ‘green’ capitalisms that do not conform to the overarching logic of the system.

We need, instead, to learn the lessons from the ‘war on terror’ and stop being cheerleaders for an even more sinister and unhinged digitalised fusion of state and corporate power that will shape our present and future.

A critical mass in Pakistan continues to speak truth to the militarised ruling class over its whittling away of the few civil liberties we still possess, including in the digital domain, whilst also resisting resource grabs and dispossession. The challenge, however, is outlined every time an episode of ‘terrorism’ is capitalised upon by the state to whip up a nationalist frenzy in which all good sense is abandoned.

If the global totalitarian regime’s march is to be halted, we must coalesce around an anti-capitalist ideological politics rooted in working people and nature. And soon.

The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.

title: Message from Nepal
author: none@none.com (Ali Tauqeer Sheikh)
content:
THREE features of the catastrophic flood that tore through Nepal on Aug 16, 2026, do not fit Pakistan’s mountain disaster strategy: it started without rains; it originated across the border; it had huge compounding factors. None of these three is a one-off. They describe a disaster category that has been forming across the region for over a decade, growing more frequent, widespread and severe. But Pakistan’s climate planning has stayed focused almost entirely on the monsoon.

A mass of rock and glacier ice broke away from an altitude of about 5,200 metres in the upper mountain range, generating seismic energy equivalent to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake. The fall produced enough friction to melt the ice on the way down, turning a dry avalanche into a slurry of mud, ice and boulders moving at up to 167 kilometres an hour at a height of 9m. The debris choked the river and formed a dam. When that gave way, a second surge followed; both hit settlements and the hydropower works below.

It started above the cloud levels. Slopes at this altitude are held up by permafrost gluing the rock and glacial ice buttressing the valley walls. Warming removes both: thawing permafrost raises pore pressure and cuts shear strength, while retreating glaciers stop bracing the slopes from outside. The rock fails on temperature’s schedule, not the monsoon’s, which is why Chamoli in Uttarakhand in India went down under clear skies in 2021 and Langtang followed five years later.

The record before both confirms a trend, not two isolated events. The 2015 avalanche off Langtang Lirung, the 2016 Gongbatongsha outburst crossing from the Tibet area into Nepal, and the 2024 Thame outburst in the Everest region struck without warning, each widening the geography of a hazard.

High-altitude disasters underscore the need for Pakistan to go beyond monsoon planning.

In Pakistan, the 2010 Attabad collapse dammed the Hunza River and submerged 24 kilometres of the Karakoram Highway. The Shisper Glacier’s ice-dammed lake breached without rain in 2022 and destroyed the highway bridge at Hassanabad. Each event has moved higher in elevation, wider in geography, and heavier in what it destroys, from one buried village in 2015 to a cascading event spread over several kilometres.

Pakistan keeps no comparable dataset on its own landslide activity. But a study in the National Science Review, covering more than 8,000 landslides across the eastern Himalayas, found a five-fold increase in high-elevation slope failures over three decades, tracking a doubling of Hindu Kush Himalaya glacier mass loss since 2000. Failures are also rising and entering the 5,000m-6,000m band that was once too frozen to fail.

The Langtang collapse struck Gyirong Port, before the debris continued into Nepal’s own river systems. The direction of travel is not new. Nearly half of the more than 25 major glacial lake outburst floods recorded in Nepal since the mid-20th century have originated across the same border, arriving from a stretch neither country monitors jointly. This event was not itself a Glof — no lake burst before the collapse — but the debris dam it left behind and the discharge that followed sit inside the same unmonitored corridor.

Pakistan belongs to the same geography, through the Kyagar Glacier’s periodic surges in the Shaksgam Valley. But China is not just Nepal’s or Pakistan’s upstream neighbour. It is South Asia’s upper riparian. It is the source plateau for the Indus, the Sutlej and the Brahmaputra — the headwaters of most of South Asia’s major rivers. That makes bilateral arrangements structurally insufficient. What this event calls for is a South Asia-wide early warning architecture, built and shared across every state whose rivers begin on that plateau, not a patchwork of separate deals each covering one border and missing the rest.

None of Nepal’s responses fixed the underlying failure. Built for a slow monsoon rise, its flood sensors were destroyed before they could warn of a moving slurry. Existing bilateral arrangements track slow glacial lake outbursts, not sudden ice-rock collapse. Nepal had no real-time alert before the surge. Pakistan, sharing the same upstream geography, has the identical gap.

What Pakistan needs: Dasu, Diamer-Bhasha and Mohmand are located in river corridors engineered for a monsoon flood profile, not the debris slurry that trapped 500 workers in Nepal. The Karakoram Highway has already been severed once at Attabad and once at Hassanabad. A third closure is not hypothetical.

Nepal rewrote its school-siting rules before rebuilding, not after. It accepted specialised help without inviting chaos. Pakistan’s community-based disaster risk management networks in Gilgit-Baltistan and KP already have the local trust that saved lives on the Trishuli corridor before state machinery arrived. What they lack is a local government signal to act on before the water reaches them.

Four steps are needed. First, convert the existing weather arrangement with China into automated, real-time information sharing on slope deformation and barrier-lake formation in the Shaksgam and Xinjiang zones — the exact category the Nepal-China arrangement missed.

Second, focus on joint satellite monitoring with the Chinese Academy of Sciences, ICIMOD and Suparco, using synthetic aperture radars across the Karakoram, Pamirs and Hindu Kush structured from the outset as a Saarc-wide facility that India, Bhutan and Bangladesh can draw on since all sit downstream of the same plateau.

Third, install seismic and hydrological sensors along the Indus and Shyok corridors calibrated for a slurry, not a rising river, so that downstream infrastructure gets lead time measured in hours instead of minutes.

Fourth, join the consortium undertaking primary technical monitoring, satellite radar analysis, and field assessments, led by ICIMOD, the United States Geological Survey, Integrated Research on Disaster Risk, Nepal Environment Society, and academic glaciologists from such institutions as the University of Michigan. They are combining real-time remote-sensing satellite tracking with ground-level hydrological stations. These entities are quantifying the initial collapse volume, utilising synthetic aperture radar to monitor adjacent unstable slopes, assessing secondary barrier-lake outburst risks, and advancing regional hazard-mapping protocols — areas of critical importance to Pakistan.

This catastrophe combines rapid- and slow-onset — the compound hazard now falling inside the mandate of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage.

The writer serves on the Board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage.

title: The confidence game
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
NOTHING gives them confidence like a pile of dollars in the reserves. Over the decades, I have seen this trend. Whoever is ruling Pakistan lacks confidence in themselves while the foreign exchange reserves are low and large debt-service payments are looming on the horizon. But the situation always turns, like these things do. After a few years of a gruelling, IMF-mandated adjustment, the reserves are rebuilt; import cover and debt service cover both rise, and with them also the confidence of the ruler.

It is happening one more time. The foreign exchange reserves have been rebuilt since July 2023. Both reserve adequacy ratios — import and debt service cover — show notable improvements since their low points between the summer of 2022 and 2023. The reserves were barely able to cover 13 per cent of scheduled maturities in the year ahead and three weeks of imports at the low point of both these ratios in December 2022. From there, they have risen and today can cover almost 70pc of scheduled maturities over the next 12 months and more than three months of imports.

The rulers have gained confidence alongside this development, to the point where they feel they are now in a position to dictate terms to their partners in government and seek a major and far-reaching change in the structure of the federation. It almost seems like they took the critique that they had failed to bring about structural reforms to heart. But in seeking to change the very structure of the state, over the objections of the parties whose support helped usher in their government, they might be acting out of a sense of overconfidence.

The improvement in the reserve adequacy ratios is real, but it is already showing signs of having peaked. Consider just what the last seven months have seen. Reserves rose during this period, but the pace of the rise decelerated. Average 12-month reserve increases remained at a high of $5.7 billion till May, then fell to $3.9bn in June and then to $2.7bn in July. More importantly, the rising reserves procured diminishing adequacy when measured against rising import requirements. Despite a billion-dollar increase in liquid reserves between January and July, import cover barely moved past 3.1 months.

Once the trajectory peaks and the reserve decline kicks in, confidence drains out of the government.

This is usually how it begins. It is not clear yet whether the recent $3bn raised via the Eurobond auction will actually stay in the country or be used to retire bilateral debt, as some of the reporting suggests. If the latter, then it will help raise the debt-service coverage ratio but will place more pressure on import cover.

These are signs that on the present trajectory, the reserve accumulation that began in July 2023 has peaked. Once the incremental reserves procure diminishing increases in the twin coverage ratios, and trade-offs begin appearing between improvements in debt-service coverage and import cover, it can be said that the organic trajectory driving reserve accumulation has hit its built-in limit.

From here on, either the trade-offs will sharpen, leading to a peak in reserves followed by a decline, or the government will find alternative sources to continue the build-up. The alternative sources could be Exim Bank financing of some sort from the US, coupled with a line from the US Treasury, assuming it comes through. It could also be more favourable rollovers of existing bilateral maturities, something we will see by December when the Saudi deposits mature.

But one thing is certain. Once the trajectory peaks and the reserve decline kicks in, confidence drains out of the government. The window in which to do dramatic things closes, the resource envelope shrinks and the government goes into defensive mode. That time may still be a little while away. But given how the reserve metrics are shaping up, it would seem that either the rulers have some large-scale inflows lined up or they have come a little late to the game of rearranging the deckchairs.

The situation is aggravated by high oil prices, brought on by the prolonged stand-off that the war in the Middle East has devolved into. With oil already touching $100, global oil inventories depleted and the Hormuz and Bab Al Mandeb straits both under fire, the outlook for oil prices is anything but sunny. Given high oil prices and the great difficulty they are having in procuring LNG cargoes, the real impact of energy prices is yet to land.

The external sector has improved over the past few years — there is no doubt about that. But three things need to be underlined again and again. First, the improvement is not on the scale needed to support a revival of growth, because the burn rates of the reserves that come with growth rates of 6pc or more in Pakistan mean these reserves will barely last 12 months. Second, the improvement is hitting a plateau and will need a fresh line of inflows to sustain itself in the months ahead. And third, a high-energy-price scenario is rapidly taking shape before us; this might be prolonged, which could aggravate the fragility of the external sector in Pakistan.

This is not the time for adventurism or for opening up unnecessary fronts domestically. Going forward, the government is likely to see a rising arc of pressure spreading across the horizon from multiple directions. At a time like this, it needs its decision-making system at home to be on an even keel. This is a bad time to be an embattled ruler, especially if that is a choice that can be avoided. All rulers in the past 25 years have succumbed to the overconfidence that comes with a healing external sector and rising foreign exchange reserves. It’s almost funny how that works: the confidence game in Pakistan is so closely tied to the quantity of dollars in its treasury. But it’s a good idea not to over-count those dollars just yet.

The writer is a business and economy journalist.

title: Beyond abeyance: rethinking the future of IWT
author: Syed Mohammad Ali.
content:
India's placing of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in "abeyance" has no legal justification. A neutral expert process and, more recently, the Court of Arbitration at The Hague reaffirmed that the 1960 treaty remains in force and rejected the notion that India can unilaterally suspend it. Pakistan has welcomed these decisions, while India has rejected them.

The result is a paradox: the treaty remains legally in force but has become increasingly dysfunctional in practice.

The Permanent Indus Commission, the principal bilateral mechanism for implementing the treaty, has not held a formal annual meeting since 2022. Its commissioners are required to meet at least once a year to facilitate communication, information exchange and cooperation. The disruption of this vital mechanism has made technical disagreements harder to manage.

Even before declaring the treaty in abeyance in 2025, New Delhi had sought its modification, issuing notices to Pakistan in 2023 and 2024. Pakistan has also challenged the design of Indian run-of-river dams on the western rivers, seeking arbitration under the treaty to resolve these disputes. A more constructive approach would have been for both countries to address these differences through bilateral negotiations.

Some experts point out how the IWT's rigid division of the rivers has encouraged a narrow, zero-sum approach to water rather than fostering genuine basin-wide cooperation. Yet, Pakistan is understandably wary of abandoning or renegotiating the treaty, especially when India is now unwilling to cooperate within its existing framework.

IWT does contain an underused mechanism for expanding cooperation. Article VII recognises that India and Pakistan have a "common interest" in the optimum development of the rivers and provides for further cooperation by mutual agreement. This offers a framework for addressing issues the original treaty did not adequately anticipate, including groundwater management, water quality and climate change.

India and Pakistan could also negotiate memoranda of understanding and technical protocols alongside the IWT without necessarily reopening its core provisions.

The division of the six rivers under the IWT in 1960 provided an imperfect but durable framework for managing India-Pakistan water relations. But the treaty was not designed to address the challenges facing the Indus Basin in the twenty-first century.

The Indus Basin is changing. Climate change is altering precipitation and snow and glacier melt patterns, increasing the risks of both flooding and water stress. The Indus delta has also suffered from reduced freshwater and sediment flows, contributing to significant ecological stress.

Climate monitoring, glacier observation and flood forecasting are practical and mutually beneficial areas of cooperation that do not require either country to resolve its broader political disputes first.

The immediate priority should be restoring the treaty's institutional machinery, including resumption of regular meetings of the Permanent Indus Commission, and restoring routine data exchange and inspections. This could set the stage for initiating discussions on climate-proofing the treaty and ensuring its long-term sustainability.

India cannot afford to view itself simply as an upstream riparian dealing with a downstream Pakistan. With the Indus originating in Tibet and its tributaries flowing through both countries, the health of its rivers, glaciers and associated ecosystems affects both. India is thus a co-riparian within a shared and increasingly stressed Indus basin.

International actors, including the United States, should encourage both countries to preserve the treaty framework rather than allow water cooperation to become another casualty of their broader security tensions. Using a water treaty as leverage in a separate security dispute risks undermining one of the few institutional mechanisms that has endured repeated crises between the two nuclear neighbours.

topic: Indus Waters Treaty: Current Challenges, Dysfunction, and Future Cooperation between Pakistan and India
whyMatters: This article offers a contemporary analysis of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), detailing its current state of dysfunction and the legal challenges faced. It critically evaluates how the 1960 treaty, while originally providing a durable framework, now struggles to address 21st-century environmental and political realities, making it essential for understanding evolving India-Pakistan water relations.
summary: The IWT (1960) established an imperfect but durable framework by dividing the six Indus rivers, assigning eastern rivers to India and western rivers predominantly to Pakistan, which initially stabilized water distribution and relations.

Despite India's unilateral declaration of the treaty in "abeyance" in 2025, international expert processes and the Court of Arbitration have reaffirmed its legal force, creating a paradox of legal validity but practical dysfunction.

The principal bilateral mechanism, the Permanent Indus Commission, has not held formal annual meetings since 2022, severely disrupting communication, data exchange, and making technical disagreements between the two nations harder to manage.

The treaty is not equipped to address modern challenges like climate change, groundwater management, and water quality, necessitating expanded cooperation through underused mechanisms like Article VII or new technical protocols, rather than renegotiation.
facts: The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) was signed in 1960.
India sought modification of the IWT, issuing notices to Pakistan in 2023 and 2024, and declared the treaty in "abeyance" in 2025.
The Permanent Indus Commission, the core bilateral mechanism, has not held a formal annual meeting since 2022.
academicReferences: International Law Commission's Articles on the Law of the Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses (1997)
World Bank's Role in brokering the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) and subsequent reports on transboundary water management
Comparative analysis of other transboundary water treaties (e.g., Nile Waters Agreement, Mekong River Commission agreements)

title: Wrong target
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THERE is a difference between enforcing immigration law and punishing students for the passport they carry. The Pakistan Medical and Dental Council’s decision to bar Afghan nationals from medical and dental admissions this session, while requiring those already enrolled to return home, crosses that line. The ostensible rationale is not difficult to discern. Relations with Kabul are badly strained and Pakistan is pressing ahead with its repatriation drive. The government has the right to regulate entry, residence and national security. But none of that explains why students studying through recognised institutions, particularly those with valid documentation, should have their education abruptly terminated. Indeed, the Foreign Office says visa-extension applications from Afghan students continue to be processed under existing rules, making the blanket nature of the PMDC directive even harder to defend.

For many Afghan students, return can amount to the destruction of an educational future. Afghanistan’s higher-education system is in tatters, while the Taliban’s restrictions have made prospects especially bleak for women. Girls remain barred from secondary school and women from university, and female medical education has also been suspended. To send students back into such an environment after they have secured places, paid fees and completed years of study is cruel. Pakistan’s anger over cross-border terrorism and Kabul’s failure to act against terrorist sanctuaries is justified. But students are not the Taliban government, nor should they be made instruments of bilateral pressure. At minimum, those legally enrolled should be allowed to complete their degrees, while new admissions can be reviewed under transparent visa and security rules. Pakistan has sheltered generations of Afghans, often at considerable cost. That history should not now end in a policy that mistakes vulnerability for culpability. Security policy can be firm without becoming indiscriminate. The state must withdraw this measure.

The state should revoke this indiscriminate measure, allowing legally enrolled students to complete their degrees and implementing transparent visa and security rules for new admissions, consistent with Pakistan's history of sheltering Afghans.

title: See for yourself
author: none@none.com (F.S. Aijazuddin)
content:
MAN proposes, God disposes. If Prometheus was punished by the gods for stealing fire, modern man is being punished by nature for harnessing free-flowing water behind dams. Dams were invented when agro-based human communities needed to store water for seasonal irrigation. The earliest known dam is the Jawa Dam in Jordan, dateable to about 3,000 BCE. The ancient Egyptians, the Romans, the early Indians, and the Chinese imperial dynasties built dams to ensure fertility.

Europe woke up late. In the 12th century, the Dutch dammed the river Amstel. They gave the word ‘dam’ permanence by including it in the names of their cities: Amster­dam, Rotterdam. The Industrial Revolution in the 19th century and the spread of Bri­tish influence saw the development of dams in Canada, India, Australia, and Egypt.

The first Aswan Dam (in its day, the largest masonry dam) was built by a British firm and financed by Ernest Cassel (better known today as the grandfather of Lady Edwina Mountbatten). Completed in 1902, it remained an engineering marvel until superseded by the present Aswan Dam, completed in the 1970s. The project became a pawn in superpower politics. Offers of financing by the US and Britain were withdrawn after they were angered by Nasser’s recognition of communist China. It was completed with Russian aid.

In the 1930s, the US government, to alleviate the social impact of the Great Depression, ordered the construction of the Hoover Dam across the Colorado River. Despite its challenging complexity, the Six Companies consortium completed the dam, two years ahead of schedule.

Nature has reminded mankind of its lethal power.

In the 1960s, because of the heavy outlay in large dam projects, the World Bank assumed the burden borne by governments. It funded large dams in Latin America, Africa and Asia. After a lull in the 1990s, triggered by ecological concerns, silting, and population displacement, it has resumed its support, funding projects in Tajikistan, Bhutan and Pakistan.

Pakistan has depended heavily on the World Bank to finance major dam projects — Tarbela, Mangla, and most recently the Dasu Hydropower Project, to which it has committed $2.3 billion. Pakistan became independent in 1947 and China in 1949. Since then, Pakistan has built over 1,000 reservoirs and dams. It has about 150 larger dams (over 15 metres tall). China has built 98,000 dams, including the massive 22,500 MW Three Gorges Dam (TGD) on the Yangtze River. (Tarbela’s capacity is around 5,000 MW.)

Structurally, they differ. The TGD is a concrete gravity dam. Tarbela is an earth-filled dam, and therein lies its geophysical vulnerability. On Aug 22, 1976, Tarbela, still under construction, developed a fault, serious enough for prime minister Z.A. Bhutto to air-dash to the site. US ambassador Henry Byroade reported to Washington that the emergency resulted from the failure of Tunnel 2. A decision was taken to open Tunnel 1 and to drain the lake (over 20 days) so that the tunnels could be inspected. Separately, Tunnels 3 and 4 had to be closed down due to “severe concrete erosion”.

Panic set in as people feared that the sudden release of water from Tarbela would destroy everything downstream, to Kara­chi. It did not help matters when the press reported that an American project engineer W. Shapiro had committed suicide, lea­­ving a note “disclosing an error in design”.

Fifty years later, nature has reminded mankind of its lethal power. On Aug 26, 2026, a catastrophe occurred on the Nepal-China border when a melting glacier collapsed in the Himalayas, precipitating an avalanche of water, rock and soil into the Trishuli River valley. The debris flow swept away everything in its path, breaking do­­­wn dams, bridges and hu­­man settlem­e­nts. More than 1,000 people have died. Over 4,500 are missing.

One is reminded of the manmade havoc caused during World War II, when on the night of May 16-17, 1943, the RAF destroyed three German dams, flooding Germany’s industrial Ruhr valley. The RAF used “bouncing bombs” that could skip across water (like pebbles) and then explode near the dam. “The resulting floods destroyed power stations, factories, mines, and downstream bridges, severely impacting German war production.”

That British tactic should be a warning to combatant nations locked in water wars. Water flow may be used as a weapon, but water dammed is especially vulnerable. No country has so far used nuclear weapons, nor dams as targets. That will not prevent some deranged Dr Strangelove from pressing the doomsday button. Twenty years ago, Al Gore warned of the impact of climate change and global warming in a documentary An Inconvenient Truth. The critic, who dismissed that documentary as “a blatant intellectual fraud”, should now be invited to help those searching for the dead in the Trishuli River valley.

Published in Dawn, September 10th, 2026

title: Following through
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
ECONOMIC policymaking requires private-sector buy-in to succeed. Yet our policymakers have rarely sought it without political prodding from the top. Even when they do, their instinct is to bury, ignore or delay implementing the recommendations.

That is precisely why the prime minister deserves credit for maintaining periodic contact with the business community. But such interactions should deliver results, not merely generate positive headlines. Still, progress is visible, though the pace remains slow. The super tax has been withdrawn, and some business costs have eased. The government also cites Rs800bn recovered through stronger enforcement over the past year without imposing new taxes on compliant businesses. That is a meaningful gain, but sustaining it demands deeper institutional reform.

The PM’s view that growth must become export-led is correct. Pakistan’s domestic-demand-driven expansions follow a familiar pattern: they last for a while but then create external imbalances and return the country to stabilisation programmes. But intent is not enough. Predictable policies, competitively priced energy, long-term financing, reliable logistics and a regulatory environment that does not punish investment are needed.

Currently, long-term investment is scarce and competitiveness continues to erode. Businessmen have pointed this out to the PM and his economic team several times during consultations. The PM and his team agree, but there is no follow-through. There is no record of which commitments from previous meetings were fulfilled. That pattern is why business confidence in these consultations continues to diminish even as the meetings go on.

The meetings have value in principle. They bring to the government’s attention the obstacles businesses actually face and can build confidence in the process. In practice, however, they tend to become crowded affairs where a long list of grievances is aired without clear priorities or a mechanism to track what happens next. That must change. Future sessions should focus on specific reforms, with each action assigned to a ministry, given a deadline and measurable target, and made the responsibility of an identifiable official.

The Prime Minister’s Office should directly oversee this process. A directive issued in a meeting room is not policy until it is recorded, assigned and pursued to completion. Too much of what is said in these forums disappears once the meeting ends. Public promises and announcements have never been in short supply — from this government or its predecessors. What has been missing is a clear and stable policy regime that allows businesses to plan and invest for the long term.

Whether these consultations change that is the only test that matters. The dialogue channel the PM has established is worth keeping open. But its purpose must now shift from reassurance and the resolution of individual grievances to reforms that change the operating environment itself.

title: Beyond speeches
author: none@none.com (Sajjad Hussain Changezi)
content:
EACH budget session follows a familiar ritual. Finance ministers announce ‘people-friendly’ budgets in the national and provincial assemblies. Social sectors are labelled priorities. Billions allocated to education and health are invoked as proof of the government’s concern for human development. The amounts are large enough to overwhelm the citizenry. But a reading of the annual budget statements for FY2026-27 on the websites of the federal and provincial finance ministries tells a complicated story.

I’ll focus here on the national and provincial education budgets, with the exception of the KP budget, where the numbers seem to be underreported. I’ll judge these budgets against three questions: did education receive more funds this year than it did last year; can this year’s money buy more after adjustment for inflation, and has education’s share of the overall government budget increased?

Starting with a year-on-year comparison of the nominal allocated budgets, Punjab’s education allocation has fallen from Rs811.1bn in 2025-26 to Rs789.2bn in 2026-27, a reduction of 2.7 per cent. Sindh’s allocation has similarly declined from Rs654.2bn to Rs635.8bn, by 2.8pc. Balo­ch­istan’s allocation has increased from Rs156.5bn to Rs171.2bn. The federal allocation has increased from Rs168.5bn to Rs194.1bn. In the case of Punjab and Sindh, suffice it to say that a budget that is lower in rupees than the previous year’s budget is a cut.

The second question concerns the comparable purchasing power of these budgets: what can the money actually buy this year? The average national consumer price inflation in FY2025-26 was 7.05pc. In other words, what you could buy with Rs100 in 2025-26, you can only buy with Rs107 in 2026-27. Building material, electricity, transport, textbooks, digital equipment and basic services have all become more expensive. When current allocations are expressed in 2025-26 prices, Punjab’s Rs789.2bn is worth around Rs737.3bn and Sindh’s Rs635.8bn comes down 
to around Rs593.9bn. In real terms, Punjab’s education resources have declined by about 9.1pc and Sindh’s by 9.2pc.

Bold claims hide the reality of education spending.

Third, and ultimately, the criterion is education’s share of the total government budget. In Balochistan, education’s share declines from 16pc to 15.7pc of the total provincial budget. Punjab’s share falls from 15.2pc to 13.4pc. In Sindh, it drops from 19pc to 17.8pc. Federally, it rises from 0.71pc to 0.77pc but still amounts to less than Rs1 out of every Rs100 spent by the federation.

These numbers reveal choices. Budget statements show what governments prioritise when resources are limited. They show whether an education emergency is reflected in financial planning or is confined to speeches. Pakistan has declared educational emergencies for years. Yet millions of children remain out of school. Learning poverty is widespread. Schools in remote communities lack teachers, safe buildings and basic facilities. Girls face further barriers, especially when moving from primary to middle and secondary school. An emergency can’t be declared in a vacuum. It must be funded sufficiently.

There is another structural problem in how education budgets are presented. They are largely gender-blind. Budget documents report aggregate education allocations but offer little clarity on how much is directed towards girls. Illiteracy is an intergenerational problem. Many out-of-school children grow up in families where their parents, particularly their mothers, were denied an education. A mother who has not had the opportunity to attend school may find it harder to navigate official systems, ob­­tain information, su­­­p­po­­rt learning at home, demand ac­­count­ab­ility or keep a child enrolled when ho­-

u­sehold re­­sources are under pressure. This is not a matter of individual failure. It is how educational exclusion can reproduce itself across generations. Girls’ education cannot remain a peripheral concern. Women’s education and empowerment are closely linked with better child health, school attendance, nutrition, household income and civic participation. If we are serious about long-term sustainable growth, girls’ education must be treated as an economic investment.

This year’s budgets offer an uneven answer. Punjab and Sindh are allocating fewer funds than last year, even before the inflation adjustment. Balochistan has increased its education allocation, but its share of the overall budget has fallen. The federation’s allocation shows an increase but education still receives less than 1pc of the total federal expenditure. Until budget statements show sustained increases in education’s share, allocations that retain their value against inflation and transparent spending on girls and the most excluded children, applause during budget speeches will remain louder than the commitment claimed.

The writer is a development professional working at Tabadlab.

A structural problem exists in 'gender-blind' budgeting, where allocation details for girls' education are scarce, perpetuating intergenerational educational exclusion and hindering long-term sustainable growth.

title: Pitfalls of referendum
author: none@none.com (Zahid Hussain)
content:
THE plot thickens. What the ubiquitous interior minister said makes at least one thing clear: restructuring the existing administrative framework is inevitable. It was apparent that he was not voicing the view of the civilian dispensation but that of the powers that be. “New administrative units will have to be created. No one can stop it,” he declared. There was also a clear hint that a referendum might be held to determine the “will of the people” on the issue.

Mohsin Naqvi, a man of all seasons, appears to have been handed yet another political project — added to a portfolio that already ranges from overseeing internal security to running cricket affairs and occasional diplomatic troubleshooting. What makes him so powerful is that he answers to neither the prime minister nor parliament. His new assignment, however, looks exceptionally challenging. The proposed ‘administrative restructuring’ plan — its contours still unclear — has generated a political maelstrom that threatens the existing political order.

It has not only divided the federal cabinet but also ruptured the ruling alliance. The PPP has already launched a campaign against any attempt to divide Sindh under the pretext of administrative restructuring. A strongly worded resolution against the plan, passed by the Sindh Assembly last week, offers some insight into the volatility of the situation in the country’s second-largest province. The brewing conflict between the province and the federal government has now exploded, threatening to bring down the present political set-up. The rupture is hard to mend.

More intriguing, however, is the response of the prime minister and the ruling PML-N on the proposed administrative restructuring — said to be floated by the establishment. While there is no word from the PM, the differing voices from the PML-N and other cabinet ministers on the proposed plan presented by the interior minister make the entire issue extremely complicated. It is a house divided on a proposed plan whose framework remains obscure.

No move to restructure governance should be separated from the democratic process.

There seems to be complete confusion in the ranks of the ruling party. While some PML-N cabinet members and party officials appear supportive of the administrative restructuring, the party’s top leadership has maintained a conspicuous silence over the proposed plan. A big question also hangs over whether the PML-N leadership is prepared to support a plan to divide Punjab — its main power base.

Matters are getting murkier, with the establishment appearing adamant to go ahead with its plan with or without political support, as Naqvi has warned. With its governments in Islamabad and Lahore fully dependent on the establishment’s support for survival, the PML-N has no choice but to toe the line.

As for the PTI — the main opposition party, arguably the most popular in the country, which also governs the troubled province of KP — it may not oppose administrative restructuring on principle, but it will not support any imposed plan. With its mandate stolen and its leaders imprisoned, one cannot expect the party to accept any proposal that would strengthen the establishment’s control.

In this scenario, it will be extremely hard for the establishment to push through a plan requiring a two-thirds majority in both parliament and the provincial assemblies, as the Constitution demands. Even a constitutional amendment would need a two-thirds majority in both Houses, and with the PPP refusing to come on board, things could get messier.

Yet it seems the powers that be are not willing to back down. Their only choice, then, would be to go for a referendum, as Naqvi has hinted. With the PML-N and other coalition partners on board, it may not be difficult to get a referendum resolution passed by parliament with a simple majority.

Pakistan has a history of referendums being used by military dictators in an attempt to legitimise their unconstitutional rule. Who can forget the infamous referendum held by Gen Ziaul Haq to perpetuate his illegitimate government? Interestingly, the question was not whether Zia should stay as president, but whether voters would like an Islamic system to be established — a ‘yes’ vote was to count as validation of Ziaul Haq as president. Ballot boxes were stuffed to cover up the thin turnout, and the mockery further exposed the illegitimacy of military rule.

Gen Pervez Musharraf held a similar referendum to legitimise his rule, though there it directly asked voters to approve his presidency. While turnout remained low, the official statement declared massive support for the military ruler. Will the present dispensation resort to the same kind of fraudulent exercise to carry out its so-called restructuring plan? There is also a strong apprehension that a referendum could be used to enshrine a constitutional role for the security establishment in the power structure — a recent bill passed by parliament has only reinforced that speculation.

There are no two views that the country needs major restructuring to improve governance, but it cannot be separated from the democratic process. In a situation where the legitimacy of the entire system is questionable, no measure, however feasible it may sound, can be acceptable. Indeed, devolution to the lower tier of local government is essential if the system is to deliver, but in the absence of democracy, any administrative restructuring would likely strengthen authoritarian rule. No referendum can confer legitimacy on an imposed administrative structure. The proposal, though still unclear, has already polarised the country, and any referendum will only intensify chaos and instability.

The best thing for the country is to hold free and fair elections and let an elected parliament decide on the critical issues of administrative restructuring and devolution of power to local governments. The present establishment-backed rule, with its questionable mandate, cannot be expected to bring democracy to the grassroots. The lessons of the past must not be forgotten — of authoritarian regimes that tried to strengthen their control in the name of reform. A reminder to the interior minister who referred to Zohran Mamdani and Sadiq Khan: the two mayors are the products of democracy, and no leader like them can emerge under semi-authoritarian rule.

The writer is an author and journalist.

title: GSP+ concerns
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S preferential trade access to the European Union could be at risk. Brussels has cautioned that Islamabad can no longer assume continued trade concessions from the bloc. The warning comes at a critical moment in trade ties between the two. The current GSP+ scheme expires at the end of this year, with Pakistan seeking to enter into a successor arrangement — that has tougher conditions. The EU ambassador’s view that the outcome is “not certain” highlights a problem that extends beyond immediate negotiations. To preserve preferential access to its largest export market, Islamabad must prove it can meet the commitments it made under the programme. As the ambassador put it, “GSP+ preferences cannot be taken for granted”. Such unusually blunt language from a diplomat is significant, particularly for a trade arrangement worth more than €7bn a year to Pakistani exporters.

The GSP+ issue is also a test of whether Pakistan is prepared to honour its international commitments. The economy has benefited enormously from preferential access to the European market since 2014. That dependence makes Brussels’ latest warning especially serious. The European Commission’s 2023-25 assessment has found regression in several areas. It noted that improvements in legislation had not translated sufficiently into implementation. Its concerns included enforced disappearances, curbs on free expression, weak judicial independence and forced labour. Islamabad’s contention that the assessment lacks balance does not address these concerns. The successor scheme raises the bar, expanding coverage from 27 to 32 conventions. Pakistan has ratified the five additional conventions. But that is only a formal requirement. Brussels is now looking more closely at whether Islamabad is implementing them and wants evidence. Disputing Brussels’ findings cannot compensate for shortcomings in implementation when the successor framework explicitly places greater weight on enforcement. Hence, Islamabad faces the tough challenge of securing entry into the new framework. To do so, it must ensure that the deficiencies identified in the assessment do not put the EU’s existing preferences at risk during the transition. Treating the matter as diplomatic disagreement would be short-sighted. The issue is one of credibility, and Islamabad must show, through concrete actions, that its international commitments are more than promises on paper.

Published in Dawn, September 9th, 2026

title: Joint tourism push
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE federal government’s plan to assume responsibility for seven roads spanning 464km across Gilgit-Baltistan is a welcome step towards improving access to one of Pakistan’s greatest tourism assets. The routes connect major destinations including Astore, Deosai, Skardu, Khaplu, Shigar and Naltar, and their rehabilitation and maintenance by the National Highway Authority could address a persistent weakness in GB’s tourism economy: unreliable connectivity. Landslides, flash floods, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods frequently sever road links, stranding visitors and residents alike and disrupting travel plans. Better roads backed by federal funding can therefore do more than shorten journeys; they can make travel safer, more predictable and more attractive to tourists. Reliable access can also encourage longer stays and repeat visits. The proposed toll on visitors may also be reasonable if locals are exempt and the proceeds are transparently used for road upkeep and related infrastructure.

However, roads alone will not unlock GB’s tourism potential. The centre and the GB government should use this initiative as the basis for a broader, coordinated strategy covering resilient infrastructure, emergency response, telecommunications, sanitation, waste management and reliable information on weather and road conditions. Tourist growth must also be managed carefully to protect GB’s fragile mountain environment. Local hotel owners, transporters, guides and small businesses should be involved in planning so that tourism generates livelihoods for communities rather than merely adding congestion and environmental pressure. Islamabad can provide resources and national-level infrastructure capacity, while the GB administration brings local understanding of regional needs. The two should also work together to promote lesser-known destinations, easing pressure on established tourist centres. Coordinated investment, regulation and promotion can make GB a safer, more accessible and sustainable destination.
