title: Chiniot dam plan
author: none@none.com (Naseer Memon)
content:
ARE Sindh and Punjab set to enter into a round of hydro tensions? This time, a string of dams on the Chenab river are being proposed. The case for one of the four — the Chiniot dam — has been presented to Irsa by Wapda. The Chiniot dam is envisioned as a multi-purpose project on the Chenab, about 100 kilometres downstream of the Qadirabad barrage and 5km from Chiniot city. According to the project’s PC-1, the reservoir will have a gross storage capacity of 1 MAF. The project envisages the storage of surplus monsoon flows, flood mitigation, the generation of 80MW of hydropower, and water supply to Faisalabad city. The structure includes an earth-fill main dam, two gated barrages, 77km of reservoir dykes on both banks, and a surface powerhouse.

Wapda, through this initiative, is quietly reviving the Cholistan project, which the Council of Common Interests halted last year. The project is riddled with serious flaws. In a technical appraisal, the federal planning ministry has made more than 50 observations regarding the project. A working paper reveals that the project will inundate about 47,000 acres of land within the floodplain of the Chenab river; the local population is deeply concerned about the loss of their agricultural land, livelihoods and residential structures.

The estimated cost of the project is Rs298 billion, of which the federal government will finance 80 per cent. Wapda will serve as the executing agency. A technical appraisal has also questioned the cost and time rationale. Wapda’s dam portfolio of Bhasha, Dasu, Neelum-Jhelum and Nai Gaj dams has been plagued by years of delays and cost overruns of several billion rupees. Wapda failed to complete any of these projects within the allocated cost and time framework.

Intriguingly, Wapda has submitted the PC-1 to the pre-Central Development Working Party meeting, without an approved environmental impact assessment. This undermines the EIA’s significance, reducing it to a mere formality. Stakeholder consultation is a critical component of the EIA. But the PC-1 is silent on whether the lower riparian, Sindh, was consulted as a highly important and vulnerable stakeholder. Wapda’s presentation before Irsa shows four dams on the Chenab at Wazirabad, Mudh Ranjha, Chiniot, and Shah Jewna, with a total storage capacity of about 4.5 MAF.

Sindh has expressed serious concerns about the dam.

Moreover, Wapda plans to increase the capacity of three upstream link canals. Recently, the Jalalpur canal was commissioned with an estimated annual withdrawal of 0.5 MAF. In the case of a project cascade, EIAs for individual projects are not advised. Instead, a strategic EIA is needed to understand the full spectrum of potential environmental and social impacts. Wapda should disclose all projects as a single package, as they will have a huge cumulative impact on the lower riparian.

Technical appraisal has also pointed to an inexplicable claim of an irrigation benefit of Rs35,768 million per year for claimed 80,000 acres. It works out to Rs447,000 per acre per year, which is four to nine times higher than the realistic agricultural revenue in Punjab. The federal ministry has said that the estimated economic internal rate of return of 18.67pc is based on implausibly inflated assumptions.

The appraisal has also raised concerns over possible dam failure in Pakistan’s third-largest city and an industrial hub downstream. It warns of an ominous scenario for a dam with storage capacity of 1 MAF behind 77km of dykes. Any dyke failure could prove catastrophic, especially as an emergency action plan is missing. During the 2025 floods, Che­nab attained a peak of 1,077,951 cusecs on Aug 27. It created a risk for the Qadirabad barrage, which has a capacity of 900,000 cusecs. The administration had to artificially breach the right marginal bund to secure the barrage structure.

Sindh has expressed serious concerns about the project. The building of the Chiniot dam will mark the start of the construction of several storage and diversion structures. The flow data of 1999-2025 reveals that Punjab’s barrages below the Rasool-Qadirabad-Sulemanki link canals received almost 16pc less than the allocated share of water in the early Kharif season. Water availability had plummeted to -36.4pc by early June. The PC-1 mentions that the filling of the Chiniot dam is to commence in June. The dam’s construction can place severe stress on downstream areas in Punjab, leading to excessive withdrawal of the Indus through link canals. The situation will be compounded when all four dams require storage. Sindh often remains water-stressed in June. Additional withdrawals will adversely affect flows of Sindh’s barrages.

The writer is a water governance expert.

Published in Dawn, September 4th, 2026

title: New AJK government’s task
author: none@none.com (Ahmed Bilal Mehboob)
content:
DESPITE hurdles, doubts, speculation, a protest movement and delayed polls on seven out of 45 directly contested Legislative Assembly seats, the task of installing a new government in Azad Jammu and Kashmir has finally been accomplished. There had been serious questions about the fairness of the elections. The bitterest criticism was from the PPP, the PML-N’s ally in the national parliament.

Even the AJK prime minister’s election was not without controversy. Barrister Iftikhar Gillani was not selected or even recommended as a candidate for the office by the PML-N parliamentary party of the AJK assembly; rather, he was picked by the president of PML-N Pakistan. The choice was resented by some senior party leaders, including Shah Ghulam Qadir, the party president in AJK, who boycotted the assembly session that elected the PM.

The key objection to Mr Gillani’s election as PM was not his relative inexperience compared to veterans such as former PM Raja Farooq Haider or former speaker Shah Ghulam Qadir but the mode of his election as an assembly member. He had lost his seat — the Muzaffarabad constituency, LA-29 — to his PPP rival in the election by over 3,000 votes. Still, he returned to the assembly on a seat reserved for technocrats. There is no legal bar to the eligibility of a member who is defeated in the general election and subsequently elected on a reserved seat to seek the PM’s office. But many politicians believe that a PM should win the confidence of his constituency before seeking the coveted position.

However, despite a turbulent electoral phase that had been ongoing for some months, the new government and PM have assumed office in AJK. Given the PML-N’s clear majority in the assembly, the election of a new AJK president of the PML-N’s choice will likely be a formality. The most important question, however, concerns the new government’s agenda and how far it can overcome the most serious challenges ever faced by an AJK government.

A negotiated solution must be found for all contentious issues.

In view of the circumstances surrounding the entire electoral process, the foremost challenge before the new government and the PM is to establish the government’s moral and performance legitimacy, even if one accepts its electoral legitimacy. Opening the lines of communication with the outlawed Joint Awami Action Committee, engaging with the saner elements within the organisation, and convincing them to abandon the agitation will be the government’s first major test. If successful, it will pave the way for legitimacy of performance. Although the outlawed JAAC can justifiably be blamed for several irresponsible and anti-state utterances and actions, the fact remains that the defunct organisation has a sizeable following, especially in Poonch division, where, despite its best efforts, including organising phased polls, the AJK Election Commission could not hold elections in seven out of 11 constituencies.

A sizeable crowd has been staging a sit-in for almost three months, partly paralysing civic life and links with the rest of AJK and Pakistan. The confrontation and deaths of some agitators and law-enforcement personnel have polarised Kashmiris not only in AJK but also among the diaspora. This confrontation has damaged goodwill and the moral standing of authorities in AJK and Pakistan. The situation, therefore, must be defused immediately and a negotiated solution found for the contentious issues.

It was unreasonable, arguably, for the outlawed JAAC to insist on immediately abolishing the 12 AJK assembly seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees settled in various parts of Pakistan. This demand became even more absurd after the AJK Supreme Court ruled in June that the legislative assembly seats reserved for refugees were constitutionally protected and could not be abolished through executive action or street protests. However, it is also true that the constitutional reforms on the allocation of seats between refugees from the occupied Kashmir valley and Jammu need to be seriously considered, along with the election procedure. The election to the AJK assembly from various parts of Pakistan is generally heavily influenced by the federal and provincial governments during the poll cycle. Now that the new legislative assembly is in place, it should seriously initiate deliberations on constitutional reforms.

In general, the outlawed JAAC’s demands are not unreasonable and are mostly directed at welfare measures and better governance. For example, the demand for a smaller cabinet and the abolition of lavish facilities for elected representatives and senior bureaucrats should be sympathetically considered, alongside calls for roads, tunnels, bridges, safe drinking water, and preventing development budgetary funds from lapsing. Demanding empowered local governments and elected students’ unions is also fair. These are not just JAAC demands, but what every Kashmiri and also many in Pakistan demand. The new government can build on the previous government’s acceptance of most demands and begin implementing the points already agreed upon.

The new PM may begin by forming a smaller cabinet and cutting back on unnecessary protocol and unproductive spending. If tangible steps are taken early for better governance, a solid foundation may be laid for broader reconciliation. In the long term, both the federal government in Pakistan and the AJK government should consider granting AJK the same rights and privileges enjoyed by the four provinces. The same goes for Gilgit-Baltistan.

A constitutional way should be found to provide interim representation to AJK and GB in federal institutions such as parliament, the Council of Common Interests, the National Economic Council and the water regulator Irsa, without compromising our position on the Kashmir dispute. The denial of these rights over the last 80 years has become a major source of grievance.

The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.

title: Beyond listings
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S request to Unesco to consider Rani Ghat and Banbhore for the World Heritage List is welcome. It follows the recent expansion of the country’s tentative list from 25 to 37 properties, with 12 new cultural and heritage sites added this year.

Both Rani Ghat and Banbhore speak to civilisations that flourished on this land long before the modern state existed, and greater international recognition could help attract scholarship, tourism and conservation funding.

Plans to take Gandhara exhibitions abroad, establish “Gandhara Corners” and facilitate longer visits to Buddhist sites are also sensible. Pakistan has for too long treated its archaeological wealth as a niche interest rather than a cultural and economic asset. But enthusiasm for adding names to Unesco’s list must be matched by equal seriousness about the six Pakistani properties already inscribed on it.

Similar vigilance is required at Lahore Fort and Shalamar Gardens, where planning and development around the property must not compromise its heritage value.

The record there is mixed. The World Heritage Committee this year acknowledged conservation progress at Mohenjodaro and Makli, while making clear that considerable work remains. Mohenjodaro still requires attention to drainage, salinity and an integrated management plan; Makli needs sustained conservation and adequate financial and human resources.

Recognition cannot become an end in itself. Federal and provincial authorities should publish conservation plans and budgets for every listed site, maintain specialist teams, improve visitor facilities, signage and access, and promote these places intelligently and consistently at home and abroad.

Tourism revenues should be transparently reinvested in preservation, with local communities given a stake in protecting the sites. Seeking recognition for Rani Ghat and Banbhore is worthwhile.

But Pakistan’s strongest case for adding new treasures to the World Heritage List is to show that those already recognised by the world are being cared for as if they matter.

Published in Dawn, September 4th, 2026

The enthusiasm for adding new sites to the UNESCO list must be paralleled by a serious and sustained commitment to the conservation and effective management of the six properties already inscribed.

Sustainable heritage management necessitates transparent conservation plans, dedicated specialist teams, improved visitor facilities, strategic promotion, and transparent reinvestment of tourism revenues with active local community involvement.
